The bridges of Rwanda open up new worlds
MUKUNGA RIVER VALLEY, Rwanda — For Naomi Nibishaka, there's life before the bridge, and life after the bridge.
On a sunny summer day, the 76-year-old crosses the rushing waters of the Mukungwa river on a pedestrian suspension bridge.
Made of concrete and cable, it's only 230 feet long — roughly the length of a city block. But it's a game changer.
The bridge connects two settlements in a valley in northwest Rwanda that are separated by the river. People cross for all sorts of reasons. Certain services are only available on one side –- a health clinic, a school, a market. Farmers may cross to seek supplies or sell their harvest. Nibishaka is on her way to see her son and grandchildren, who live across the river from her settlement.
Before the bridge was built, there were crossing options — none of them great. You could hire a boat but it was expensive. Local authorities would rope together timber logs for a makeshift bridge, but in the rainy season, the logs would grow slippery and floods would wash them away.
The other alternative was hiking to a narrower crossing — but that took 3 hours each way.
"When someone [who attempted the crossing] went missing, we would look for them, but if it was a rainy day, we would ask the other side if that person slept over," 
Nibishaka says. "And if they can't find them, we would look for the body."
Many people in the community drowned, Nibishaka says. Fearful parents pulled their children out of school if a river crossing was part of their commute. Farmers unable to cross saw their business suffer.
Then in 2025, this footbridge — called Cyangoga — was built. It's one of 96 built in Rwanda since 2020 by the bridge-building nonprofit Fika. The name for this Kigali-based charity means "to arrive" in Swahili. Funding for the program came from the Rwandan government and donors like the U.S. Agency for International Development, before it was dismantled by the Trump administration.
Until now, researchers had not studied the impact of the bridges Fika built. The Rwanda project offered an opportunity to assess what this simple piece of infrastructure might be able to accomplish.
Evan Thomas, professor of environmental engineering at the University of Colorado Boulder, is one of the researchers. "We collected tens of thousands of surveys from hundreds of villages and thousands of households to try to figure out: What changes when you get a bridge?"
Results are in
Their results, released in July, attest to a remarkable series of improvements.
"We found an increase in household consumption, an increase in household income, an increase in the amount of land people are cultivating, an increase in use of fertilizers, even an increase in the number of children going to school," Thomas says.
For Nibishaka, the bridge has brought her freedom to move around — and a full stomach.
"Before, I would have to wait for my grandkids to bring me food every day. Some days I would be very hungry" she says. Now, the children can easily get food to her, and she can cross the river herself to visit them.
A tough terrain
Rwanda, known as the land of a thousand hills, is particularly challenging for infrastructure projects.
"The whole country is very mountainous, very steep and very wet," says Devin Connell, Fika's vice president of programs. "So to build infrastructure, or provide electrification across the country, it's just a logistical and physically difficult task to do."
The group mainly builds two types of bridges.
"This one is a suspension bridge, which is the type of bridge we build in valleys," says Connell. "It has steel towers and a dead man anchor buried in the ground. And brings the walkway up above the floodplain."
The other kind of bridge is built for steep gorges, with hills on both sides.
"That's where we build a suspended bridge and the cables sag down below, kind of classically like an Indiana Jones-style bridge," he says.
Because of the challenging terrain, the bridges are designed to be constructed without heavy machinery.
On average, each bridge costs about $100,000. Thomas says it's a cost-effective figure, especially considering the price of building in Rwanda's terrain.
The results of the study offer up many instances of the power of the bridges.
In the Mugunkwa river valley, farmers who make banana wine more than tripled their output. And since services such as a health clinic, school and post office are only on one side of the bridge, communities on the other side have easier access. The health clinic saw a 40% increase in the number of people coming in.
The rate of return on investment was 120%, meaning the bridge paid for itself and more in the year since it was built.
The impact on schools is especially striking, says Marie Gorette Mutuyimana, a primary school teacher of 28 years who crosses the river twice every weekday to get to and from work.
For years, Mutuyimana had worked with parents in the valley, encouraging them to send their children to school, but deep down she knew it was the river that kept drop-out levels high.
"Sometimes I invested my own money in renting bicycles for those students for a faster commute, and the parents were relying on me to ensure their safety," Mutuyimana says.
"If it started raining while we were at school. I wouldn't be able to concentrate on teaching, I would just worry about how we were all going to get home," she says. The responsibility weighed heavily on her.
Now she says things are different: More than 134 students re-enrolled in the school. She says they're excited to be back with their friends. And she can focus on teaching.
Lessons learned
The research shows how transformative infrastructure investments can be, according to Edward Miguel, a development economist at the University of California, Berkeley, who was not part of the research team.
"Solving that one fundamental transportation problem changes lots of economic decisions, farming decisions, and the payoff can be really big in the long run," Miguel says.
It's especially relevant, he says, in light of the funding shortages that have rocked the world of development assistance after the Trump administration's overhaul of U.S. foreign aid. USAID used to be a big supporter of programs like this all over the world, Miguel says. Now, many lower income countries are struggling to fill the gap. A study like this can show them what's worth investing in, according to Miguel.
"If I were in the government of Rwanda, looking at how important these investments are, in next year's budget, I would start thinking about maybe allocating more money to transportation investments," Miguel says.
What else is needed
Yet a bridge can't solve all challenges that face remote communities.
Asked what they need for a better life, villagers told NPR they urgently needed roads, electricity and clean water. Miguel says the problems facing rural populations can be daunting.
"And sometimes people look at it and throw up their hands and go 'oh my god, we solved the bridge, but now we need the road … we need electricity," says Miguel. "But every time you make one of those investments, you improve people's lives."
For schoolteacher Marie Mutuyimana, the bridge was the start.
"Primarily, we needed to ensure the safety of ourselves and our children, and the ability to access services," she says. "Now that we have that peace of mind, we can ask for the other things we need to improve our lives."

Arteta joins elite 250 club - but where does he rank?
- Published
When thinking of the greatest managers of the Premier League era, Arsene Wenger, Sir Alex Ferguson and Pep Guardiola are names that belong high on the list.
They are three of the rare breed to have managed 250 games with a single Premier League club, and Mikel Arteta is now the 10th member of that elite group.
Monday's 1-0 win over Aston Villa was the 250th top-flight game in charge for Arteta with the Gunners, and his champions delivered a trademark performance.
At full-time at Villa Park, the travelling supporters sang about how they are going to win the league again with Arteta in charge.
With Arsenal coming into this season as trophy holders, and with transition affecting rivals Liverpool, Manchester City, Chelsea and Manchester United, it is hard to see how the fans' partisan prediction is going to be proved wrong.
Arsenal conceded the fewest goals in the league last season as they won the title for the first time in 22 years.
And during Arteta's nearly seven years in charge, the Gunners have become renowned for their defensive excellence.
Against Aston Villa they showed it again, without allowing a shot on target against them as Bukayo Saka's second-half goal secured victory.
The latest win not only puts Arteta in the 250 club. He also has the fourth-best win percentage among those bosses, with only Guardiola, Ferguson and Jurgen Klopp ahead of him.
No 'passengers' but plenty of drive
Arteta is the longest-serving current Premier League manager and with his longevity has come an Arsenal identity.
Arsenal have become renowned for being difficult to break down and new players repeatedly say that they are impressed and sometimes overwhelmed by the level of detail coming from Arteta.
This is the fifth season in a row where Arsenal have won their first two Premier League matches and they again have a solid platform to build another title challenge.
The Gunners have only faced three shots on target in their first two Premier League games. Villa drew a blank in that regard.
During their title triumph last season, the Gunners did not allow their opponents a shot on target in six league matches, the joint-most of any side in a campaign on record since the 2003-04 season.
Goalkeeper David Raya has won the the Golden Glove award for the most clean sheets in each of the past three seasons, while William Saliba and Gabriel Magalhaes have been voted in the PFA team of the year for the past three seasons too.
Since the start of March, the Gunners have kept eight Premier League clean sheets – three more than any other side and the only side in Europe's big-five leagues to have kept more are Juventus with nine.
"It's how they defend as a team and how they attack as a team," Arsenal's record goalscorer Thierry Henry told Sky Sports after the game.
"One thing is sure with Arsenal - everybody needs to run. You don't have any passengers in that team. This is how you win a title. You can see they are so good at it."
Arteta builds on firm foundations - still business to be done?
Arsenal have one of the best squads in Europe.
The Gunners spent £250m last summer bringing in eight players as they won the title and have already spent about £200m this year, turning Piero Hincapie's loan deal into a permanent one (£34.5m), signing Bruno Guimaraes from Newcastle United (£75m), Christos Tzolis from Club Brugge (£34m) and bringing in Ezri Konsa from Aston Villa (£55m).
"That is what we need," Arteta said, speaking to Sky Sports when asked about his squad depth.
"The players that come in make the difference. All of them contributed to create more dominance and more momentum.
"The level of focus and the way they want to contribute to the team, that is going to be decisive in the season."
Arsenal's strength in depth cannot be understated, but one area they may still look to strengthen in is the forward area.
The Gunners have been on the hunt for an elite forward to lift their attack and still could be active on Tuesday's deadline day.
They had an unsuccessful pursuit of Real Madrid winger Vinicius Jr, while they also have a long-standing interest in Atletico Madrid striker Julian Alvarez.
"We are trying to improve the squad and until tomorrow night we will try to do it," Arteta said.
"I have been disconnected from the world for the last 24 hours because my energy has to be on the match, but I will get back on it now."
When pushed about a deal for Alvarez, Arteta said: "I don't know, that's for the people upstairs."
Whatever happens in Arsenal's search, they are going to be hard to keep off the top of the table with Arteta at the helm.

'I've never been to Afghanistan': Six million deportees forced to start over under the Taliban
- Published
The elderly grimace, hobbling on crutches, and wide-eyed children stare, cradling chickens carried from homes they were forced to leave behind.
"It feels good to be in my own country," 35-year-old Nazia says, just minutes after she crosses from Pakistan, where she was born, into Afghanistan.
The Torkham crossing, known as "Zero Point", is where one hard life ends and another begins.
"But I've never been to Afghanistan before and many people here don't even have enough bread to eat," Nazia sighs as she heads, two of her children in tow, toward registration counters festooned with white and black Taliban flags.
Nearly her entire family, eight sisters and their offspring, were deported to Afghanistan this year from Pakistan or Iran.
They are part of the biggest cross-border movement of people anywhere in the world.
Millions of Afghans have fled across the borders to Pakistan and Iran for decades – seeking refuge or employment - and the number escaping Afghanistan has continued to rise since the Taliban takeover in August 2021.
Most are now being forced to return as these two neighbours crack down on undocumented migrants. Nazia and her family were undocumented but the UN and human rights groups say the security sweep is reaching far beyond that group to include registered Afghans too. Even Pakistan now publicly says that Afghans with Proof of Registration cards are not exempt.
The expulsions show no sign of stopping.
The number forced to return this year from Pakistan and Iran has already reached another million, according to the UN's Refugee Agency, the UNHCR.
"In a little under three years, we've seen six million people, a population that is itself the size of a small country, come back to Afghanistan," observes Charlie Goodlake, spokesperson for the UNHCR in Afghanistan.
"We've never seen in recent history a return movement on this scale," he underlines, standing in the baking heat in the tented village close to the border.
It's a desolate landscape of tarpaulin and plastic shelters, many now tattered and torn, erected by the UN and other aid agencies to provide refuge for a few nights for a people arriving with nowhere to go.
Many returnees have not set foot in Afghanistan for decades; many like Nazia have never been here at all.
"I left 45 years ago during the Soviet invasion of Afghanistan and most of my brothers were born in Pakistan," explains Sarwar, who arrived a few days earlier with seven brothers and their families in a convoy of 40 people and the jumble of their worldly goods packed into a lumbering Pakistani lorry.
"We spent a long time there, so of course I felt heartbroken when they forced us out of our home," he says.
"But, despite all that pain, I am also happy because I am finally free of harassment by Pakistan's police."
Every family we met told us they had experienced prejudice and harassment by authorities in Pakistan.
The Pakistan government has not responded to the BBC's questions, but a foreign ministry spokesman told a briefing in Islamabad on Sunday that "the Government of Pakistan undertakes the necessary measures to prevent any instance of harassment or maltreatment of Afghan nationals in Pakistan. If such incidents have taken place, they are sporadic and are dealt with fully in accordance with the law".
Both Pakistan and Iran say it's past time for Afghans to go home, accusing some of posing a security risk, and others of being a financial burden.
The expulsions from Pakistan and alleged abuse intensified after a major escalation in fighting between Pakistan and Afghanistan last October. In February, Human Rights Watch highlighted "door-to-door raids, late-night home searches and arrests without warrants".
In Iran, which claimed last year to host more than four million undocumented Afghans, the mass deportations were accelerated after its 12-day war with Israel and the US in June 2025.
The New York based Centre for Human Rights in Iran accused the authorities of using the post-war climate to "cast suspicion on Afghan migrants - accusing them of espionage and branding them as potential spies for Israel".
The UN's refugee agency continues to underscore the humanitarian principle that any return should be "voluntary, safe and dignified".
But in Torkham, Sarwar's sister-in-law Zarina laments the precarious future they face: "We have no resources to start a business or earn a living, and we don't even own a tent to live in".
Inside the barren transit tent, which provides little escape from scorching 41C heat, Zarina sits alongside an anxious huddle of women and their children.
Are they worried about the future for women and girls in a country where the Taliban has barred women from much of public life, including secondary school and university?
Forty-year-old Zarina turns to make a sweeping gesture with her arm: "Look at them, they're all girls. Of course I'm worried."
Some returnees are not just worried; they're terrified.
"I don't leave this house," a former Afghan security guard, first deported from Iran and then Pakistan, nervously tells us when we meet him far from the border in what he hopes is a safe house.
"We are all living in fear including my wife and children who are also afraid to go outside."
He dismisses the Taliban government's amnesty, announced days after their return to power which declared that former government officials, security personnel and civil servants would not face retaliation and were encouraged to return to work.
"I have no trust in their amnesty because many of my colleagues have been killed." He says his case had been registered with the UN but was deported before he could be transferred to a safer country.
Financial hardship magnifies the pain. The steep cuts in foreign aid worldwide are especially sharp in Afghanistan where the Taliban are still stuck in sanctions linked to terrorism and human rights.
Pakistan confirmed on Sunday that 16,000 vulnerable Afghans have now been granted, on humanitarian grounds, a temporary exemption from being deported – a decision welcomed by the UN.
But sources estimate that the number of Afghans in Pakistan at risk of serious harm, including women and girls who would be denied education, could be as high as 250,000.
At the graceful foreign ministry compound in Kabul, Taliban Foreign Minister Amir Khan Muttaqi tries to put on a brave face.
"There's no doubt that we need some help," he admits. "There is pressure due to their return but in the long run, it will benefit them as well as Afghanistan."
In the first years after the Taliban swept to power in 2021, some of their ministers made light of humanitarian issues, saying God would provide.
The UN now estimates that 21.9 million people, nearly half the country, need assistance this year to survive. The UN's children agency, UNICEF, said last week that one million children faced "life-threatening" malnutrition.
"No country in the world could handle this kind of crisis on its own," UNHCR spokesperson Goodlake assesses, while acknowledging Taliban government efforts to help returnees as they arrive.
But, he adds, "We also know that many of the restrictions and edicts they put in place, particularly on women and girls, don't help us elicit international support".
Muttaqi reiterates his government's line that matters like girl's education are "internal issues" for Afghans to resolve.
The severe restrictions on the lives of girls and women is one of the major issues in the Taliban's international relationships and that has cost them. Five years on, only one country, Russia, has formally recognised their rule.
But when asked about this, Muttaqi points to the deepening diplomatic and economic ties with neighbours such as China and India, as well as Central Asian states.
As for Kabul's relative isolation from western nations, he asks, "those who didn't have relationships with us over the past five years, what have they achieved?"
He answers his own question: "Nothing."
We heard that word - "nothing" - from every family we met at Zero Point, but in a much different sense.
All were embarking on the hardest of homecomings, beginning all over again - with almost nothing.

A study across the various units of a premier eye care hospital in southern India has found that using advanced air filters in operation theatres offers no added benefit to infection prevention in cataract surgery. The study, Comparison of Cataract Surgery Endophthalmitis Rates in Operating Rooms with and without Laminar Air Flow and HEPA Filters, authored by Sheena Song, David F. Chang et al., was published in the American Journal of Ophthalmology in August.
Aravind Eye Care System (AECS), which has a network of 14 regional hospitals in south India, performs around 50% to 60% of cataract surgeries on indigent patients at little or no cost to the patients.
AECS system has operating rooms of varying types depending on the hospital location and its age. Since the hospital has standardised surgical protocols, antibiotic prophylaxis, instrument processing and environmental safety across its units, it decided to examine if installation of laminar air flow (LAF) and high efficiency particulate air filters would reduce the rates of postoperative endophthalmitis (POE).
POE is a complication that can occur after cataract surgery. Infection is mainly due to invasion of the globe by microbial flora, bacteria, or fungi from the adnexa (structures surround and support the eye ball) and environment during the surgery If not treated promptly, it could lead to vision loss.
The study
Researchers at ACES conducted a retrospective study of the 4,52,770 cataract surgeries performed at its 14 hospitals in India in 2023.
“The retrospective analysis reviewed the cataract surgeries, all performed using identical surgical and infection-control protocols, including periocular povidone-iodine and intracameral moxifloxacin. Surgeries were performed in operating rooms with varying air-handling units: LAF with HEPA, central AC with HEPA, central AC without HEPA, and split AC without HEPA,” explained R. Venkatesh, chief medical officer at Aravind Eye Care Hospital in Puducherry and one of the authors of the study.
The multicentre, retrospective study, found that using LAF or HEPA filtration for cataract surgery offered no infection reducing benefit.
Also Read: Insurance can better cataract surgery outcomes for India’s elderly: study
Across all groups, the overall POE rate was extremely low at 0.016%, with no statistically significant differences between the different ventilation systems—even when analysed separately by surgical method: phacoemulsification vs manual small incision cataract surgery MSICS or patient category: paying vs non-paying, the researchers said.
“This contradicts mandating these more expensive air handling unit systems for ophthalmic surgery. Recommending or requiring LAF or HEPA unnecessarily imposes additional infrastructural barriers for ophthalmic operating rooms in resource-limited settings and for office-based surgery in high-income countries,” the study concluded.
Towards safe surgeries
The study noted that the results of the analysis showed that safe cataract surgery is achievable without an expensive LAF or HEPA system, provided rigid aseptic protocols are followed.
“This could remove unnecessary infrastructure barriers in resource-limited settings and make cataract surgery more accessible across all types of surgical facilities worldwide,” said Dr. Venkatesh.
A similar result came up in an earlier study conducted nearly a decade ago. That study was conducted by Shalinder Sabherwal of the Department of Community Ophthalmology and Public Health Research at Dr. Shroff’s Charity Eye Hospital, New Delhi.
Dr. Sabherwal, Deepali Chaku et al. had published their findings in the Indian Journal of Ophthalmology in May 2020, based on their analysis of surgery outcomes for five years between 2013 and 2018. The study, published as the article Are high-efficiency particulate air (HEPA) filters and laminar flow necessary in operating rooms to control acute post-operative endophthalmitis? relied on a retrospective analysis of medical records of 88,297 cataract surgeries conducted in a single network of a tertiary and four secondary hospitals across north India. It identified cases of endophthalmitis from the records between January 2013 and June 2018.
The analysis found that the incidence at secondary centres, without LAF and HEPA filters, were comparable to that found in the tertiary centres with these facilities.

A specific cadence for contemporary group chats eludes me. The rapid-fire tempo of texts combined with custom stickers, often based on inside jokes, leaves me behind. My digital fate: the silent lurker. As I let the notifications wash over me, I am a ghostlike figure haunting the group chat, a silent watcher who rarely responds without a specific invocation.
Group chats are dominating the social lives of younger Americans. In a recent YouGov poll, 34 percent of adults under 30 said they are in at least four group chats, whether via text or other messaging app. Power texters are spending hours juggling multiple message threads—3 percent of adults under 30 said they are in more than 20 distinct group chats.
These group chats are not just for the young folk, though. All attempts at social interactions now spark a new group message. A WhatsApp thread for our monthly book club. An Instagram group for that weekend getaway. A bulbous iMessage chat with random cousins attempting to plan a family reunion. Group chat hell is everywhere you turn.
Here are a few tips for maintaining your sanity during the reign of the group chat, without becoming a textless social pariah. Hint: It’s all about boundaries.
Core Compromise
Maybe you thrive in the chaos of hundreds of notifications, but I don't. I started by choosing which text threads were most important to me. A text thread with my immediate family is nonnegotiable. A group message about a trip that's in one month is actually helpful for logistics. A random thread where people are throwing out Halloween ideas might be fun, but it's on the chopping block. Make a short list of what you actually want to participate in and stay there.
Walk Away
For the others, you can leave the chat. It really is that easy. Especially for event-based group chats, I’m quick to leave the conversation after it's all wrapped and any outstanding bills are settled. Much like I’m not going to be the last person to leave an afterparty, I’m walking away from group chats without hesitation. If there's a specific aspect of the conversation I want to keep going, I'll follow up with those people.
Mute It
You've picked your core group chats you don't want to give up, and you've walked away from the rest. Now is your time to play with the notification settings and see what your smartphone offers. It's worth looking into the settings overall, as well as the options for individualized threads inside apps, especially if some notifications rarely come through while other text threads are more active.
If you balk at the idea of notification distractions, consider Do Not Disturb settings. Be forewarned that being this unreachable can sometimes become a headache for those closest to you.
Get Creative
For those group chats you decide to stay in, why not spruce up the place a bit? Whether you're on an iPhone or Android, there are plenty of options for making your group chats more specific to your context and potentially just more fun to use. Right now I'm watching Game of Thrones from the beginning for the first time. I have a group chat with friends to process some of our reactions and update the background image to whatever character I’m currently rooting for.
Go Direct
I mentioned earlier that when I leave a group thread and I want to keep some aspect of the conversation going, I'll follow up directly with people. This seems to be the better direction to take overall. While you may get a dopamine rush from shooting off hilarious memes and receiving reaction emojis in the group chat, cultivating relationships often happens best with one-on-one moments. Directly texting someone feels like a worthwhile compromise to escape from group chat hell, without fully excluding yourself from modern messaging. Though a face-to-face chat always feels best.

Tropical Storm Edouard has formed in the Gulf and will make landfall later today along the southeastern coast of Texas. While the storm will be relatively short-lived, it could flirt with becoming a hurricane later today as it makes landfall near the Texas - Louisiana border. Here’s what to know right now.
Current Status Of Tropical Storm Edouard
The National Hurricane Center has been watching the storm closely over the past few days. “Although it only has about a day over the very warm Gulf waters, strengthening is expected within a generally low shear environment,” wrote National Hurricane Center forecasters on Monday afternoon. At that time, the storm was a Tropical Depression. The small size of the storm made it more likely to intensify given the favorable conditions for development.
“The intensity forecast today is problematic. Edouard has managed to develop a small core that could be prone to rapid changes in intensity,” noted NHC forecasters early Tuesday morning. They are not ruling out the possibility of the storm reaching a Category 1 hurricane intensity. Even if not, it will be an impactful high-end tropical storm event. At the time of wroting at 4:15 am Central Time, the storm was moving west-northwestward at 8 miles per hour with sustained winds of 40 miles per hour.
What’s Expected?
A strong tropical storm or even Category 1 hurricane will bring impacts to the Upper Texas and southwestern Louisiana coasts, east-central Texas, and southwestern Louisiana on Tuesday and Wednesday. According to NHC, "A Storm Surge Warning is in effect for High Island to the Vermilion/Cameron Parish Line. Tropical Storm Watch is up from Port Bolivar to the Vermilion/Iberia Parish Line. In case the storm continues to strengthen, a Hurricane Watch is in effect for High Island to Cameron, Louisiana.
Edouard is expected to make landfall near the Texas and Louisiana border, which keeps the center of the storm and its worst conditions east of the Houston metropolitan area. The most likely impacts will be related to rainfall as both flash and river flooding are possible. Up to 4 feet of storm surge is also possible from western Louisiana to High Island, Texas.
Tropical Storm Edouard is the fifth named storm of the Atlantic hurricane season. Typically, the fifth named storm of the year happens around August 22nd. Forecasters have called for below-normal activity due to El Niño. The Atlantic basin has been relatively quiet. As we enter the month of September and the first day of meteorological fall, the Atlantic season activity typically ramps up. The peak of the season is around the second week in September.
As Edouard produces rain in the region, the remnant moisture from Tropical Storm Dolly provided much needed relief for drought-stricken Puerto Rico. Parts of Texas have also been in drought conditions, so rainfall is needed. However, 3 to 6 inches of rainfall falling on dry conditions will certainly produce flood hazards for the region. It’s a bit of a “Jekyll and Hyde” situation. However, our NASA-sponsored research at the University of Georgia has shown that these are the perfect drought-busters. “Shepherd and colleagues found that while major hurricanes (Category 3, 4, or 5) dump more rain in a single day than other storms, weaker hurricanes, tropical storms, and depressions contribute more to the cumulative total throughout the hurricane season,” said a NASA press release.

I met the darkest parts of myself during postpartum psychosis. The Lindsay Clancy trial meant I couldn’t stay silent
Moms who have been closely following the Lindsay Clancy murder trial reflect on their experiences of postpartum mental health crises and tell Rhian Lubin why the case has them speaking out about the failures of America’s maternal healthcare system
Editor’s Note: This report deals with postpartum mental health disorders and includes references to infanticide and suicide, which might be distressing for some readers. Please take care when reading.
With her baby boy sitting happily on her lap, Stormi Griffin looked at the camera and smiled.
The photo, which she posted on TikTok along with images of her other two children, was not about “Pinterest-perfect” motherhood, she said, but to illustrate what she looked like in the throes of postpartum psychosis.
“You can look completely fine,” Griffin, 23, told The Independent. “It's not just a crazy lady rocking herself in a straitjacket.”
The mental health condition of postpartum psychosis has burst into public discussion with the murder trial of Massachusetts mother Lindsay Clancy, a former labor and delivery nurse, accused of killing her three children — 5-year-old Cora, 3-year-old Dawson, and 8-month-old Callan — and then trying to take her own life in 2023 at their Duxbury home.
Clancy’s defense team has argued that the 36-year-old is not criminally responsible for the murders, which took placeduring the onset of her postpartum psychosis. The prosecution portrayed the killings as a premeditated, deliberate act.
Griffin was one of three mothers who experienced their own postpartum mental health crisis and spoke to The Independent after following Clancy’s trial.
On one hand, the case has seen an outpouring of support for Clancy with allies flocking to court in pink T-shirts reading: “She Needed Help.” But there has also been fierce condemnation from others who call Clancy “a monster.”
The case has sparked a national conversation about the failures of maternal care — and raised questions about how women are treated by the healthcare industry more widely in the U.S.
The reality of postpartum psychosis
Griffin, a former medical assistant and now a dance teacher, has Thomas, 4, Ethan, 1 and stepdaughter Ava, 6.
She was diagnosed with postpartum psychosis last year, a few months after Ethan’s birth. The mental health condition, a medical emergency which occurs in approximately one to two women per 1,000 births worldwide, is linked to hormonal changes, sleep deprivation, and stresses that follow childbirth, according to medical experts.
Postpartum psychosis is temporary and treatable with the right medication. It also differs from postpartum depression, which affects approximately one in seven women after they have a child.
At its most severe, Griffin, from Paris, Texas, said her symptoms included hearing voices and hallucinations that made her “lose touch with reality.”
Griffin, who said that mental illness runs in her family, was one of hundreds of women sharing their postpartum experiences on social media during Clancy’s trial. She posted the smiling picture with Ethan on her lap to show how “normal” you can appear from the outside.
“The main thing was just to show it's not just a crazy lady rocking herself in a straitjacket,” she told The Independent. “You're not just itching yourself and going crazy. You can look completely fine.”
Experts agree that mothers suffering from a mental health disorder around the time of giving birth often keep up appearances.
“She could be going about everyday tasks and errands while having intrusive thoughts, hearing voices,” said Wendy Davis, executive director of Postpartum Support International. Davis said the behavior is referred to as “masking.”
“From the outside, it's often impossible to tell that things are very hard for her, that she's suffering and possibly in danger. And the mother herself might not realize what she is experiencing is a mental health disorder that is temporary and treatable,” she explained.
‘I'm hearing voices, and I know they're not there’
That was true for Griffin, who began to feel symptoms of depression and anxiety in July 2025, about two months after she had given birth. She was put on antidepressants and anti-anxiety medication, and said she improved for a short period. But then more alarming symptoms emerged in late September, lasting on and off until November.
“I suffered from visual and auditory hallucinations daily; I couldn’t sit still on [some] days; I had thoughts that were not my own, and I met the darkest parts of myself,” Griffin posted on TikTok.
The symptoms did not happen overnight, but “very much crept up” on her, she told The Independent.
“I heard voices that almost sounded like me, and then voices that I've never heard,” she said. “It made me question reality. The best way to describe it is it felt like I had an alter ego who just kept popping up, and the inside of me was like, ‘This isn't right. This isn't you.’”
She was diagnosed with postpartum psychosis and bipolar 2 disorder in September 2025 after her colleagues at the pediatric office where she then worked became concerned. Griffin returned to work six weeks postpartum due to the financial needs of her family, she said, and stressed that her former employer had offered her more maternity leave.
The nurse practitioner she worked for called her husband, Blake, and together they sat her down in a room and asked her what was going on. “I'm hearing voices, and I know they're not there. I'm seeing things,” Griffin recalled telling them.
After that intervention, which Griffin credits with saving her life, she was put on different medication and met regularly with a therapist. But even after getting help, the mom “couldn’t seem to escape” the psychosis. She had a particularly dark period for a few weeks September and October.
“It was like being in a corn maze with no real end in a horror movie,” Griffin explained. “I just couldn't get out of it.”
Mood stabilizers helped bring Griffin “back to reality,” she said. But out of caution, her husband was able to take time off from work to be at home, so that she was not left alone with the children.
“As much as I’m terrified of the sentence, I was a danger to myself. I was a danger to others,” Griffin said. “I could have easily been a danger to my children. And if I didn't have that help, if I didn't have those people fighting for me, I'm confident that I would not be here.”
“I had people putting their lives on pause to come sit with me, just to make sure that I was okay and to make sure that my children were okay,” she added.
It took time, but once doctors had Griffin on medication that worked for her, she started to improve. The mom said she fears what could have happened had her doctors left her on the medication that was proving ineffective at the start of her psychosis.
“I absolutely would have hurt myself, possibly someone else,” she said.
“Whether that was in a fit of rage and I wrecked my car into someone, if I intentionally took my own life, and if I could have been in a rage and snapped at my children out of despair and depression, which is why I'm so grateful that everyone else around me was able to see that I was not ok and take what I said seriously.”
Griffin doesn’t even recognize the woman she was nine months ago, thanks to her supportive family and the medical care she received.
Mental health professionals testified that Clancy didn’t show signs of psychosis. Prosecutors in Clancy’s trial alleged the mom “lied” to her mental healthcare providers about her dark thoughts, purposely didn’t take the correct dosage of medication, and argued that she received an “abundance of help, an abundance of care.”
They said the U.S. healthcare system was “not on trial here.”
In closing arguments, Clancy’s defense attorney, Kevin Reddington, said the mom’s mental health spiraled because of “that damned medicine and the lousy medical care that she got.”
Griffin said she believed that “luck” played a significant role in the care she received.
“It's why the Lindsay Clancy trial is heartbreaking…to know that I went through something so similar, and so many doors were busted down for me,” Griffin said. “And to know that there was another woman who went through that who didn't have [the] same is why it's so controversial and upsetting.”
“It makes me very much want to get up and scream that all moms deserve help,” Griffin added.
Staying consistent with her medication, therapy, and doctor's visits every month is essential, but now Griffin said she is in “a much better place.”
‘I just wanted them to take that baby away from me’
At first, Wisconsin mom Onna Wallace struggled to follow Clancy’s trial because it triggered memories of her own postpartum mental health struggles eight years ago. During that time, the 38-year-old makeup artist said she felt like a “failure” as a mom and at her lowest point considered taking her own life.
Wallace, from Madison, had always dreamed of becoming a mom, but after a difficult pregnancy and a traumatic birth with her firstborn, Lachlan, now 8, the image she had of motherhood was nothing like the reality.
“The second they laid that baby on my chest, it was like a switch flipped. It was just the strangest feeling, and I just wanted them to take that baby away from me,” she recalled.
There was more trauma after the birth when Wallace developed postpartum preeclampsia, a serious condition related to high blood pressure that can cause strokes and blood clots. Her mental health spiraled.
“I got more anxious and more sad. I couldn't eat. I could hardly sleep. I was so exhausted, but I just couldn't,” Wallace said. “And even though I needed some sort of break, I couldn't leave my baby, and couldn't trust her with anybody else, but yet at the same time, I felt like I didn't want her.”
Wallace said she felt alone and, despite having a supportive family, none of them understood what she was going through. “I was so embarrassed, and it just got to a point where I wanted to die,” she recalled. “I didn't want to hurt my child. I wanted to hurt myself.”
The intensity of those first six months, when her baby had colic and cried “for six straight months,” was too much to bear. In a moment of crisis, Wallace said she texted a number for support that she found online.
“I always say that number saved my life because I texted it, and they talked me down,” she said. “Just to have somebody say, ‘You're a good mom, you're not alone, this is okay, and other moms feel this way too.’ I’d never heard that before.”
The memories from that time had faded until Clancy’s trial.
“I just was like, this will break me to read, because I know exactly how she was feeling,” Wallace said of Clancy. “I just could not fathom being in that much of a darkness. I think just how terribly she was failed by the medical system.”
‘My brain was constantly creating these horrific scenarios’
Sarah Curtis, a 37-year-old mom from Florida’s Treasure Cove region, has been listening to daily podcasts about Clancy’s trial. She opened up about the intrusive thoughts she experienced postpartum 10 years ago in light of the case.
Curtis, mom to a boy and a girl aged 10 and 12, said she struggled with postpartum depression, anxiety, and OCD with both children that stemmed from losing her first child in 2011 after a miscarriage at 14 weeks.
“I am in no way minimizing the devastating loss of three innocent children. Three babies lost their lives. There are no words for that,” she said. “What we are supporting is the fact that this mom was begging for help and she was failed by her providers,” she said of Clancy. “I think about how differently my own story could have ended if someone hadn’t finally listened.”
The mom, who runs her own photography business, faces additional barriers to healthcare due to being self-employed.
While Curtis praised the “fantastic” care of a midwife and the hospital where she gave birth to her first child, she described a postnatal checkup with a nurse at home two days after being discharged as a “30-minute in and out.” After that, the next time she saw a health professional was six weeks later, when she said the nurse seemed more concerned about quizzing her on birth control than her mental health.
Instead, she would like providers to ask mothers more questions about how they are coping mentally, and make routine appointments in those early weeks and months more accessible. “Because that's when I started really getting into darker thoughts and anxious,” she said. “But we don't have anything.”
When Curtis was at home alone with a newborn and a toddler, she had disturbing thoughts that were “controlling her life.”
“I was so scared that something was gonna harm my children,” she said, emphasizing that she never experienced thoughts of hurting her kids.
“Anytime I would get in the car, I would envision a semi truck hitting us. I would get up constantly in the middle of the night because I was so scared someone was either coming in their window or watching through their window, kidnapping them out of their beds, or they would have a seizure and stop breathing,” she recalled.
Curtis struggled with intrusive thoughts for five years before a major panic attack finally pushed her into confiding in her husband, a veteran, who brought her to see his therapist. She was eventually diagnosed with generalized anxiety disorder, OCD, and panic disorder, which doctors told her all stemmed from postpartum.
When excerpts from Clancy’s journal entries were read to the court, where she described feeling as though she was “drowning every day” and “completely overwhelmed trying to take care of the three kids,” Curtis had to fast-forward.
“They were very hard to sit through,” she said. “Because it catapults you back into that moment where you're sitting in such darkness and wondering, ‘what is wrong with me?’”
If you or someone you know needs mental health assistance right now, call or text 988, or visit 988lifeline.org to access online chat from the 988 Suicide and Crisis Lifeline. This is a free, confidential crisis hotline that is available to everyone 24 hours a day, seven days a week.
To learn more about postpartum mental health, visit Postpartum Support International at postpartum.net.
In the UK, you can speak to the Samaritans, in confidence, on 116 123 (UK and ROI) or visit the Samaritans website to find details of your nearest branch.

Kalshi issues George Santos a lifetime ban and $71,356 fine over suspicious trades
President Donald Trump commuted the disgraced ex-Congressman’s prison sentence last year
Prediction platform Kalshi has handed former U.S. congressman George Santos a lifetime ban and fined him $71,356 over allegations of insider trading.
According to a disciplinary filing released by the firm, its compliance team determined there was reasonable cause to conclude that the former lawmaker participated in unlawful trades.
The decision comes amid a surge in questionable transactions across prediction markets like Kalshi and Polymarket, creating fresh oversight hurdles as law enforcement and regulators step up their focus on the expanding industry.
In June, Kalshi referred Santos to the U.S. Department of Justice following the discovery of unusual account activity.
Fresh out of prison for wire fraud and identity theft, Santos allegedly began a new scheme by fixing the odds on a bet of whether he would attend President Donald Trump’s State of the Union address in February, unnamed sources told NPR at the time.
He posted on X a day before Trump’s speech saying that he would be at the U.S. Capitol for it. But the next day, he said he would instead be watching the speech from an airport TV, writing on X that it was “not part of the plan!”
Before his announcement, Santos had allegedly placed bets on Kalshi that he was not going to attend the State of the Union, NPR reported.
Several social media users immediately accused him of running another scheme.
Santos agreed to a $35,000 settlement with federal investigators to resolve the DOJ inquiry. In a statement at the time, Santos’ lawyer said his client had a “genuine intention” to attend the State of the Union, even booking a hotel and plane ticket before a winter storm scuttled the plans.
“Mr. Santos concealed neither his intention to attend, nor his change of plans to not attend the SOTU, from anyone," attorney Joseph Murray said. “There was absolutely no intent to deceive any person, nor intent to manipulate any market."
Santos addressed complaints about the SOTU bets on his podcast in March, saying, “I guess people lost money. Some people made unexpected money. That’s to show you how fragile these markets are.”
Santos was ousted from Congress following charges of identity theft and fraud. He pleaded guilty to fraud and identity theft in 2024 and a federal judge in New York sentenced him to 87 months in prison. The judge said the former congressman showed no remorse for campaign donors and voters he lied to and swindled out of money.
U.S. President Donald Trump commuted his prison sentence in October, after the 37-year-old former Republican congressman served just 84 days.
“George Santos was somewhat of a ‘rogue,’ but there are many rogues throughout our Country that aren’t forced to serve seven years in prison,” Trump wrote on Truth Social.
He went on to praise Santos for having “the Courage, Conviction, and Intelligence to ALWAYS VOTE REPUBLICAN!”

The Indian Medical Association (IMA) on Wednesday (August 26, 2026) issued a public health advisory on the seasonal surge in Influenza A (H1N1), or swine flu, during the monsoon, urging people not to self-medicate with antibiotics and antivirals and advising immediate medical attention in case of severe symptoms.
The IMA said India is witnessing a seasonal increase in H1N1 cases, with metropolitan centres such as Delhi recording more than 1,770 laboratory-confirmed cases, alongside cases reported in Maharashtra, Karnataka and West Bengal.
The advisory said surveillance by the Indian Council of Medical Research (ICMR) has confirmed that the circulating virus remains seasonal Influenza A (H1N1), with no novel genetic mutations detected.
“India is witnessing a seasonal surge in Influenza A (H1N1) / Swine Flu cases during the monsoon period,” the IMA said, adding that while heightened vigilance is necessary, “there is no cause for panic”.
The medical body said the majority of H1N1 infections are mild and self-limiting.
According to the advisory, H1N1 typically presents with sudden onset of high-grade fever and chills, persistent dry cough and sore throat, severe muscle aches and fatigue, headache, runny or congested nose, and, more frequently in children, nausea, vomiting or loose stools.
The IMA stressed that Influenza A (H1N1) is a viral illness and antibiotics do not kill viruses.
“Do not consume Azithromycin, Amoxicillin-Clavulanate, Cefixime, or other antibiotics for flu symptoms,” it said, warning that indiscriminate antibiotic use during viral surges can destroy protective microbiome flora and fuel lethal Antimicrobial Resistance (AMR).
The IMA clarified that antibiotics should be used only when a qualified physician diagnoses a secondary bacterial infection based on clinical and laboratory findings.
On antiviral medication, the advisory said Oseltamivir is a prescription-only drug and should be used only for specific clinical categories under medical supervision.
“Do not self-administer antivirals,” the IMA said.
The medical body also listed several warning signs requiring immediate emergency medical attention, including difficulty in breathing, shortness of breath or rapid breathing, chest pain or persistent pressure, and bluish discolouration of the lips or fingers.
Patients experiencing coughing up blood, drowsiness, confusion, extreme sleepiness or seizures, persistent vomiting and inability to tolerate oral fluids should also seek emergency care, it said.
For children, inability to feed, lethargy, grunting or severe chest retractions have been listed as red-flag symptoms requiring urgent medical attention.
The IMA advised people to follow preventive measures, including frequent handwashing with soap and water for at least 20 seconds or using an alcohol-based hand sanitiser.
It also recommended covering the mouth and nose with a tissue or bent elbow while coughing or sneezing and wearing a well-fitted mask in crowded and enclosed spaces.
“Stay Home When Sick: Avoid schools, workplaces, and social gatherings for at least 24 hours after fever has resolved without fever-reducing medications,” the advisory said.
The IMA also strongly advised annual seasonal influenza vaccination for healthcare personnel, pregnant women, the elderly and people with underlying chronic medical conditions.

As online services get better at blocking malicious traffic, the attackers and scammers behind them have been forced to find new ways to reach their targets. The alternative of choice is now what are known as residential proxy networks. These systems funnel millions of home Internet connections into a unified network, and the proxy operators allow attackers to route their malicious traffic through these connections for a fee. The online services see only IP addresses with good reputations and geolocations that don’t stand out.
More often than not, the home users have no idea that their connections are being used to facilitate crime and occasionally even nation-state attacks. Users who do know often don’t care much. In exchange for leasing out part of their unlimited bandwidth to others, many get free movie and TV show streaming. Several less tech-savvy people I know who own such digital media players have told me, after I explain how the media players piggyback off their connections, that the bonanza of content is worth it. They find the tangible benefits outweigh the abstract harm they pose.
Infecting already compromised devices
Research published Monday brings the threat into much clearer view. Security firm Plume cataloged a vast ecosystem of malware that preys squarely on users of SuperBox, just one of many media players offering pirated content. These malicious apps can be surreptitiously installed by remote attackers even when the devices are positioned behind a router. While Monday’s deep-dive analysis focused exclusively on SuperBox, Plume warned that dozens of similar streaming devices pose precisely the same threat.
“Our researchers found that these residential proxy networks are not simply monetization tools,” Plume researchers wrote. “They are actively being used as a target for additional malware delivery, enabling cybercriminals to infect already-compromised devices with entirely new malware families while remaining largely invisible to the device owner.”
The Android-based SuperBox is configured with almost all the OS-based security protections turned off. Apps that come pre-installed, or those that are available through the SuperBox app store, then run as root, meaning they have unfettered administrative system rights on the device. Paying proxynet customers can also gain root by issuing a handful of Linux commands. With that, either the app or the paying customer can install their own apps and surveil and join the local network the device is connected to, where they have the same system rights as any other connected device.
The SuperBox neuters default Android defenses, including signature verification, the “unknown sources” restriction, the permission-review dialog, and Play Protect scanning. As a result, the box’s ADB (Android Debug Bridge) is exposed to the Internet. Worse, the su binary—the code that provides the command-line interface allowing users with low-level system rights to temporarily gain administrator-level access—is set to grant root without any authentication. The combination of the ADB being exposed to the Internet and the lack of authentication for root access means that both apps and users of the proxy service can execute virtually any command they want on the device.
More often than not, users position their SuperBox behind their home router, where they may think their device is safe from Internet-connected remote attackers. In fact, that sense of security is completely false. The binary that provides proxy functions inside many SuperBox apps opens an outgoing connection to a proxy server and keeps it open as a communication channel indefinitely. Routers are unable to block the communications because the connections they rely on are outbound and encrypted between the SuperBox and the proxy server. Even users who are savvy enough to monitor traffic on their network never see anything that looks like an inbound connection to the ADB port.
“The open ADB port plays the central role,” Plume researcher Gergely Eberhardt wrote in an email. “Combined with root access, a single pm install command can silently install any APK. This bypasses every one of Android’s default protections at once: signature verification, the “unknown sources” restriction, the permission-review dialog, and Play Protect scanning.”
Intruders at gates
The open ADB, along with the default presence of apps that have built-in proxy functionality, creates a dangerous mix that makes SuperBox a potent threat.
“This combination results in further infections involving additional residential proxies or IoT botnets, and the attackers are often the very customers of the primary proxy network,” Plume wrote. “The device owners get multiple bots they never asked for and are not aware of, all competing for the same hardware, and an IP address whose reputation now reflects whatever those bots utilize it for.”
Some of the proxy networking services that make use of SuperBox take measures to prevent their customers from accessing the local networks of SuperBox users. The recently disrupted Popanet, for instance, blocks local IP address ranges from outside the local network. Even then, Popanet users can access local IPs by specifying the special wildcard address 0.0.0.0, which Android then routes to the SuperBox IP 127.0.0.1. From that vantage point, proxy users can access the rest of the local network.
Monday’s post also reported that even the Popanet network was facilitating live exploit attempts. Plume wrote:
The internal-network protection issue that we described in the previous part isn’t just a theoretical concern. To confirm whether anyone is actually exploiting it, we ran a controlled experiment. We joined the Popanet network as a residential exit node and instructed the host that any connection coming through the tunnel targeting either port 5555 or 5858 (these are the most common ADB ports) would be redirected to our local honeypot. From the operator’s perspective, our node looked like any other regular residential endpoint serving customer traffic; from the inside, every attempt aimed to reach an ADB port through our node was captured.
We let the node run for over three weeks; over that period, the honeypot recorded 1,352 distinct attempts at reaching the ADB through the gap we identified earlier. All the attacks could be split into two families of loopback addresses targeting the local machine. The first is 0.0.0.0, supplied either as a raw address or embedded in a hostname via a wildcard DNS service such as nip.io. The second is 127.0.0.1, which the proxy blocked via isLoopbackAddress() as we explained earlier.
An email sent to info@mysuperboxtv.com seeking comment didn’t receive a response before this story’s publication.
Intruding traffic attempted to install multiple malicious apps that made SuperBoxes a node in yet another proxy network or join botnets for use in DDoS attacks. The three primary apps were CECbot, a variant of Mirai, and Maskify.
It’s hard to walk away from Monday’s report with anything other than the strong conviction that SuperBox—and virtually all of its peers—pose a tangible and imminent threat to the networks they’re connected to. Even savvy people who think they can be cordoned off from the Internet are at risk. If you’re using one, you should disconnect it and throw it away. If you find a family member using one, you should intervene. With the Popanet proxy service alone running through 2 million devices, according to Google, chances are good that a home network near you is, too.

'Ghana was the crime scene': The country leading the demand for slavery reparations
- Published
This year has seen a dramatic change in tone in the global conversation about the transatlantic slave trade.
The demand for formal apologies, debt relief and financial compensation from nations and institutions that benefited from slavery has become increasingly forceful.
In March, a resolution was passed at the United Nations recognising slavery as "the greatest crime against humanity" - though the United States voted against the resolution and every European nation abstained from the vote.
The UK, which alongside Portugal dominated the transatlantic slave trade, has consistently rejected the idea of paying reparations, which is perhaps unsurprising given estimates of what Britain "owes" in damages to nations affected run into many trillions of pounds.
This resistance has not deterred the country that has become the leading voice on reparations: Ghana.
Ghana cannot afford to be silent on ensuring that we hold perpetrators accountable"
It was Ghana that tabled the UN resolution, and in June, a summit on reparations was held in its capital, Accra, with delegates from around 80 countries, who concluded that recompense was long overdue.
"Ghana has always been a pan-African leader. We're the first country to attain independence in sub-Saharan Africa and to prove that it is possible to fight imperial might, and win," Foreign Minister Samuel Okuzeto Ablakwa tells me.
Ghana has been given special responsibility by the African Union to be "champion for reparatory justice" and it is clearly a role the country's political leadership is taking seriously.
In part that is because about 10-15% of the estimated 12 million Africans who were forcibly removed from their homes, torn from their villages, and dehumanised on a scale never before seen, were from what is now Ghana. Even more were shipped from its shores.
"Ghana was the crime scene where these atrocities took place, so Ghana cannot afford to be silent on ensuring that we hold perpetrators accountable," Ablakwa says.
The minister has called for a system of reparatory justice that funds educational grants, venture capital for young African entrepreneurs and research into enduring health issues that some argue may trace their roots back to the severe malnutrition and inhumane conditions of enslavement.
And though he insists that this is not about direct financial gain for African leaders, one of the demands laid out at the recent summit on reparations clearly talked of debt relief and debt cancellation.
He also wants individual institutions that benefited from the slave trade to be held accountable and pay compensation. Among these is the Church of England.
In the 18th Century, the Church's missionary wing ran plantations and owned hundreds of slaves, which helped fund its work across the Americas and beyond.
Many Church of England clergy independently owned slaves, and a recent report by the Church's endowment fund reported the institution made large investments in the slave trade from which it made huge sums of money.
In July, the leader of the Church, the Archbishop of Canterbury Dame Sarah Mullally, visited Ghana in one of her first international visits in the role.
She travelled to Cape Coast Castle, one of the many coastal fortresses that had been run by the British, and where enslaved people were held before enduring the brutal "Middle Passage" to the Americas.
As she toured the dungeons where slaves were held and walked through "the door of no return" through which they were forced before being loaded on to ships, Dame Sarah looked emotional and stopped to pray.
"I felt the weight of the depth of evil that the transatlantic slave trade was. You can't help but be deeply moved by the horrific conditions that people were kept in," the Archbishop said.
She also prayed in a 17th Century chapel that was positioned directly above the dungeons.
"For me that is such a stark illustration of the way the Church was involved in the slave trade," she says. "How can the church have sat above the horrors that were going on below?".
"The Church of England has apologised for the part that we played in the transatlantic slave trade but we've also said there needs to be action that relates to that," Archbishop Sarah said.
The Church has set up a £100m ($135m) social impact fund designed to benefit communities thought to continue to feel the enduring legacy of the slave trade today.
But within the Church, the establishment of the fund has encountered resistance, just as the global push for nations to pay reparations has done.
One of the key counter-arguments centres on the fact that some Africans were themselves complicit in the capture and sale of their fellow people.
But Foreign Minister Ablakwa emphatically rejects this narrative. "I think that there's a strategy to divide and conquer and to create a very contrived confusion," he argues.
He stresses that the entire architecture of chattel enslavement was curated by Western slave-owning powers, who simply utilised local actors to help carry out their plans.
The foreign minister points out that when the laws, insurance policies, and financial architectures of the trade were being drafted, "there was no African at the table".
"We denounce and totally reject those claims that Africans are as guilty and complicit as those who masterminded this whole atrocity," he says.
Yet, within Ghana itself, the conversation around African complicity is far more nuanced, and for some traditional leaders, acknowledging the past is a vital prerequisite part of healing.
King Tackie Teiko Tsuru II, the Ga Mantse, leader of Ghana's Ga people, recently took the step of publicly apologising for his ancestors' involvement in the slave trade.
"I think that the transatlantic slave trade was the greatest crime against humanity, and ancestors also took part as players in that trade," says the king.
The Ga people became middlemen who traded with Europeans. They sold gold, ivory and ultimately enslaved Africans, often those captured in local conflicts, in exchange for the manufactured goods brought mainly by the British and Dutch, including textiles, alcohol and guns.
But the king felt he needed to say sorry not just for his own people's complicity, but the complicity of other Africans too.
"I stand on the same point of apologising on behalf of all traditional authorities and my ancestors and forebears for the part they also played in the slavery of our brothers and sisters.
"It has affected lives and societies up to now, and to be able to go forward, you have to look at your past. It dawns on us to admit our fault and correct it," he says.
The king believes strongly in the need for those who benefited from the slave trade to pay reparations and acknowledges that he, too, needs to commit to making financial amends.
"I believe that it underpins a state of moral courage and credibility."
For the Ga Mantse, admitting fault does not dilute the guilt of European empires; rather, it solidifies Africa's moral standing and sets an example as to how to move forward.
But Ghana is leading the way in another aspect of trying to heal the damage done by the slave trade. The country has run a high-profile campaign inviting the African diaspora - particularly African-Americans - to visit the continent.
It has been promoted as a means of bringing people together in the shared story of their traumatic past, with "reparations" quite literally focussing on "repair" at a very human level.
Yaw Asare, now a Ghanaian PhD student at Howard University, previously worked within the President of Ghana's Diaspora Office, which ran the campaign.
Initially, the gathering of black people from across the globe was, he felt, "a beautiful, profound experience devoid of capitalist motives". But he says in some respects the initiative soon morphed.
"The Ghana Tourism Authority also latched on to it and then used it to enhance their tourism project," Asare explains, saying the initiative started to become less about "repair" and more about hitting tourism quotas.
Asare says the campaign has often viewed the returning diaspora simply as a means of foreign cash flow, raising prices and negatively altering local economies.
"Now (local) people are finding that they cannot afford basic things," Asare says, describing how local Ghanaians were economically sidelined.
More devastatingly, he feels the commercialisation of the initiative overshadowed the deep, psychological work that is desperately needed for locals as well as "returning" members of the diaspora.
"We are dealing with humans, we are dealing with people. We cannot reduce them to, 'come see this site, pay this entrance fee'," Asare says.
He also questions - in an initiative that was partly supposed to be about addressing the trauma of Africans in the diaspora - why they were required to pay entrance fees at the same rates as European tourists at, for example, the coastal castles where slaves were trafficked.
He says all of this means a missed opportunity to address deep-rooted trauma some of which he feels is etched into the very geography and psychology of modern Ghana.
"Go to Jamestown (in Accra), people are huddled together because there is the fear of 'if I live far away, I could be taken'," Asare says, pointing to how centuries-old concerns dictated why people built their houses so closely together.
Jamestown is one of the oldest districts in the city, a community originally built around a British coastal fort where slaves were brought, traded and then sent on ships to the Americas.
For Asare, true reparatory justice must prioritise human connection and healing over financial transactions.
"We have to remove the band-aid and then look at the sore, the gaping wound that's present," Asare says about what he sees as real "reparations". "And see how we can dress it and nurse it and heal".

A Tibetan advocacy group says hundreds of homes were destroyed on the Tibetan side of the border in last week’s deadly floods, raising questions about Beijing’s official account of the scale of the disaster.
Public discussion about the flash floods has been restricted, with security officials in Tibet announcing on Sunday that it had penalised at least 10 people for sharing “false disaster information”. There was no further information on the nature of the penalties.
Chinese authorities say 16 people have been confirmed dead and 546 are missing, including 261 foreign citizens. But the International Campaign for Tibet says its sources believe the number of casualties is significantly higher, with at least 300 homes destroyed.
Tencho Gyatso, the president of the campaign group, told the Guardian: “What is visible in Nepal exposes what is being concealed in Tibet. Four villages – Sale, Serchung, Labi and Rizi – were among the hardest hit, with approximately 300 homes reportedly destroyed and many people still missing.”
She said the “little information that we can gather from the ground” suggested the numbers affected were “far higher” than Chinese officials had reported.
On 26 August, the collapse of a glacier triggered deadly floods along the Nepal-Tibet border, destroying entire villages. The death toll on the Nepal side has passed 900, with more than 4,000 missing. Tourists from India, the US, Britain, Australia and Canada among others remain unaccounted for in the mountainous region that is popular with trekkers and pilgrims.
Advocacy groups say there has been a stark contrast in the amount of information presented on either side of the border. Chinese coverage has been dominated by official state media reports, with few unofficial accounts about the scale of the disaster and its aftermath.
Independent verification is extremely difficult in Tibet, where foreign journalists face severe restrictions. Tibetans can face imprisonment for sharing information with journalists and advocacy groups outside China.
Gyatso said: “Officially released glimpses, however important, cannot tell us what is happening across all affected communities.”
Her Tibetan advocacy group said several sources reported that survivors had been moved to Gyirong, which is about 30km (18 miles) from the border crossing that was hit by the flooding. They are said to be under strict management and restricted from communicating freely.
According to a report posted on 27 August on the Tibet Daily, a state-run newspaper, two Tibetans were detained for questioning for posting “rumours” that more than 1,000 people had been swept away close to the border.
Gyatso said: “The Chinese government portrays it like it’s only happening in Nepal and there’s nothing across the border. For any type of crisis, the way China handles it is that there is no crisis. The party is in control.”
Posts relating to the disaster continued to trend on Chinese social media on Monday, with many comments echoing official narratives and supporting rescue efforts.
A Weibo post by Hu Xijin – a prominent Chinese commentator and former chief editor of the state-run Global Times – attracted more than 300 comments and thousands of likes. He accused a small number of voices of seeking to “stir controversy by fabricating baseless claims”.
However, one comment under his post questioned why all the updates were coming from the Nepali side of the border.
On Sunday, Tibetan public security officials said they had penalised people for sharing misleading information or “disrupting online order” with posts about the disaster.
In one case, a user identified only as Zhang disputed the official death toll, posting: “Clearly thousands of people were swept away, yet the authorities reported only three deaths and 265 people missing.”
Another user named Zhou said: “In this wave of mudslides, one entire village was wiped out. It was definitely more than a thousand [deaths].”
Maya Wang of Human Rights Watch said: “The instinct of the Chinese government is always to kind of control and to ensure the narrative which is to portray itself as a very efficient government.
“There have been questions raised over how the development of the valleys in an ecologically fragile and geologically fragile area may have related to this disaster.”
Human rights groups say that Beijing maintains tight controls over movement, religion and information in Tibet. Tibetan groups in exile have long been critical of large-scale development in the region, which they consider geologically fragile.
A Chinese foreign ministry spokesperson said on Monday that the release of information about the floods and mudslide near its border with Nepal was transparent and timely.
“Malicious smear campaigns and hype using the disaster situation does not align with popular sentiment,” said Guo Jiakun, in response to allegations that China censored videos of the disaster and understated the number of missing people.
When asked about allegations that China ignored warnings from scientists over hydropower construction, he said: “We firmly oppose such baseless and malicious speculation.”
Additional reporting by Yu-chen Li in Taipei
