The Women Obsessed With Lindsay Clancy
Horrific crimes have always attracted attention, but the women who have filled the courtroom are seeking something beyond spectacle.
Updated at 7:35 p.m. ET on August 31, 2026
On one of the final days of the trial, dozens of women streamed into the back of a Plymouth, Massachusetts, courtroom, filling two long rows of wooden benches. They stood and watched the judge and jury take their seats. Then they strained for a view as a nurse wheeled in the defendant, Lindsay Clancy, who has admitted to strangling her three young children to death in her suburban Boston home in January 2023, before swallowing prescription pills, slashing her wrists and neck, and throwing herself out of a bedroom window headfirst.
Seeing her there in a wheelchair, one woman crossed herself and whispered, “Please, God.” As an officer gaveled the court into session, others pulled out notebooks, folders, and scraps of paper. “WHY,” Marta Quijano wrote as a prosecutor called a psychiatrist to the stand. “Motivation,” she added, starring the word as the doctor began explaining his opinion that Clancy was not in the throes of psychosis on the night of the killings, as her defense has argued, but deeply suicidal and still capable of knowing right from wrong. In the back row, a woman who had flown in from Cleveland shook her head. She had a true-crime novel in her lap and turned to a blank page at the end. “Stupid experts,” she wrote.
Americans have long been obsessed with murder trials, especially those involving the primal nightmare of mothers who kill their children. The public loves to watch mothers on trial and partake in their judgment. There was Susan Smith, who had drowned her three children in a South Carolina lake and was found guilty of murder in 1995, despite having a history of trauma and sexual abuse. And there was Andrea Yates, who had drowned her five children in a bathtub and was convicted of capital murder in 2002 and then retried in 2006, when she was found not guilty by reason of insanity after witnesses testified that Yates had experienced severe postpartum psychosis and schizophrenia.
The Clancy trial is now part of this sadistic American tradition, but it has also become something else for the women who have been showing up in person. It was not enough for them to watch the proceedings on television, or listen to some lawyer on YouTube, or even stand outside the courthouse wearing pink and waving signs in support of Clancy, as hundreds of women did one day earlier this month. They did not want to be outside rendering judgment; they wanted to be inside, on the third floor, sitting on the wooden benches, as close as possible, in case they could notice some detail, some gesture, some pause or expression or word that might reveal a truth they could recognize from their own experience. Each was there for their own reasons.
A jury of nine women and three men will decide in the coming days whether Clancy, a 36-year-old former labor-and-delivery nurse, is criminally responsible for killing her children or not guilty by reason of insanity. The two prosecutors have argued that the killings were the premeditated decision of an entitled and controlling woman who had been frustrated that she could not master her worsening depression and sought a way out of a life that she no longer wanted. Clancy’s defense attorney, Kevin Reddington, has cast her as a loving mother failed by a fragmented mental-health system even as she repeatedly sought help for intensifying depression, anxiety, and insomnia after giving birth to her third child.
Clancy saw her psychiatrist 14 times, tried 13 different medications, called a suicide hotline, went to an emergency room, tried to enroll in an inpatient program, and confided to her husband that she’d had thoughts of harming her children. Defense experts testified that doctors had missed an underlying bipolar disorder and prescribed pills that made Clancy’s symptoms worse, starting a downward spiral that culminated in a rare condition called postpartum psychosis that can cause hallucinations. Clancy has said that she heard a male voice telling her to kill her children, Cora, Dawson, and Callan, on January 24, 2023.
After being resuscitated following her suicide attempt, which left her paralyzed from the waist down, Clancy was handcuffed, placed under armed guard, and arraigned from her hospital bed. A judge allowed the moment to be livestreamed from the courtroom; a video screen showed her unblinking eyes above a white surgical mask. The trial itself has also been livestreamed, fueling conspiracy theories that have tended to blame the killings on Clancy’s husband or an intruder, attempting to find clarity where there is little, as many women at the trial already understood. At first, only a few showed up. By last Monday, they were waiting in an hour-long line to get into the courthouse, and another that stretched down a bright hallway to the courtroom doors.
“I can’t imagine what’s going through her head,” one woman was saying to her friend.
“It’s not just cold-blooded murder,” the friend said.
“I had suicidal thoughts, clear as a bell,” a retired teacher named Dottie Kiley told another woman in line, explaining her experience with antidepressants. “So bad I called the police and told them, and they had a cop come down and sit with me. It was a small town, and they had time to do that.”
The woman behind her nodded. “She could be any one of us,” she said as the courtroom doors opened.
Inside, the women listened to Avram Mack, a psychiatrist and prosecution witness, explain his clinical opinion that Clancy, having made up her mind to kill herself, then made the decision to kill her children to prevent their suffering a life without her—a theory called “altruistic filicide.” Quijano leaned over to the woman sitting next to her.
“What is the validity of this three years later?” she whispered, shaking her head.
After the morning break, she stood in line again for the afternoon session.
“With my first daughter, because it was so difficult breastfeeding, I had insomnia and anxiety—I was worried the baby is hungry,” Quijano told a woman she had just met. “I remember one time—she was a cranky baby—and I remember not so much shaking her but going like this,” she said, demonstrating how she squeezed her daughter’s shoulders and screamed. “They are called intrusive thoughts because your brain says something, and you don’t recognize it.”
Ashlyn Rizzo, who’d been attending the trial for two weeks straight, nodded.
“I had been planning to run away,” Rizzo said, referring to a moment after her first child was born. “I liquidated all my 401(k) and squirreled the money away. I was going to go without the baby. I figured everyone was better off without me. I had delusions. I couldn’t tell wake from sleep. I didn’t confide to anyone. I wrote a note.”
“My cousin had a plan,” Quijano said, not needing to finish.
“I was just going to start driving,” Rizzo continued. “Stay in hotels.”
As it happened, Rizzo said, she had called her psychiatrist, who that very day got her into the same specialized program in Rhode Island that had rejected Clancy one month before she killed her children. “Saved my life,” Rizzo said.
On Tuesday, the line was longer.
“I wonder, what does justice look like in this case?” a retired teacher named Lisa was saying. She had been keeping the livestream of the trial on in the background of her daily life all month, until she decided to come to see it for herself. She had driven up from Virginia.
“My daughter had a moment,” Lisa, who didn’t give her last name, told the woman standing behind her, referring to postpartum depression. “I’ve been there, trying to get psychiatric appointments.”
“I had a miscarriage in the second trimester and drifted into depression,” Sheila Sullivan replied, explaining that she’d wound up committed to a psychiatric facility in the 1970s. “They gave me shock treatment. Back then, they didn’t know.”
“I’m sorry,” Lisa said, hugging her.
“Thank you,” Sullivan said.
“They don’t do any research on how hormones affect mental health,” Lisa said.
“She didn’t have any symptoms until they put her on the drugs,” Sullivan said.
“It’s all interconnected,” Lisa said as the courtroom doors opened and the women filled the back benches.
“Can you tell us what peritraumatic disassociation is?” a prosecutor asked an FBI forensic psychiatrist, Gregory Saathoff.
“It’s when you feel things are unreal, not you—like you’re watching yourself,” Saathoff began.
A woman wrote down, “Witness staring at jury,” and whispered, “I think that’s weird.”
Sullivan took out her notebook.
“Moral judgement??” she wrote.
She listened as Reddington, the defense attorney, questioned Saathoff, going through his 75-page résumé and pointing out that he had treated only two women with postpartum depression, and that that had been decades ago. Reddington went over the times that Clancy had described feeling “like a zombie” and had been in a “disassociated state,” and asked why health-care providers had not asked more questions when Clancy indicated that she was suicidal.
“She was trying hard to get help,” the doctor acknowledged.
“I can relate to all of this,” Jodi Fournier said as she stood in line later that afternoon. “Not at the extreme, but I can understand.”
For several days, she had been driving to court with two friends from a town 30 minutes away.
“The other thing is, when you work in health care, you learn not to trust the doctors,” her friend Susan Hatfield said. “She was questioning her doctors. She didn’t trust them, and neither did I.”
“See that woman over there?” Fournier said, noticing a blond woman standing by herself and praying at a window outside the courtroom.
“She’s does it every day,” Hatfield said.
Sullivan joined the line behind them.
“I had a miscarriage, then depression, then thoughts of suicide,” she began, retelling her story, and soon they went inside.
Every day, the court officer gaveled in the session, a call to order that ended with the phrase “You will be heard.” Every day, a nurse wheeled in Lindsay Clancy.
“That’s her,” Fournier whispered.
On Tuesday afternoon, Reddington continued questioning Saathoff. “Do you remember Linsday talking about how she can’t feel love? She can’t feel fear?” Then he quoted from Clancy’s journal: “It takes all the effort in the world just to breathe,” she had written, as well as “I want help” and “I want to be well.”
In the back benches, the women leaned forward so they could hear. They pulled out notebooks.
“WTF,” one woman wrote as Reddington went over Clancy’s medication list.
“I am afraid,” another woman wrote down on Wednesday, quoting something Clancy had said.
Rebecca Olszewski, a pharmacist and mother of three, had flown in from Cleveland to attend the trial. She told me that she was recovering from anorexia, bulimia, and generalized anxiety disorder, all of which she said she had learned to mask, as Clancy had apparently done at times. Prosecutors submitted into evidence photos of her smiling with her kids. “There would be outings, and my mom would be like, ‘You seem in good spirits,’” Olszewski said. “And I’d say, ‘Mom, I’m just here going through motions.’”
She wrote down a list of questions: Why hadn’t the people who’d answered the suicide hotline asked Clancy more questions about her suicidal thoughts—not simply whether she had a plan at that moment, but whether she’d ever had a plan? Why hadn’t doctors placed her in an inpatient program? Why hadn’t they paid closer attention?
Now Olszewski sat on the wooden bench, studying the jury to see whether they were paying attention. Then she watched the judge, noticing how he looked at Clancy and the witnesses.
On Thursday, the day of closing arguments, the line was longer than it had been all week. Not everyone could get into the main courtroom, so another one was made available, and women filled more wooden benches, including Joni Villemez-Comeaux, a mental-health counselor there from Texas.
“This is shining a very poor light on our field, and it needs to,” she was saying, and now several women began asking her about how she would have handled Clancy—which sorts of details mattered, and which didn’t. “Every fucking thing matters,” Villemez-Comeaux said, and soon the courtroom was quiet.
In closing, Reddington once again went over all the ways that Clancy had sought help. The medications. The psychiatrist visits. The journal in which she’d chronicled her worsening symptoms until her handwriting had turned into what he described as “chicken scratch.”
“My God, what does she have to do?” Reddington said, and when he finished, women clapped and cheered, and then listened as the prosecutor for the Commonwealth, Jennifer Sprague, delivered her closing argument.
“This case is not about the mental-health system,” she began.
On the wooden benches, a woman quietly said to herself, “Yes, it is.”
After that, Sprague continued for nearly an hour. She talked about how depressed and suicidal Clancy had been but emphasized how much support she’d had. Her parents, a nanny, health insurance. “She had more access to care and treatment and support than most people do.” She once again painted Clancy as an entitled woman who’d known that what she was doing was wrong, who’d decided to strangle her children anyway, leaving them “discarded on the basement floor like broken toys because she was done playing the game.”
By the time she spoke those words, though, many of the women who’d stood in line and listened to days of testimony had already left the courtroom. They had heard enough.
This article originally misidentified Kevin Reddington as Patrick Reddington.

Srinagar, Aug 31: Deputy Commissioner (DC) Srinagar, Akshay Labroo, on Monday visited the Institute of Mental Health and Neurosciences (IMHANS) to review the preparedness for implementation of the Phase-I rollout/Pilot of the Rehabilitation & Socio-Economic Reintegration Scheme for Drug Abuse Victims, 2026.
The pilot programme is being coordinated by the Social Welfare Department aimed at testing the rehabilitation model on the ground, identify operational gaps, refine the Standard Operating Procedures (SOPs) and generate necessary learnings for its subsequent expansion across Jammu and Kashmir.
During the visit, the Deputy Commissioner took detailed stock of the arrangements for implementation of the pilot phase in Srinagar District and reviewed the availability of rehabilitation services, coordination mechanisms among the concerned Departments and institutions and other necessary arrangements to ensure effective implementation of the programme and its successful execution in the District.
The DC emphasised the need for a holistic, coordinated and outcome-oriented approach towards rehabilitation of drug abuse victims, with focused attention on their recovery, rehabilitation and socio-economic reintegration into mainstream society. He stressed that all concerned Departments and Institutions must work in close coordination to ensure seamless delivery of services to beneficiaries. He also underscored the importance of registration of the affected persons of the drug abuse, proper documentation of field experiences, identification of implementation challenges and timely corrective measures so that the learnings from the pilot can contribute towards strengthening the programme before its wider rollout.
 The DC further called for effective monitoring and regular assessment of the rehabilitation interventions to ensure that the intended objectives of the scheme are achieved and beneficiaries receive sustained support throughout the rehabilitation and reintegration process.
The visit was a part of the Government initiative and the District Administration’s ongoing efforts to ensure effective preparedness and coordinated implementation of initiatives aimed at addressing drug abuse and strengthening rehabilitation and reintegration services in the District.
The Deputy Commissioner was accompanied by the Additional Deputy Commissioner, Aadil Fareed, IAS Probationer, Aakash Garg, Tehsildar South, Sajad Rasool Shah, Prof (Dr ) Arshid Hussain Head of Department , Dr Ajaz, Medical Superintendent SMHS Hospital, Dr Andleeb, In-charge Drug De-Addiction Centre, SMHS Hospital, Dr. Yasir Hassan Rather and other concerned Officers and Officials.

Jury convicts a man of first-degree murder for the 1996 killing of rap icon Tupac Shakur
LAS VEGAS — A jury found Duane "Keffe D" Davis guilty of orchestrating the 1996 killing of rap icon Tupac Shakur, finally bringing a measure of resolution to a case that had gripped hip-hop fans and lingered in the public imagination for decades.
The 63-year-old Davis was convicted Monday of a single count of murder with a deadly weapon and could be sentenced to life in prison. The jury deliberated for less than three hours after a weekslong trial in Las Vegas.
After the verdict was read, Shakur's sister, Sekyiwa "Set" Shakur, cried and hugged the prosecutors. Davis' son covered his face with one hand.
Chief Deputy District Attorney Binu Palal told jurors in closing arguments earlier Monday that Davis acquired a gun and "went hunting" for Shakur and Death Row Records co-founder Marion "Suge" Knight after the men had beaten up Davis' nephew earlier that night.
"He is responsible of the murder of Tupac Shakur," Palal said. "Tell him you hear him. Find him guilty."
Prosecutors said that while his story had changed over the years, Davis repeatedly placed himself inside a white Cadillac from which the shots were fired. And they said that while he did not pull the trigger, evidence showed he'd called for the gunfire as a powerful gang leader the younger men in the car, including his nephew, were going to listen to.
Defense attorney Michael Sanft asked jurors if there was any evidence that Davis had ever called the shots before or after the shooting.
The panel of 16 jurors, four of whom are alternates, heard testimony from 24 prosecution witnesses and three defense witnesses over nine days.
The prosecution said the state would dismiss a gang enhancement charge due to witness logistics. Prosecutors declined to comment following the verdict, and members of Shakur's family said they were waiting until sentencing, which is scheduled for October.
The decades-old case has drawn the attention of hip-hop fans and crime experts alike
The trial brought to a head a decades-old case that for years has drawn the attention of hip-hop fans and true crime experts alike. Shakur, who was considered one of the most influential rappers of all time, was in Las Vegas on Sept. 7, 1996, and stopped at a red light when a white Cadillac pulled up beside him, and shots were fired. He died six days later from his wounds. Knight was also wounded but survived.
For years, nobody had been charged in the rapper's death until Davis began making public statements, saying he was in the Cadillac and gave the gun to others in the backseat, calling the shooting a retaliation for the earlier beating of his nephew. Davis is the only person still alive among the four men prosecutors say were in the Cadillac.
Witnesses described the hostile rivalry between the Los Angeles gang sects Mob Piru and Davis' Southside Compton Crips leading up to Shakur's death and how the gangs became affiliated with Knight's Death Row Records and Sean "Diddy" Combs' Bad Boy Records.
Defense argued public statements were untrue, and physical evidence was lacking
Sanft, Davis' attorney, argued there was no physical evidence connecting his client to the shooting. He said the book Davis co-authored and the public statements he made were dramatized bravado designed to make money, not to tell the truth.
Throughout the trial, Sanft poked holes in prosecutors' narrative. He said investigators did not back up the claims made by his client, and he repeatedly pointed out a lack of physical evidence, such as phone records, that showed Davis was the shot caller.
"They have nothing in this case that says that man was here in Las Vegas on Sept. 7, 1996," Sanft said during his closing argument.
In a rebuttal argument, prosecutor Marc DiGiacomo pointed to a scrapbook Davis kept containing articles about Shakur.
"This guy's scrapbooking his murder, for God's sake," DiGiacomo told jurors.
Davis' own words were front and center
Palal held up Davis' 2019 memoir, "Compton Street Legend," and played an interview in which Davis encouraged people to buy it to get the "real truth." Although the book contains a disclaimer saying some facts were changed, prosecutors argued the central account did not.
Sanft also turned to his client's memoir during his closing argument. While reading an excerpt, he said the N-word aloud, prompting people watching in an overflow courtroom to recoil and shake their heads.
In multiple interviews, Davis said he handed the gun to the back seat, but in others as well as in his book, Davis wouldn't say who pulled the trigger.
Gang and record label rivalries provided the backdrop
While insisting Davis' words alone were enough to convict him, prosecutors said a gang rivalry helped explain why the shooting happened.
Witnesses described the hostile rivalry between the Los Angeles gang sects leading up to Shakur's death, and how the gangs became affiliated with two rival labels — Mob Piru with Knight's Death Row Records and the South Side Compton Crips with Sean "Diddy" Combs' Bad Boy Records.
The shooting death of Bad Boy's the Notorious B.I.G. six months after Shakur came up many times during the trial, with law enforcement witnesses saying Davis was briefly a suspect in that killing before being discounted. That case, which has also been an obsession of hip-hop fans, remains unsolved.

బుర్ఖా ధరించిన ఒక మహిళ కాషాయ రంగు బైక్ను ధ్వంసం చేస్తున్నట్లుగా ఉన్న వీడియో (ఇక్కడ & ఇక్కడ) ఒకటి సోషల్ మీడియాలో ప్రచారంలో ఉంది. ఈ ఘటన నిజమైనదని, బైక్ రంగు నచ్చకే ఆ ముస్లిం మహిళా ఇలా చేసిందని వైరల్ పోస్టులో పేర్కొన్నారు. దీనిలో ఎంత నిజముందో ఇప్పుడు చూద్దాం.
క్లెయిమ్: బుర్ఖా ధరించిన ముస్లిం మహిళ కాషాయ రంగు బైక్ని ధ్వంసం చేయడాన్ని చూపుతున్న వీడియో.
ఫాక్ట్: ఇది ఒక స్క్రిప్టెడ్ వీడియో, నిజమైన ఘటన కాదు. వినోదం కోసం ఇటువంటి వీడియోలను చిత్రీకరిస్తుంటామని, ఈ వీడియోలో నటించిన శివాన్ష్ యాదవ్ తన ఫేస్బుక్ బయోలో పేర్కొన్నారు. కావున, పోస్టులో చేయబడిన క్లెయిమ్ తప్పు.
ముందుగా వైరల్ వీడియోలోని దృశ్యాలను రివర్స్ ఇమేజ్ సెర్చ్ చేయగా, దీనికి సంబంధించిన పూర్తి వీడియోను (ఆర్కైవ్) ‘shivanshyadav_prank‘ అనే ఇన్స్టాగ్రామ్ పేజీలో అప్లోడ్ చేసినట్లు గుర్తించాం. ఈ పేజీని పరిశీలించగా, ఈ వీడియోలోని వ్యక్తి బుర్ఖా ధరించిన మహిళతో ఉన్న మరిన్ని వీడియోలను (ఇక్కడ & ఇక్కడ) చిత్రీకరించినట్లు గుర్తించాం. అలాగే, ఈ పేజీలో వివిధ మహిళలతో చిత్రీకరించిన స్క్రిప్టెడ్ వీడియోలు, ప్రాంక్ వీడియోలు (ఇక్కడ & ఇక్కడ) కూడా ఉన్నట్లు చూడవచ్చు.
ఈ పేజీకి సంబంధించిన ఫేస్బుక్ ఖాతాను పరిశీలించగా, తాను ఒక ఆర్టిస్ట్నని, వినోదం కోసం కామెడీ వీడియోలు చిత్రీకరిస్తుంటానని వైరల్ వీడియో నటించిన శివాన్ష్ యాదవ్ తన ఫేస్బుక్ బయోలో పేర్కొన్నారు. దీన్ని బట్టి, వైరల్ వీడియో నిజమైన ఘటన కాదని, అదొక స్క్రిప్టెడ్ వీడియో అని స్పష్టమవుతోంది.
చివరిగా, కాషాయ రంగు నచ్చక ముస్లిం మహిళ బైక్ను ధ్వంసం చేసిందంటూ ఒక స్క్రిప్టెడ్ వీడియోని నిజమైన ఘటనగా షేర్ చేస్తున్నారు.

The standard explanation for why rain causes corrosion is that water carries dissolved salts and acids to a surface, constant drumming of raindrops abrades whatever protective coating is on it, and oxygen does the rest. Nearly all our tools to prevent this—paints, polymer films, or oxide layers—are built around this idea. But we’ve apparently been missing something important about the rain.
A new study led by Zhongyuan Ni, Rüdiger Berger, and Hans-Jürgen Butt at the Max Planck Institute for Polymer Research in Mainz, Germany, has shown that water drops routinely arrive at a surface carrying an electrical charge large enough to punch through an insulating coating. Not scratch it. Not slowly dissolve it. Electrically blow a hole in it, the way a spark jumps a gap.
Charged rain
The starting point of the study is a phenomenon called “slide electrification,” which has only been properly quantified in the past few years. When a water drop slides across an insulating surface like a leaf, a painted wall, a windowpane, or a plastic panel, it strips charge from that surface and leaves an opposing charge behind. The voltages involved are not trivial. Drops charged this way have been measured at up to 9,000 volts.
The question Ni, Berger, Butt, and their colleagues asked was what this charge does to the surface that the drop lands on next. To find out, the team released 35-microliter water drops, about the size of a large raindrop, containing a pinch of salt to mimic rainwater, onto a surface tilted at 50 degrees. The drops slid about four centimeters, picked up a charge, rolled off the edge, and then fell five millimeters onto a copper plate coated with a 60-nanometer film of Teflon, which is one of the most chemically resistant coatings on the market today.
The tilted surfaces were mostly chosen to mimic raindrops in the real world. One was a leaf from a Tradescantia spathacea plant growing in one of the researchers’ offices. Another was a PVC foam board from a hardware store. The third one was a sheet of transparent polystyrene sold as window glazing. Only the fourth one, the fluorinated coating on quartz, was more of a lab creation than something people usually see everywhere around them. The charges the drops picked up ranged from 0.2 nanocoulombs off the leaf to two nanocoulombs off the fluorinated quartz. A nanocoulomb in something the size of a raindrop works out to be a few thousand volts.

OpenAI’s ChatGPT will have to comply with tougher EU rules such as removing illegal content or face potential fines, the European Commission said on Monday, as Brussels grapples with how its existing digital regulation applies to rapidly evolving AI services.
The Commission said the chatbot, social media forum Reddit, and gaming platform Roblox would be classified as so-called very large online platforms under the EU Digital Services Act, its landmark online safety regime.
The designation means all three services will face additional obligations such as removing illegal content and protecting the privacy and security of minors and could face fines of up to 6 percent of their global revenue if they fail to comply.
The decision marks a further expansion of the DSA into generative AI, with X’s AI chatbot Grok already facing an investigation under the law.
“ChatGPT, Reddit, and Roblox will now be held to a higher standard of scrutiny and accountability in the European Union, in line with their large impact on our citizens and society,” said the EU’s tech chief Henna Virkkunen.
The move comes after all three services surpassed 45 million monthly users in the EU, the threshold for enhanced scrutiny under the DSA. They now have until the end of December to comply with the additional obligations.

Russia says it helped to repel Niger attempted coup
- Published
Russia has said its forces helped to repel Saturday's attempted coup in Niger.
Explosions and gunfire rang out across capital, Niamey, early in the morning, including at a key military airbase and the presidential palace.
Hours later, Niger's authorities said the rebellion had been contained.
Nigerien forces had repelled the attack "with the assistance of servicemen of the African Corps of the Russian Ministry of Defence", the foreign ministry in Moscow said on Sunday.
The ministry also said it would continue to support Niger in its fight against "extremists", but that the situation was now under the control of the legitimate authorities headed by President [Gen Abdourahmane] Tiani".
Russia's African Corps has become a key security partner for multiple military governments in the Sahel, who have been struggling to contain long-running jihadist insurgencies.

The Alliance of Sahel States - composed of Niger, Mali and Burkina Faso - said the attempted coup was "a betrayal by a group of soldiers involved in an attempt at destabilisation".
The authorities have not said how many soldiers were involved in the attempted coup, nor how many casualties there were.
Niger's military ruler, Gen Tiani, who was sworn in as its president last year after he deposed its elected leader, has also not publicly addressed the incident.
The nation's state broadcaster showed footage of several alleged mutineers being arrested by the Presidential Guard.
On Sunday, Niger Press Agency reported that commercial activity was returning to normal, with petrol stations, shops and other businesses reopening.
Supporters of the government gathered at a public square in central Niamey in support of the security forces and Tiani's government.
Air Base 101, the military site attacked on Saturday, is part of the Diori Hamani airport complex.
It hosts Nigerien military aircraft and drones, as well as an Alliance of Sahel States counter-terrorism unit. Russian and Italian forces are also based there, according to news agency Reuters.
Niger, Mali and Burkina Faso are all military-ruled countries that have cut ties with Western partners and strengthened their co-operation with Russia.
But jihadist violence remains widespread in all three countries, despite the shift in alliances.
For Niger's government, Saturday's mutiny highlights that the military is dealing not only with an external insurgency, but also signs of discontent within its own ranks.
The airbase where the mutiny began had itself been targeted twice by jihadists this year – once by an Islamic State affiliate and later by an al-Qaeda affiliate.
Nigerien authorities say security forces have increased patrols around key sites in Niamey following the attempted takeover, including the main airport entrance and the presidential pavilion.

President Trump yesterday demanded that the Federal Communications Commission punish or rebuke an NBC journalist for saying he has “mixed results” in his election endorsements. In the latest example of how Trump is using the FCC to harass reporters and news organizations that he dislikes, he said Meet the Press host Kristen Welker “will be reported to the FCC for rebuke or punishment” for what he claimed was a “purposeful inaccuracy.”
“Kristen Welker, the Unpopular ‘Hostess’ of the once great Meet the Press, now considered Meet the Fake Press, just stated that Donald Trump has ‘mixed results’ on his Endorsements of Candidates, when the recent WINS of Darline Graham and Mike Mazzei, stand at 100% for the U.S. Senate, and 98% for the U.S. House, recently and over the longterm. How can anyone be allowed to say this, working for freely given Public Airwaves? Results are attached. Because of this purposeful inaccuracy, she will be reported to the FCC for rebuke or punishment,” Trump wrote in a Truth Social post.
A separate post from Trump yesterday said, “THE FAKE POLLS USED BY OUR CROOKED MEDIA ARE OUT OF CONTROL, AND SOMETHING MUST BE DONE ABOUT IT. FCC TO THE RESCUE! President DJT.” Trump also posted a rant on Friday about New York Times journalist Maggie Haberman, calling her “an unattractive person both inside and out” who “should be forced to turn over any and all money that she’s made through her fake reporting on me.” Trump referred to Haberman throughout his post as “Maggot Haberman.”
Trump’s post about Welker included an image purporting to show he has near-perfect results in his endorsements this year. “The Press is a Disgrace to our Nation, and I hope that Chairman Brendan Carr, and the fine people of his Commission, will take this Threat to our Country very seriously,” Trump wrote.
Perhaps indicating that he will refer additional journalists for FCC punishment, Trump wrote that Welker “is not the only one. The Radical Left News is going out of their way to harass, demean, and libel anything ‘TRUMP.’”
Trump’s FCC chair has eagerly obeyed orders
The idea of the FCC punishing reporters for basic analysis of election results would have seemed far-fetched in previous administrations. The FCC website says the commission “cannot prevent the broadcast of any particular point of view,” and that it “generally will not intervene” in complaints about “one-sided news reports” because “it would be inconsistent with the First Amendment to replace the journalistic judgment of licensees with our own.”
Even during Trump’s first term, then-FCC Chairman Ajit Pai said that under the First Amendment, “the FCC does not have the authority to revoke a license of a broadcast station based on the content of a particular newscast.” Pai made the comment less than a week after Trump called on the FCC to revoke broadcast licenses from NBC and other networks for “fake news.”
An FCC investigation of Welker over an ordinary statement about election results seems much less far-fetched under Carr, who has embraced his role as Trump’s chief censor. Carr has made it clear he takes orders from Trump, abandoning his previous position—which he held under Democratic presidents—that the FCC must operate independently of White House interference.
Welker said in an appearance on NBC 4 Washington that Trump “has endorsed a slate of candidates in the primaries” and that “he’s had some mixed results but most recently his pick of Senator Darline Graham, of course the sister of the late Senator Lindsay Graham, was successful in her primary battle.” Trump’s post attacking Welker claimed that “the story of [Graham’s] Victory was hardly covered by anybody,” despite Welker mentioning it in the very statement that triggered Trump’s wrath.
Poynter Senior Media Writer Tom Jones writes, “What Welker said about Trump’s endorsements having mixed results was true. Trump just didn’t like it.” While Trump praised himself for his successful endorsements, he didn’t mention primary losses by Republican gubernatorial candidates Burt Jones in Georgia and Randy Feenstra in Iowa and the failed re-election bid by Rep. Cory Mills (R-Florida).
Carr uses news-distortion policy to threaten networks
An NBC News spokesperson told several media outlets that “Kristen is one of the best in the business and we stand by her.” We contacted NBC News and will update this article if it has any further comment.
Welker is hardly the first TV journalist to discuss Trump’s mixed endorsement results. “Already, just this month alone, six of the president’s endorsed candidates have lost their races, and so there are questions about the power of his endorsements,” CNN White House correspondent Alayna Treene said on Inside Politics.
In June, Trump abruptly ended an interview with Welker after she challenged his claims of election rigging in California. Trump stated that “all I have to do is look” when Welker asked him for evidence of cheating. “That’s not evidence,” Welker responded.
If Carr does investigate Welker, he could do so under the FCC’s news distortion policy. Carr has repeatedly invoked the rarely enforced news distortion policy and a rule against broadcast hoaxes in various threats to Trump’s perceived enemies in the media. We asked the FCC chairman’s office today if the commission will investigate Welker and will update this article if we get a response.
Previous FCC leaders set such a high bar for proving news distortion that the policy was all but abandoned until Carr made it a focal point of his attempts to punish broadcasters. In September 2025, Carr threatened to revoke ABC station licenses for news distortion if they continued airing Jimmy Kimmel’s show.
Trump and FCC try to reshape the media
While Carr can cause trouble for licensed broadcasters and networks simply by issuing threats, he went far beyond mere threats in the case of ABC. The Carr FCC ordered ABC to file early license-renewal applications for the eight TV stations it owns and operates and justified the proceeding by accusing ABC of violating anti-discrimination rules with diversity, equity, and inclusion (DEI) practices.
ABC owner Disney is fighting back with a lawsuit against Carr and the FCC, saying it has faced a campaign of censorship in retaliation for the protected speech of its journalists and network programs. Both conservative and liberal groups have urged the FCC to back off.
The Trump administration has also sought to reshape the media through merger approvals. Paramount won FCC approval to buy Skydance after agreeing to install what Carr called a “bias monitor” at CBS. Paramount later won Justice Department approval to buy Warner Bros. Discovery, months after CEO David Ellison reportedly told Trump administration officials that he would make big changes at the Warner-owned CNN.
In March, Trump and Carr demanded more positive media coverage of the Iran war, with Carr claiming without evidence that broadcasters aired “hoaxes and news distortions.” Last year, Carr accused Comcast of news distortion when its subsidiary NBC refused to adopt the Trump administration narrative on the deportation of Kilmar Abrego Garcia.
FCC Commissioner Anna Gomez, the commission’s only Democrat, responded to Trump’s latest threat yesterday. “As I’ve said many times, the FCC has no authority to punish journalists this administration doesn’t like,” Gomez wrote. “These threats to press freedom are dangerous. They undermine the foundation of our democracy, and they have no place in it.”

Paris-based film and television studio SND, part of French media group M6, has picked up world sales on the high-end period drama “Alice: Pioneer of Cinema,” in which Oscar-nominee Bérénice Bejo (“The Artist”) stars as Alice Guy, the very first female fiction filmmaker. 
The six-parter, ordered by HBO Max and France Télévisions, is due to world premiere at the Toronto Film Festival‘s Primetime section on Sept. 14, ahead of its airing in December. 
	France’s Wild Bunch and Ligne de Front are producing along with Belgium’s Panache Productions, La Compagnie Cinématographique and Canada’s Sphere Media. 
The big-scale series, created by Tim Loane (“Versailles,” “Das Boot”) and Claire Lemaréchal (“The Bureau”) from a script by André Gulluni (“Rematch”), will also play on the leading Spanish pay TV/SVOD service Movistar Plus+, HBO Max in Belgium and the streamer Crave in Canada. 
	
Popular on Variety
Helmed by Virginie Verrier and Guillaume Lonergan, “Alice: Pioneer of Cinema” tells the true story of Alice Guy, who turned from secretary for Gaumont to the first female fiction filmmaker and movie mogul in the late 19th to early 20th century.
After rising through the ranks at French banner Gaumont, she moves to the U.S., where she builds the first film studio owned by a woman. Despite her extraordinary achievements, she ends up losing it all, and her name fades into oblivion.
A century later, her film pioneering role is finally recognized when she receives a posthumous Lifetime Achievement Award from the Directors Guild of America, handed out by Martin Scorsese. Then in 2024, at the Paris Olympic Games, her golden statue rises from the Seine, alongside other female luminaries Simon Veil and Simone de Beauvoir.
Besides Bejo, the stellar cast takes in Oscar Lesage (“The Substance”), Thibaut Evrard (“Paris Police 1900,” “No Man’s Land”), Irène Jacob (“The Affair; “The Double Life of Véronique”), Sophie Nélisse (“Yellowjackets,” “The Book Thief”) and François Arnaud (“The Borgias,” “Yellowjackets”).
“Every so often, a series arrives with a story so extraordinary you cannot believe it has never been told,” said Alexis Reybet-Degat, SND head of international TV series distribution. “‘Alice’ has the scale and craft of a major production, and a heroine whose fight feels strikingly modern. It is prestige and popular at once, and we are proud to bring it to broadcasters around the world.”
Caroline De Jenlis, producer at Ligne de Front said, “We are thrilled to partner with SND. With their incredible expertise, we are fully confident they will give Alice’s extraordinary story the global showcase it deserves.”
SND will start negotiating the series at the 32nd Unifrance Rendez Vous in Le Havre, unspooling over Sept 7-10. Another prime drama on the sales banner’s slate includes the nuclear warship thriller “R91.”
In Toronto, “Alice: Pioneer of Cinema” will be showcased together with nine premium shows from major players such as A24, Amazon MGM, Netflix and Apple.

Body odour is a normal part of life. Contrary to popular belief, sweat in itself does not usually smell. The familiar odour develops when bacteria and fungi that live on the skin break down substances in sweat, particularly secretions from glands in the armpits and groin. In most cases, body odour is harmless and may vary depending on factors such as heat, physical activity, diet and hygiene.
However, a new or persistent change in body odour should not always be dismissed as a hygiene issue, doctors say. In some cases, an unusual odour may be linked to an underlying health condition and may need medical evaluation.
Heat, food and hormones
Several everyday factors can alter body odour. Hot weather and physical activity increase sweating, while tight or synthetic clothing can trap moisture. Garlic, onions, spicy foods, alcohol and certain medicines can also affect body odour.
Hemanath M. J., consultant, internal and family medicine, Apollo Speciality Hospitals, Vanagaram, Chennai, says the apocrine glands in the armpits, groin and scalp contribute more to odour than the eccrine glands, which cover most of the body. Stress can stimulate the apocrine glands and intensify odour.
Hormonal changes can also play a role. Puberty, menstruation and menopause may temporarily alter sweating and body odour. Puberty is one common situations in which changes in body odour are routinely seen. An overactive thyroid, which can cause excessive sweating, may also make odour more noticeable.
A change is more likely to be temporary when there is a clear trigger and the odour settles after the trigger passes. “If somebody develops an odour after eating a particular food, drinking a particular drink, starting a medication or strenuous exercise, or during a period of hormonal change, and it returns to normal after some time, the context helps explain the change,” says Narayanan A., consultant, dermatology, SRM Prime Hospital, Chennai..
Body odour as a health clue
A persistent or unexplained change can sometimes be associated with a skin condition or an underlying medical problem. Skin infections in the armpits, groin or other moist areas can alter odour. These may be accompanied by redness, soreness, itching, peeling or discharge.
“An infection in the groin or axilla (armpit) or excessive growth of bacteria or fungi can alter the odour,” says Dr. Narayanan.
Dr. Hemanath says conditions such as erythrasma and fungal infections can produce a distinct smell, particularly in warm, moist areas. Excessive sweating, or hyperhidrosis, does not itself cause odour but can provide more moisture for bacteria to act on.
Certain metabolic conditions have also been associated with distinctive smells. Uncontrolled diabetes can produce fruity or sweet-smelling breath because of ketone build-up. A rare condition called trimethylaminuria can cause a fish-like odour because the body is unable to break down certain compounds properly.
Odour changes have also been described in advanced kidney and liver disease. But doctors caution against treating these smells as diagnostic tests.
“Some distinctive smells have been described with complications of diabetes, liver disease or kidney disease, but these are clues rather than reliable diagnostic tests,” says Dr. Narayanan. The overall clinical picture, including symptoms, examination and biochemical investigations, is what guides diagnosis.
Need for evaluation
The first step when there is a change in body odour is to look for an obvious trigger. Regular washing, changing sweaty clothes, washing clothes properly and using an antiperspirant can help determine whether the problem responds to routine measures.
But a sudden change in body odour without a clear cause is reason to consult a doctor.The physician would first consider what changed at the same time as the odour. If there is no obvious trigger and the change persists or keeps recurring, a deeper evaluation may be required.
A sudden unexplained increase in sweating, night sweats without an obvious reason, or sweating that interferes with daily activities should also prompt medical attention. Experts list other warning signs such as unexplained weight loss, excessive thirst or urination, fatigue, swelling, fever, night sweats or skin changes. A fruity odour with excessive thirst, frequent urination, nausea, vomiting or confusion requires urgent assessment.
Depending on the symptoms, a doctor may conduct a physical and skin examination and consider tests such as blood glucose and HbA1c, kidney and liver function tests and a thyroid profile. Skin scraping or culture may be considered if an infection is suspected.
Doctors say, body odour should not be used to self-diagnose a disease. Most changes have an everyday explanation, but a smell that is new, persistent, unexplained or accompanied by other symptoms is worth discussing with a doctor

Water was released from the Mettur Dam in Salem district after water levels reached the required 90-foot mark, bringing crucial relief for farmers in Tamil Nadu's Cauvery Delta region. The opening, delayed by nearly 80 days from the customary June 12 schedule due to low rainfall and delayed inflows, provides irrigation support for kuruvai, samba, and thalaidi crops. The Tamil Nadu government has planned a water release for 45 days, subject to storage and continuous inflows. However, concerns remain regarding long-term water security for the state's agricultural belt, which remains heavily dependent on sustained southwest monsoon rains and water releases from upstream Karnataka. The broader inter-state conflict over Cauvery river water sharing and the proposed Mekedatu dam project continues to be a subject of contention and legal dispute before the Supreme Court.
At the Shanghai Cooperation Organisation summit, Prime Minister Narendra Modi called upon member states to dismantle the entire ecosystem of terrorism, including terror financing, recruitment, radicalisation, and safe havens. Highlighting the need to move beyond an action-reaction mindset, he stressed that there can be no room for double standards on terrorism and that no nation should use terror as an instrument of state policy or consider it a strategic asset. The Prime Minister underscored that tackling terrorism and transnational crimes such as narcotics trafficking is essential for regional security, Eurasian connectivity, and economic opportunity. He also addressed the West Asia crisis, advocating for dialogue and diplomacy as the way forward. Emphasising a long-term vision for the organisation, he urged member nations to work together transparently to build a secure environment across the Eurasian landmass over the coming decades.
A green-painted house has emerged as one of the most striking images from the devastating floods in Nepal, standing almost completely intact while buildings, vehicles and other structures around it were swept away by raging floodwaters. India Today reached the house, located in the flood-hit Trishuli region, which became the focus of viral footage showing floodwaters and debris surging around it as a terrified family remained trapped on its balcony. The family was later rescued. Reports, citing an analysis by architectural experts, suggested that the house was built with a reinforced-concrete frame and continuous steel reinforcement, giving it a rigid structural skeleton capable of withstanding the powerful lateral forces generated by the floodwaters. Its location, slightly away from the main debris channel and on relatively higher ground, may also have helped, allowing the water to split around the building rather than hit it directly. The solitary house, surrounded by widespread destruction, has since been dubbed a "miracle house", a striking symbol of survival amid one of Nepal’s worst recent flood disasters.
A special five-judge bench of the National Company Law Tribunal has stayed an earlier order concerning the settlement of Essel Group's 22,000 crore rupee debt for 6.5 crore rupees. The tribunal issued notices to Essel Group chief Subhash Chandra and lenders in the Zee Entertainment insolvency case, clarifying that the earlier approval of the resolution plan was not a final or majority view. The bench observed differing opinions among earlier members and ruled that the guarantor cannot sell or alienate any assets. The special bench will hear all lenders and stakeholders on the matter.
At the Shanghai Cooperation Organisation summit in Bishkek, world leaders gathered against the backdrop of global geopolitical conflicts to strengthen regional stability, connectivity, and economic collaboration. Top priorities on India's agenda include energy security amid uncertainties regarding the Strait of Hormuz, combating terror funding and radicalisation, curbing drug trafficking, and enhancing Central Asian regional connectivity. The summit also focuses on diversifying supply chains, leveraging digital public infrastructure such as India's Unified Payments Interface, and promoting sustainable peace and trade cooperation across member states and partner nations.

The 31st Busan International Film Festival (BIFF) has unveiled a guest lineup headlined by Isabelle Huppert, Maggie Gyllenhaal, Kore-eda Hirokazu, Fan Bingbing and Michelle Yeoh.
Huppert brings her latest film, “All About Corinne,” to Busan audiences. Gyllenhaal makes her first visit to Korea with “Flesh Impact,” a project created to mark the centenary of Marilyn Monroe’s birth. Fan Bingbing joins fellow Chinese stars Shu Qi and Zhou Xun in Busan, while also curating a Carte Blanche selection of Park Chan-wook’s “The Handmaiden.” Yeoh, the first Asian performer to win the Academy Award for best actress, returns to the festival after 15 years to receive the Asian Filmmaker of the Year award and appears in the gala presentation title “It’s My Time.”
The broader guest roster runs deep. Hong Kong’s Ann Hui will accept the Camellia Award, and Indonesian icon Christine Hakim will also attend. Iranian director Majid Majidi, known for “Children of Heaven,” makes his first trip to Korea with competition entry “Midday Meal.” Animator Rintaro returns to discuss his work on “Metropolis,” and Filipino director Lav Diaz comes back to Korea after a decade away. Japan’s Kore-eda Hirokazu arrives with “Look Back,” Taiwan’s Tsai Ming-liang returns for a second straight year with a new entry in his “Walker” series, and French filmmaker Bertrand Mandico brings “Roma Elastica,” starring Marion Cotillard. Korean auteurs Lee Chang-dong, Na Hong-Jin and Kim Jeewoon round out the lineup, the latter appearing as one of this year’s three Carte Blanche curators.
Popular on Variety
Japan sends a large delegation of stars led by Nagasawa Masami, including Emoto Tasuku, Ishibashi Shizuka, Kuroki Haru, Yokohama Ryusei, Yamazaki Kento, Matsushita Kouhei, Sawajiri Erika, Maruyama Ryuhei and Nagayama Eita. A younger group of international names is also set to attend, among them Yeh Shuhua, Michelle Mao, Jin Ha and Thai star Davika Hoorne.
BIFF’s gala presentation section will screen five films with their directors and casts in attendance. Kore-eda’s “Look Back” adapts Fujimoto Tatsuki’s manga for the screen. “All About Corinne,” from director Marc Fitoussi, marks his fourth collaboration with Huppert. Judith Godrèche’s “A Girl’s Story” revisits Nobel laureate Annie Ernaux’s most intimate memories to follow a young woman’s coming of age. “It’s My Time,” from director Bai Xue, casts Yeoh as a 70-year-old woman taking on an unexpected challenge. July Jung’s “Dora,” which premiered at Cannes’ Directors’ Fortnight, closes out the section.
BIFF’s competition section, its main Asian cinema showcase, features 14 films from Korea, Japan, China, Taiwan, Iran, Uzbekistan and Indonesia, four of them directorial debuts and four from women filmmakers. Majidi’s “Midday Meal” anchors an international lineup that includes Kato Takuya’s “The Day After Sunday,” Chen Jiwen’s “Descendants,” Gu You’s “The First Taste of Loneliness,” Hirose Nanako’s “Between Two Lovers,” Eddie Cahyono’s “Ibuku,” Okita Shuichi’s “Satoko Always,” Yosep Anggi Noen’s “The Sea Speaks His Name,” Kim Jung-hoon’s “Shaving” and Lee Yun Chan’s “To Be Ordinary.” The four debut features come from Lim Hayeon, Botir Abdurakhmanov, Youm Kyubock and Tanaka Miki. The section serves as the entry point for BIFF’s New Currents Award, given to a standout directorial debut.
Alongside competition, the festival’s Window on Asian Cinema section adds 28 further titles from established and emerging filmmakers working across Asia and its diaspora, many of them multi-country co-productions. The lineup includes Wayne Wang’s “Diary of a Mad Old Man,” Kamila Andini’s “Four Seasons in Java,” Rima Das’ “Not a Hero” and Fujii Michihito’s “You, Like a Star,” alongside a broad spread of titles spanning India, Japan, Taiwan, Thailand, Vietnam, Kazakhstan, Iran and beyond.
BIFF’s Icons section, its sidebar for works by established masters of world cinema, presents 35 films this year. The lineup brings together Hamaguchi Ryusuke’s “All of a Sudden,” Pedro Almodóvar’s “Bitter Christmas,” Werner Herzog’s “Bucking Fastard,” Lukas Dhont’s “Coward,” Cristian Mungiu’s “Fjord,” David Lowery’s “Mother Mary,” starring Anne Hathaway, and Brad Bird’s animated “Ray Gunn,” featuring the voices of Sam Rockwell, Scarlett Johansson and Tom Waits. It also includes Korean auteurs Hong Sangsoo and Lee Chang-dong, Taiwan’s Tsai Ming-liang, and Kogonada’s U.S.-Hong Kong co-production “Zi,” which will have its international premiere in Busan.
The festival’s guest and program announcements follow a run of earlier reveals for this year’s edition, including the “The Table: Day and Night” opening film, the Vision-Korea and Vision-Asia lineups, the Korean Cinema Today and On Screen selections, the Carte Blanche curators, a tribute program for the late Ahn Sung-ki, and market-side news from the Asian Contents & Film Market, including Thailand’s debut as Country of Honor, the InnoAsia technology program and new additions to the Asian Project Market and Busan Story Market.
The 31st Busan International Film Festival will run Oct. 6-15 at the Busan Cinema Center and venues throughout Busan, with the 21st Asian Contents & Film Market held Oct. 10-13.

Former Republican congressman George Santos has received a first-of-its-kind lifetime ban from the prediction market platform Kalshi, which has also fined him $71,356 for violating its rules around insider trading and market manipulation.
According to the notice of disciplinary action Kalshi posted today, the former politician placed trades in markets related to whether he would attend President Trump’s State of the Union address in February 2026. He then “began making a series of public statements regarding his attendance at the event in an attempt to influence the price” of certain contracts, some of which were “false or misleading,” per the notice.
The day before the address, Santos posted, “I'm going to be there for the State of Union in the gallery, guys” on X. During the speech, he sent a follow-up noting that he was actually at an airport watching the address on television. “FML,” he wrote.
Kalshi’s enforcement team flagged the trades, froze Santos’ account, and referred the case to the Commodity Futures Trading Commission, the federal agency that oversees prediction markets. This summer, he settled with the CFTC for $35,000 over these suspicious trades; a little over $17,500 was returning the profit he made, with an additional $17,500 fine. At the time, his lawyer issued a statement stressing that Santos settled to “put this matter behind him” and that he had done so “without admitting the Commission’s allegations, findings or conclusions.”
Through his legal representative, Santos declined to comment to WIRED. However, on social media, he already weighed in, sarcastically thanking Kalshi “for the lifetime ban from your gambling platform,” adding, “Let’s see how much longer you guys are around for 💋,” a nod to the prediction market’s ongoing battles with state authorities over how it is regulated.
Once upon a time, Santos had a rosier relationship with the industry; he was once paid for promoting Kalshi’s rival Polymarket, but Polymarket severed ties with him once federal regulators began looking into his behavior around February’s State of the Union.
This is far from Santos’ first brush with the law. He was expelled from Congress following an ethics investigation in 2023, and eventually pleaded guilty and served time in federal prison for embezzling from campaign donors, lying to Congress, and defrauding campaign contributors. He was released from prison in 2025 after President Trump commuted his sentence.
According to today’s notice, the prediction market found that Santos successfully influenced the pricing of several markets. Kalshi also issued four additional notices of enforcement actions today, but Santos was the only person penalized who did not settle with the company.
“He wouldn’t talk to us, and actively dodged us,” Kalshi spokesperson Elisabeth Diana tells WIRED.
In the past year, Kalshi has issued a number of other enforcement actions against politicians who it found had broken its rules. In this most recent round of enforcement actions, it fined North Carolina Congressional candidate Laurie Buckhout, California gubernatorial candidate Stephen Kloobeck, and Maine gubernatorial candidate Ben Midgley for attempting to trade on contracts related to their races; they are all temporarily suspended.
“I bet on myself. Literally. It was a dumb mistake, and as soon as I learned there was an issue, I worked to make it right. Safe to say my career as a Kalshi trader was short-lived,” Buckhout, a retired military officer, told WIRED in an email. Kloobeck and Midgley did not immediately respond to WIRED’s request for comment.
Previously, it fined US Senate candidate Mark Moran for insider trading; at the time, Moran told WIRED that he “did it on purpose” and did not intend to cooperate with Kalshi.
Kalshi’s Diana says that Santos can expect “legal action” if he does not pay.

A common way to deal with emotions is through food, says Lakshmi Venkatraman, consultant psychiatrist and assistant director of Psychosocial Rehabilitation Services at SCARF (Schizophrenia Research Foundation). Dieting and restrictions on food are also culprits. The vicious circle begins when people tend to eat more, end up feeling guilty at their act, reduce their self-esteem, because of which they binge eat and feel more guilty.
Simple measures such as eating regular meals with all foods, including favourites in moderation, helps. “When we realise emotions are pushing us (to eat), finding ways to tackle the emotions will help,” Dr. Lakshmi explains. “Be mindful while eating, focus on what we are eating, take it quite slow while eating which helps to prevent binge eating,” she points out.
R.M. Anjana, managing director of Dr. Mohan’s Diabetes Specialities Centre, cites the various studies done by the Foundation at various intervals of time, to explain the importance of regulating “what we put into our mouth”. When a person finds that they binge once a week and this persists for three months then it should trigger an alarm, she says. “Diet and physical activity alone can prevent 50% of diabetes,” she said and cited studies that state that binge eating contributes to about 15 to 20% of type 2 diabetes.
A bariatric surgeon aims to moderate the gut hormones, says P. Praveen Raj, consultant and head of the Department of Minimal Access Bariatric and Robotic Surgery in the Department of Surgical Gastroenterology, GEM Hospital and Research Centre, Coimbatore.
The first step is to take a thorough history of the person’s issues. There are various hormones in the gut that regulate satiety, trigger appetite and aid digestion. An imbalance in any one of them could be the cause for obesity. The aim is to treat the cause, he explains. “You rule out the psychological reasons, and the pathological abnormality. Once this is understood we can start to treat it (the condition),” he adds.
The specialists were panelists at a webinar on “The Binge: Learning to handle addictive behaviours,” organised on Sunday by The Hindu. The webinar can be viewed at https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=Cl4wxf7_HRI

New Delhi, Sep 01: Prime Minister Narendra Modi on Tuesday commended the people for the 7.8 per cent GDP growth rate, noting that the feat was accomplished despite wars, instability, and supply chain disruptions.
In a video message on Instagram, the prime minister said that if people continue to stress on Swadeshi and self-reliance, the country's youth will be presented with a developed India in the 100th year of Independence.
He also asked people not to go for foreign holidays, host weddings abroad, or buy gold unless necessary.
"I want to congratulate the people of the country for 7.8 per cent GDP growth. It has been possible due to their collective resolve and efforts. India has achieved this milestone despite conflicts, wars and instability everywhere," Modi said.
The prime minister said that since the 2020 COVID Pandemic, there has been no stability anywhere, but India progressed well.
He said certain people in India have been trying to spread negativity and falsehood, but the country grew all the same.
"We have to maintain the speed of our growth. We have to grow. And for that we must become self-reliant. The youth's dreams need our hard work to be realised. Let's not be lacking in efforts," he said.
Modi said his government's policies are good, its intention clear, and that is why the country is reaching new heights of progress.
India's economy grew at a faster-than-expected 7.8 per cent in the April-June quarter, showing resilience against concerns of an economic downturn over the war in West Asia.
Gross domestic product (GDP) growth in the first quarter of the 2026-27 fiscal year slowed from a barnstorming 8.6 per cent in the previous quarter, but remained well above expectations when the conflict erupted and disrupted energy markets.

In Summary
- As concerns around smart glasses and privacy grow, Meta has ensured that users cannot use the cameras on its smart glasses if they cover or tamper with the LED that lights up during recording.
- While Meta’s move is a step in the right direction, it still does not go far enough to address the privacy issues posed by smart glasses.
- Smart glasses brands need to do more to prevent misuse. This includes informing and educating not just users, but also the public, who could unknowingly end up in footage shot on these devices.
Smart glasses have existed for a while but have attained a whole new dimension of popularity since Meta invested in them. For those of you who might not be aware (welcome to high-tech planet, folks), smart glasses look like regular glasses but come with a number of tech add-ons, such as displays, speakers, and most notably, cameras. These smart glasses can take photos, record videos, handle phone calls, play music, let you speak to an AI assistant, figure out your way around town, get recommendations, and more.
Table of Contents
Smart glasses? Pervert glasses, more like!
Sound uber cool, cutting-edge and futuristic, don’t they? Unfortunately, this tech rose comes with a stack of thorns that would make a cactus turn even more green with envy. While the tech world and content creators may be going gaga over all these smart glasses can do, more and more people are beginning to refer to them as “pervert glasses.” There is a sound reason for this – these glasses are increasingly being used to record people (often women) without their consent and knowledge, resulting in a massive breach of a person’s privacy. There have been a number of incidents in which people have been recorded without their knowledge and the footage shared in public or private groups, causing severe trauma to those who appeared unknowingly in the footage.
What’s worse, the onus of figuring out that they are being recorded fell on the person being recorded. Being vigilant, actively looking for signs of someone wearing smart glasses, and catching up on tech cues were all part of the package – we also did a story on ways one could find out if they are being recorded as smart glasses moved from being content creators to destroyers of privacy. As incidents of “secret recordings” through these glasses increase, pressure has finally started building on the brands making these devices to make them safer not just for their users, but also for those in their vicinity.
Meta finally moves, but is it enough?
Recently, Meta finally fixed a flaw that was making it easier for users to covertly record others. In a post made on Threads (https://www.threads.com/@ahimel/post/DcjTatTGyn-), Alex Himel, Vice President of Wearables and Vice President of Augmented Reality at Meta, said that the camera on the glasses would stop working if the LED on the glasses was covered.
He was referring to a small LED indicator on the glasses that lights up when the glasses are recording. While the cameras on the glasses would not allow users to record if the LED was covered, many users found ways around this. One method was as simple as covering the LED light after starting to record the video. Following Himel’s announcement, an update will ensure that if the LED is covered at any stage (before or after starting a video recording), the glasses will automatically stop recording the video or taking photos. What’s more, if users tamper with the LED light and destroy or disable it, the glasses will now disable the camera feature permanently.
While this is definitely a step in the right direction, it does not really solve the biggest issue around these glasses. We have seen Meta’s glasses in public, and it is very difficult to spot when they are recording, especially in daylight or if the person is some distance away. The LED light is bright, but can easily be missed if one is not looking for it. What’s more, one can place a hand in front of it to stop others from seeing it, without actually covering it. We really think more needs to be done to safeguard the privacy of users in the vicinity of these devices. Brands need to come up with stronger measures that can help people spot those who may be wearing smart glasses and steer clear of their line of vision, if they so wish.
Making smart glasses safer: five more things brands can do
Given how limited the LED indicator can be, here are five measures that tech brands can take to make smart glasses safer for those in front of them:
Just make them look different…VERY different
One of the reasons why it is extremely difficult to find out if a person is wearing smart glasses is because they look exactly like usual glasses. Clear, tinted, or even running smart glasses all come with designs/frames that make them look like “normal” glasses. This makes them difficult to spot and enables users to record footage without being noticed.
We think that, given the privacy nightmares they can potentially pose, smart glasses need to look fundamentally different from everyday glasses. Visible badging, colors, even frame size or design should make them easy to spot. Who knows, this might even catch on as a style statement, but at least it will alert those in the vicinity that the person is walking around with a camera literally on their eyes!
Better, brighter (and maybe even more) LED lights
An LED light blinking while recording or taking photos is currently the only way to find out if someone is recording video or taking photographs from their smart glasses. As we have said before, a single light can be missed or even discreetly covered. The solution? Brands could perhaps use multiple LEDs of different colors, and which are of larger size, to pretty much advertise that a smart glasses’ camera is in use. Something like Nothing’s Glyph UI would be very handy!
Pump up the volume
Smart glasses should also give clear audio signals when their cameras are functioning. It should not be possible to take photographs without a loud camera shutter sound, and adding low but constant beep sounds when video is being recorded would also alert people to the presence of a camera in their vicinity.
Mandatory identifying apps
There are already apps like Zuckoff in the market that notify users if they are around someone wearing smart glasses. But these are unofficial and a little hit and miss. We think it would be wonderful if smart glass manufacturers took the initiative to come up with an app that can alert people in a small radius (say, 10 meters if based on Bluetooth), letting them know that they are in the presence of someone wearing smart glasses. Yes, it does violate the privacy of the person wearing smart glasses, as it is likely to make people in their vicinity notice them, but then that’s the price one pays for wearing such a device.
Better marketing and awareness
Brands have been pouring sackfuls of money into normalizing and promoting smart glasses. It would be great if they could allocate some of these funds to also highlight the dangers they can pose, and how they can be misused. Some might think this is counterproductive, but we feel this is the socially responsible thing to do – to make people aware that the device has its dark side too. And it is best that the brands do it themselves before they are forced to do it by Governments around the world.
The Government needs to step in as well. While new tech does make lives easier, there are always people who can find ways to misuse it. It happened with the Internet, it happened with smartphones, it is happening with AI, and it is happening with smart glasses too. To make sure that technology is not misused, there need to be strict privacy laws that are implemented effectively and come with stringent punishments. Perhaps statutory warnings on devices, advising consumers not to misuse them, might be an option worth considering. People need to realize that with great tech comes great responsibility.
Smart glasses need a Meta-morphosis, pun intended. They do not need to blend in, but to stand out and make people realize that they are present in a room. People need to know that they could be on camera. And the onus for this lies not just on those doing the recording, but on the brands who facilitate this.

"There's a thin line between being a hero, and being a memory." — Optimus Prime, Transformers (2007) The line, delivered by Optimus Prime in the first Transformers film is a quiet reflection on the price of courage. It speaks to the uncertainty that comes with standing between danger and the people who need protection. A hero may be remembered for what they accomplished, but the possibility of becoming a memory is always close behind. Optimus Prime is, at his core, a leader defined by responsibility. As the commander of the Autobots, he repeatedly places himself in danger to protect both his own kind and humanity. His heroism is not simply about winning battles. It is about making difficult choices when there is something greater at stake. That is what gives the quote its weight. Being a hero is not presented as a permanent state. It can be fragile. One decision, one sacrifice or one final battle can separate a living hero from the memory they leave behind. The words have also acquired another layer of poignancy following the death of Peter Cullen, the veteran voice actor who became synonymous with Optimus Prime. Cullen died at the age of 85, leaving behind a career that stretched across animation, film and television. His voice was central to the character's identity, giving Prime a combination of authority, restraint and warmth. Cullen was not defined solely by the Autobot commander. He was also widely recognised as the voice of Eeyore in Winnie-the-Pooh, creating an unmistakable contrast between the stoic optimism of Optimus Prime and the melancholy personality of the much-loved donkey. That range makes the quote feel particularly fitting when considering Cullen's legacy. Voices become part of childhood memories. Characters endure long after the people who created them are gone. And eventually, even those who gave fictional heroes their voices become part of the history they helped create. Another memorable Optimus Prime line from the franchise captures that sense of purpose: "Freedom is the right of all sentient beings." Together, the two lines reveal what makes Optimus Prime such an enduring character. His heroism is rooted not in glory, but in sacrifice, freedom and responsibility. And as audiences continue to return to the Transformers films, the distinction between a hero and a memory becomes increasingly meaningful.
