‘Alpha,’ ‘beta’ and ‘Low T’ — the strange masculinity war consuming the midterms
"Democratic voters want a candidate who will fight," said Beth Reingold, an Emory University professor who specializes in gender and politics
While major policy disputes over inflation, health care, taxes, tariffs, immigration, and the war in Iran dominate headline debates this midterm election cycle, an underlying cultural question is quietly shaping key congressional battles: what defines a real man?
This surge in aggressive posturing follows the brand of politics introduced over a decade ago by Donald Trump, who used a distinct style of masculinity to belittle primary rivals and defeat two female Democratic opponents during his White House campaigns.
Seeking to regain power, several Democratic candidates are now asserting their own version of manhood—or striving to more confidently deflect conservative attacks.
"Democratic voters want a candidate who will fight," said Beth Reingold, an Emory University professor who specializes in gender and politics. "And that’s conceived as a sort of masculine demand, a more masculine approach, especially in response to Trump."
The dynamic is playing out across several key races. In Michigan, Democratic Senate nominee Abdul El-Sayed accused his Republican rival, Mike Rogers, of "beta energy" as they traded jabs over their high school football backgrounds.
Down in Texas, conservative figures have targeted Democratic Senate nominee James Talarico, labeling him "Low T Talarico" in reference to testosterone.
The 37-year-old Talarico, who is campaigning against 63-year-old Ken Paxton, brushed off the insult by saying, "I don’t think guys my age are really concerned about that kind of thing."
Reingold noted that gender discussions in campaigns typically focus on how female candidates choose to present themselves. "What’s different in this election," she said, "is that there’s even more of an incentive for these male candidates to make their masculinity present in some way, shape or form."
Projecting stamina and hiding physical weakness has a long history in American politics. Franklin Roosevelt hid his wheelchair and partial paralysis from the public.
John F. Kennedy, the youngest elected president, cultivated an image of youth and strength by being photographed sailing and playing football, while keeping his severe back pain and medication routine secret. Similarly, Ronald Reagan, then the oldest president ever to serve, was routinely depicted riding horseback.
Donald Trump, however, introduced a much more aggressive tone. He frequently applied derogatory nicknames to opponents, such as Marco Rubio—now Trump’s secretary of state—whom he called "Little Marco," and Jeb Bush, now retired from politics, whom he dubbed "Low Energy Jeb."
During a 2016 primary debate, he even publicly defended the size of his genitalia.
When Trump entered the Republican National Convention in 2024, speakers played James Brown's "It’s a Man’s Man’s Man’s World." He had recently survived an assassination attempt at a rally in Butler, Pennsylvania, where he stood on stage with a bloodied face, pumping his fist and telling supporters to "fight! fight! fight!"
Data from AP VoteCast showed that Trump increased his support among male voters to 55% that November, up from 51% in his 2020 race against Democrat Joe Biden.
In Michigan, the gender debate emerged after Rogers, a former Republican congressman, released a campaign commercial claiming Democrats want to permit "men in women’s sports." He criticized El-Sayed as overly liberal for the state while highlighting his own high school football background.
El-Sayed responded on social media over the weekend, writing: "Clearly your teammates didn’t vote you captain. If they did, you would have said it in the ad. Probably had that beta energy back then, too. I was captain. Football. Wrestling. Lacrosse."
Rogers pushed back in the exchange, writing: "Nothing screams ‘alpha’ quite like a 41-year-old desperately reminding everyone he was popular in high school. Looks like someone peaked in high school."
El-Sayed frequently posts videos of himself lifting weights in fitted black T-shirts, though he also shares clips of himself singing and dancing while rejecting conservative views on masculinity.
"Being a man is not about how you show up in the gym," he said in an interview with Lever News, a progressive news site. "It’s about how you show up for your family. It’s about how you show up in your community."
In Texas, famous for cowboy boots and swagger, masculinity became a focal point soon after state representative Talarico won the Democratic Senate nomination.
Republican Sen. Ted Cruz, who is not up for reelection this year, remarked on Fox News that "if you were making a list of 1,000 adjectives to describe this guy, ‘masculine’ would not be one of them" and claimed that "if a stiff breeze came by it would blow him over."
A political action committee supporting Paxton later aired an ad touching on transgender politics. It opens with a stern, heavily bearded man in a hard hat, accompanied by a voiceover stating: "This is Texas." The ad then cuts to a clip of Talarico saying there are more than two biological sexes, as the narrator adds, "This is not."
Paxton’s campaign is banking that personal attacks and their cultural associations will resonate with voters in a state that embraces the slogan, "don’t mess with Texas."
"When one party or one group says that another candidate isn’t masculine, or isn’t masculine enough, they are not really just talking about that candidate," said Joshua Blank, research director for the Texas Political Project at the University of Texas at Austin.
"It’s a way to say that this candidate is allied with groups and individuals who hold nontraditional views about the roles of men and women in society, and even the definition of male and female."
Talarico generally dismisses the taunts, arguing that they "don’t meet the needs of Texans" struggling with the costs of groceries, gas, and insurance.
Instead, he tries to reframe the debate as "about what it means to be a real man" by describing how his adoptive father, Mark Talarico, spent every Saturday mowing the lawns of both his own home and the elderly widow next door.
"He never talked about it. He just did it — because that’s what a man does," Talarico tells voters on the trail. "Call me old fashioned but a real man takes responsibility."
He then uses the narrative to highlight corruption allegations against Paxton, which Paxton denies. "Real men serve others," Talarico says. "Weak men serve themselves."

Did a goat herder's lucky $200 nugget spark a gold rush in western Kenya?
- Published
A goat herder from a remote area of western Kenya has told the BBC his discovery of a golden nugget has sparked a gold rush, overwhelming his small village over the last few weeks.
When people found out that 33-year-old Manasse Lomachar had sold his three grams of gold for 36,000 Kenyan shillings ($280; £205) several weeks ago, he believes this led to thousands of prospectors arrived in Cheporor.
And it is true that what last month was just bushland and rough grazing ground near the village is now scarred by pits, mounds of earth and makeshift mining camps.
It is not clear if was Lomachar's lucky find or other recent discoveries that sparked the excitement. But local authorities estimate that about 10,000 people arrived at the height of the rush.
Even a small amount of the precious metal can transform the futures of these men and women - from Kenya and neighbouring Uganda - many of whose precarious lives rest on an unreliable farming income.
People do sometimes pan for gold in these parts - but rarely find anything significant.
Lomachar's says his discovery came about purely by chance. While he was searching for a missing goat he encountered a group of women panning along a riverbed.
"I joined them, and that's how [the village] realised there was gold in this area," he says.
Farmer and herder Patrick Lokolia, from neighbouring Napawoi village, joined the gold rush hoping to earn some extra money to support his family.
"I have children in school, and paying school fees has been a big problem for me," he tells the BBC wearing an old Chelsea football top and standing amid the mining activity.
Eighteen-year-old Abigael Chelengat says she had never mined before coming to Cheporor from a nearby district, but arrived hoping to find enough gold to pay her school fees and help keep her younger siblings in school.
Behind her hundreds of people work side by side, hacking into the rocky ground with hoes and shovels.
Others carry the earth to a nearby seasonal river, where mostly women crouch in the murky water, washing and sifting mud and sand hoping to detect a tiny trace of the element.
Some of the more experienced miners are deep in holes excavating the earth and drilling at rocks with the same goal.
Hope is kept alive by stories of those for whom the effort has paid off - like Lomachar.
Samuel Kiarie, the deputy commissioner of West Pokot county, says he thinks the rush began after two notable discoveries.
"Young men found what appeared to be a substantial amount of gold. The following day, women made another significant find in the same area," he tells the BBC.
Kiarie explains that women have been finding small quantities of alluvial gold along the same seasonal riverbed for years, typically earning $8-$23 a week.
But the uncovering of larger quantities at the beginning of August is what caught the attention of many people.
Kiarie reckons as rumours spread, the number and size of the discoveries were exaggerated - drawing in ever larger groups of people with little or no mining experience who hoped to replicate the reported early successes.
Since the initial rush, the number of prospectors has gone down to around 2,500 as some have given up the search.
While there is little doubt that some gold has been found in the area, questions remain about the size of the deposit in the earth and its commercial potential.
"I can confirm that small-scale gold traders told us they received an average of about 100 people every day," the deputy commissioner says - though whether the finds were actually gold is not known.
Individual discoveries reportedly range from amounts worth a few hundred Kenyan shillings to one find valued at approximately 78,000 shillings ($600).
West Pokot county borders Uganda, and communities on both sides have long-standing social and family ties.
Mugisha Godfrey, an artisanal miner from Busia in eastern Uganda, travelled to Cheporor after hearing about the discovery from a friend.
He immediately set out for the village spending about 100,000 Ugandan shillings ($27) to get there.
However, the living conditions in Cheporor are not favourable, he says.
"We sleep under the trees, and when morning comes, we continue working. Sometimes we work both day and night," Godfrey tells the BBC.
So far, he has found nothing. But he is not discouraged.
"We can't return unless we find something. Only when we have found what we need can we go back home," he says.
For others, the gold rush has created opportunities without requiring them to dig.
More than 200 businesses have emerged around the site, according to local officials, selling food, water and other essentials to the village's new population.
Irene Ameja travelled from neighbouring Baringo county to cater to the crowds. She sells bottled water, soft drinks, bread, milk and other foodstuffs.
"I am hoping that when I leave, I will have made enough money to continue with my business and expand it," she says.
But the rapid growth of the settlement has also exposed the area's lack of basic services.
"This is a forest and we are in the middle of the mountains," she says. "We don't have clean water to drink or even to bathe."
For women, she adds, the challenges become greater after dark: "You have to find somewhere safe to stay because most of the people sleeping here are men."
Local officials admit the influx has placed enormous pressure on an area with little infrastructure, no piped water and limited sanitation.
Public health officials have been deployed to monitor conditions and help prevent disease outbreaks.
The authorities say they have also increased security patrols amid concerns over sexual violence and the vulnerability of women and girls at the site.
Officials are also worried that children could be drawn into mining activities as schools prepare to reopen in September.
Measures are being put in place to discourage young people from remaining at the site once the new school term begins.
Those still searching are increasingly turning to deeper excavation.
Several truckloads of material have already been transported to nearby Ortum town for processing, with the authorities awaiting the results.
Until then, the size and commercial viability of any mining remain uncertain.
For Lomachar, the answer is not to stop the mining, but to make it more organised.
He wants the government to help local miners establish safer and more effective ways of finding and extracting the gold.
"We would ask the government to help us with things like metal detectors, which could help us find out whether there are other minerals here, so that our community can develop," he says.
He points to the homes nearby as evidence of the area's poverty.
"If you look around, there are hardly any houses with iron-sheet roofs; most are just thatched houses."

'This star is for Africa' - Angélique Kidjo on making Hollywood Walk of Fame history

Five-time Grammy award winner Angélique Kidjo, who made history on Tuesday to become the first African musician to get a star on the Hollywood Walk of Fame, has told the BBC she wants to dedicate the accolade to the continent of her birth.
"This star is for all the continent of Africa. Because if I was not African, would I be here?" said the 66-year-old musical icon from Benin.
She reiterated her message, made at the ceremony in Los Angeles to mark her four-decade career, about the importance of Africans to the world of music.
"Without the blues brought by the slaves in America, there's no R&B, there's no rock and roll, there's no soul music, there's no jazz. All of it comes from Africa."

Kidjo told BBC Focus on Africa TV that Africans themselves needed to appreciate what they had given the world, and nurture talent at home.
"Let's celebrate our artists in their own right on the continent. Let's give them visibility, strength, because music creates economy," she said.
Most African artists - besides mega stars who have a global fanbase - struggle to make a living as they rarely get paid the royalties they are owed.
"We need to recognise our artists and create a system for them to make money on their continent and to participate also in creating jobs."
As her illustrious career was immortalised in Los Angeles, Kidjo became emotional - wiping away tears.
"At that moment, I'm like, dad, mum, I wish you were here with me to see [this]" the songstress explained to the BBC.
"I couldn't take the emotion. They were not here to taste the fruit of what they've created. How they have nurtured my curiosity, my love for music."
Kidjo - who has taken African sounds to global audiences, blending influences from home with funk, jazz and pop - grew up in Benin and then went to Paris aged 23, citing oppression from the country's then-communist government.
At her Walk of Fame ceremony, she was joined by other family, friends and stars such as Hollywood actors Willem Dafoe and Djimon Hounsou, who is also from Benin, and Nigerian musician Adekunle Gold.
The gathering was filled with singing and dancing in celebration of her career, which has included collaborations with big names such as Burna Boy, John Legend, Bono and Alicia Keys.
Her latest album, HOPE!!, was released earlier this year with tracks produced by Pharrell Williams, and collaborations with Ayra Starr, Quavo, Nile Rogers and Diane Warren.
Kidjo has released 18 albums in total and has been nominated for 17 Grammy awards, which she has won five times.
She also won the 2023 Polar Music Prize, and two years earlier was named as one of Time's 100 Most Influential People.
"She is without a doubt the hardest working woman in showbusiness," Dafoe said at the ceremony.
"The first time I saw Angélique perform live, I thought her music, her dancing, her commitment were incredible."
The Spider-Man star likened her energy to that of soul singer James Brown, who he called the "hardest working man in showbusiness".
"She's not only an incredible performer... songwriter and musician, but also an incredibly kind and giving person and a real deal activist."
Kidjo is a Unicef and Oxfam goodwill ambassador, and is the co-founder of the Batonga Foundation, which helps vulnerable young girls and women in Benin.
At the Los Angeles gathering she was also praised by Harvey Mason Jr, the CEO of Recording Academy - the organisation that also oversees the Grammy awards.
"She's connected cultures, she's crossed borders, she's reminded audiences everywhere that while we may come from different backgrounds, her music unites in a way that few other things can," he said.
During her interview with the BBC, the musician's phone kept ringing with those wanting to congratulate her.
"Yesterday I received the call of the president of Benin," she said.
"Today I received the call of Chris Blackwell, the founder of Island Records, the producer of Bob Marley, the maker of U2 and so on and so forth."
Kidjo explained how fundamental Blackwell, who signed her in the 1990s, had been to her success - launching her breakthrough album Logozo.
"I said to him at that moment… 'Can I do the music I want to do and keep my cultural identity without anyone imposing any other music on my shoulder?' He said… 'It's no brainer.'"
Kidjo joins Charlize Theron, a white South African actress, in representing Africa on the Walk of Fame, which comprises more than 2,800 stars.
She said she was amazed to hear a year ago that she had been nominated for a Hollywood star, telling Focus on Africa she did not believe the news given to her by her husband until she said she had seen it on the BBC.
And when asked about the significance of becoming the first African musician with a star, she replied: "Changes that last take time."

Subdivided-flat registration rate at 42.5% as ‘early bird’ phase deadline passes
Industry observers say ownership complications and low awareness have slowed landlords’ applications under Hong Kong’s new housing regulations
Property-ownership complications and low public awareness have slowed landlords’ registration of Hong Kong subdivided flats under new housing regulations, industry observers have said, after the government received only 42.5 per cent of the applications expected in the first phase.
Monday marked the deadline for the initial six-month “early bird” registration phase under the Basic Housing Unit Ordinance. Landlords who applied during this period were eligible for a waiver of HK$3,000 in certification fees per subdivided flat for each of the first three years.
The legislation came into force in March to phase out substandard subdivided flats. The government estimates that about 80,000 flats across the city could be accredited, but only about 34,000 units were registered during the first six months.
Scott Leung Man-kwong, deputy chairman of the Legislative Council’s housing panel, described the 42.5 per cent application rate as acceptable but said the HK$3,000 discount was not a significant incentive for landlords to apply early.
“For inherited properties, sometimes the verification of legal ownership could delay the application,” he told a radio show on Tuesday.
“We’ve seen cases where a son inherited a flat from his father that is already subdivided. The tenants continued to pay rent and they did not process the legal transfer of the property. But now, with the application for basic housing units, they will have to do so.”

లోక్సభలో ప్రతిపక్ష నేత రాహుల్ గాంధీకి సంబంధించిన ఒక వీడియో సోషల్ మీడియాలో వైరల్ అవుతోంది. ఈ వీడియోలో ఆయన మహిళలు, అత్యాచారాలకు సంబంధించి వివాదాస్పద వ్యాఖ్యలు చేసినట్లు ప్రచారం చేస్తున్నారు. వైరల్ వీడియోలో రాహుల్ గాంధీ, “80 శాతం అత్యాచారాలకు మహిళలే కారణం. భారతదేశంలో అత్యాచారాలు జరుగుతాయి, కానీ ‘భారత్’లో అత్యాచారాలు జరగవు.” అని చెప్పినట్లు వినిపిస్తోంది. అయితే, ఈ వీడియో నిజంగా రాహుల్ గాంధీ చేసిన వ్యాఖ్యలను చూపిస్తుందా? ఈ వైరల్ వీడియో వెనుక ఉన్న నిజమేంటో ఈ కథనంలో తెలుసుకుందాం.
క్లెయిమ్: లోక్సభలో ప్రతిపక్ష నేత రాహుల్ గాంధీ “80 శాతం అత్యాచారాలకు మహిళలే కారణం. భారతదేశంలో అత్యాచారాలు జరుగుతాయి, కానీ ‘భారత్’లో అత్యాచారాలు జరగవు” అని అంటున్న వీడియో.
ఫాక్ట్: ఈ వీడియోను ఎడిట్ చేశారు. అసలు వీడియోలో రాహుల్ గాంధీ స్వయంగా ఈ వ్యాఖ్యలు చేయలేదు. ఆర్ఎస్ఎస్ చీఫ్ మోహన్ భగవత్, మాజీ హర్యానా ముఖ్యమంత్రి మనోహర్ లాల్ ఖట్టర్ గతంలో చేసిన వివాదాస్పద వ్యాఖ్యలను ప్రస్తావిస్తూ, వారి అభిప్రాయాలను రాహుల్ గాంధీ విమర్శించారు. అయితే, వైరల్ వీడియోలో ఆయన ఎవరి వ్యాఖ్యలను ప్రస్తావిస్తున్నారో చెప్పిన భాగాన్ని తొలగించి, ఆ వ్యాఖ్యలు రాహుల్ గాంధీ స్వయంగా చేసినట్లుగా చూపించారు. కాబట్టి, ఈ పోస్టులో చేస్తున్న వాదన తప్పు.
వైరల్ వీడియోలోని కీలక ఫ్రేమ్లను ఉపయోగించి రివర్స్ ఇమేజ్ సెర్చ్ చేయగా, కాంగ్రెస్ పార్టీ అధికారిక యూట్యూబ్ ఛానల్లో 22 ఆగస్టు 2026న అప్లోడ్ చేసిన అసలు వీడియో మాకు లభించింది. అదే రోజు పుణెలో జరిగిన కాంగ్రెస్ “ఛాత్రోన్ కీ గూంజ్” కార్యక్రమానికి సంబంధించిన వీడియో ఇది. అసలు వీడియోలోని 1:00:12 టైమ్స్టాంప్ వద్ద వైరల్ క్లిప్లోని దృశ్యాలు కనిపిస్తాయి. అయితే, అసలు వీడియోలో రాహుల్ గాంధీ ఆ వ్యాఖ్యలను స్వయంగా చేయడం లేదు. ఆర్ఎస్ఎస్ చీఫ్ మోహన్ భగవత్, మాజీ హర్యానా ముఖ్యమంత్రి మనోహర్ లాల్ ఖట్టర్ గతంలో చేసిన వ్యాఖ్యలను ఆయన ప్రస్తావించాడు. అత్యాచారాలు “ఇండియా”లో జరుగుతాయి కానీ “భారత్”లో జరగవని మోహన్ భగవత్ చెప్పారని, 80 శాతం అత్యాచారాలకు మహిళలే కారణమని మనోహర్ లాల్ ఖట్టర్ వ్యాఖ్యానించారని రాహుల్ గాంధీ పేర్కొన్నారు. అనంతరం, ఇలాంటి వ్యాఖ్యలు తాము వ్యతిరేకిస్తున్నానని ఆయన తెలిపారు.
మోహన్ భగవత్, మనోహర్ లాల్ ఖట్టర్ పేర్లను ప్రస్తావించిన భాగాన్ని వీడియో నుంచి తొలగించారు. ఆ వ్యాఖ్యలను రాహుల్ గాంధీ స్వయంగా చేసినట్లుగా కనిపించేలా వైరల్ వీడియోను రూపొందించారు. దీంతో వైరల్ వీడియోను ఎడిట్ చేసినట్లు స్పష్టమవుతోంది.
తదుపరి, గూగుల్లో కీవర్డ్ సెర్చ్ చేయగా (ఇక్కడ, ఇక్కడ) ఉన్న వీడియోలు లభించాయి. వీటి ప్రకారం, 4 జనవరి 2013న ఆర్ఎస్ఎస్ చీఫ్ మోహన్ భగవత్ అసోంలోని సిల్చర్లో పర్యటించిన సమయంలో అత్యాచార ఘటనలపై వివాదాస్పద వ్యాఖ్యలు చేశారు. “ఇండియా”లో ఇలాంటి నేరాలు ఎక్కువగా జరుగుతాయని, “భారత్”లో తక్కువగా జరుగుతాయని ఆయన చెప్పినట్లు వార్తలు వచ్చాయి. ఈ వ్యాఖ్యలు అప్పట్లో వివాదానికి దారితీశాయి. తర్వాత అప్పటి ఆర్ఎస్ఎస్ అధికార ప్రతినిధి రామ్ మాధవ్ వివరణ ఇచ్చారు. మహిళలను గౌరవించే భారతీయ సంప్రదాయాల గురించి మోహన్ భగవత్ మాట్లాడారని, ఈ విలువలకు దూరమైనవారు నేరాలకు పాల్పడే అవకాశం ఉందని ఆయన చెప్పినట్లు రామ్ మాధవ్ వివరించారు.
అదేవిధంగా, 2018 నవంబర్లో అప్పటి హర్యానా ముఖ్యమంత్రి మనోహర్ లాల్ ఖట్టర్ అత్యాచారం, వేధింపుల ఘటనలపై వివాదాస్పద వ్యాఖ్యలు చేశారు (ఇక్కడ, ఇక్కడ). వార్తా కథనాల్లో ఈ వ్యాఖ్యలకు సంబంధించిన వివరాలు ఉన్నాయి. అత్యాచారం, వేధింపుల ఘటనల్లో 80–90 శాతం వరకు ఒకరికొకరు తెలిసిన వ్యక్తులే ఉంటారని ఖట్టర్ అన్నారు. అలాగే, కొన్నిసార్లు చాలా కాలంగా సంబంధంలో ఉన్న వ్యక్తుల మధ్య వివాదాలు తలెత్తిన తర్వాత ఇలాంటి ఘటనలు జరుగుతున్నాయని ఆయన సూచించారు.
చివరిగా, అత్యాచారం, మహిళలపై రాహుల్ గాంధీ వివాదాస్పద వ్యాఖ్యలు చేసినట్లు చూపిస్తున్న ఈ వైరల్ వీడియో ఎడిట్ చేసినది.

About 1,600 federal employees who work at the General Services Administration have been forced to relocate from their office on F Street in Washington, DC, to the Theodore Roosevelt Federal Building, roughly two blocks away. Workers say the new building, which also houses staff from the Office of Personnel Management has mice, a caved-in bathroom ceiling, and drinking water that needs to be run for five to 10 seconds before it is clear.
The federal workforce has been rocked by changes made by Elon Musk’s so-called Department of Government Efficiency (DOGE) since January 2025. DOGE effectively fired tens of thousands of workers and forced those who remained to commit to in-person schedules and, in some cases, zero-based budgeting. GSA, the agency in charge of the federal government’s IT services and real estate assets, was hit early by DOGE, and in addition to major workforce cuts also rolled out plans to sell hundreds of federal office buildings. A year after the cuts, GSA announced it planned to hire about 400 workers.
“We’ve all been through a lot, but this really made me finally understand that they don’t care about us,” says one GSA employee who asked to remain anonymous, as they aren’t authorized to speak to the press. “We’re left wondering what else is going to collapse or break—do we need to look at the ceiling before going to the bathroom? Can we actually trust the water is safe to drink?”
Photos obtained by WIRED show a toilet in a men’s room on the third floor covered in debris from the ceiling, a gaping hole in said ceiling, and a dead mouse caught in a trap. Workers said the mouse wasn’t “entirely shocking” since many federal buildings allegedly have vermin, but the ceiling pushed them over the edge. An additional sign in the office recommends workers filling up water bottles to “run the water without your bottle for 5-10 seconds and wait for the water to run clear.”
GSA and OPM did not immediately respond to a request for comment.
GSA leadership, including administrator Ed Forst, has told employees they should expect to work in the OPM building—which is slated for “accelerated disposition,” or a quick building sale—until December 2028. Their prior building, located at 1800 F Street, is undergoing extensive renovations. The initiative is part of a “government-wide effort to reduce underutilized space and fortify the federal real estate footprint,” according to a GSA press release.
While Musk himself has stepped back from his public role in the Trump administration, DOGE affiliates have continued working in government, embracing austerity measures and AI initiatives. Others have gone back to the private sector, working in AI, data centers, and manufacturing.

MONTEREY, Calif.—Last week, we brought news of the Bentley Torcal, a new electric vehicle that the luxury automaker has been cooking up at its HQ in Crewe, England. The company wants to attract new customers with its first battery EV, part of a plan to make sustainability as much a part of the brand’s character as its high-end fit and finish. W12 engines have given way to V8 plug-in hybrid power, and the new Continental GT is all the better for it.

Or all-wheel drive—something that has been a characteristic of every new road-going Bentley since the turn of the century. That would certainly cut the curb weight. So, too, would leaving out the rear seats. That sort of idea leads down a well-trodden path for some OEMs, and Porsche in particular is famous for making stripped-out road cars inspired by its race cars and making money from them, too.

Then again, Bentley still knows a thing or two about racing, most recently conquering the challenging and prestigious Bathurst 12 Hours race in 2020 with a GT3 version of the Continental GT3. And like that race car, its new Supersports settles for the relative simplicity of a 4.0 L twin-turbo V8 under the hood, powering just the rear wheels. There’s even more extreme aero than you expect to see on a road-legal car with a flying B badge, too.
The lightest Bentley since 1941
The engine is actually a new variant of Bentley’s 4.0 L V8, with a strengthened engine block, new cylinder heads, and larger turbos. There’s also a dual-mass flywheel, but it remains wet-sumped. With 657 hp (490 kW) and 590 lb-ft (800 Nm), the Supersports isn’t the most powerful Bentley ever made, but it may be the most driver-focused. Both front and rear axles feature 48 V active anti-roll bars that can react in a third of a second, applying up to 960 lb-ft (1,300 Nm) of reaction torque to keep the car flat. The twin-valve dampers and air suspension have been recalibrated in Touring, Bentley, and Sport modes. And on the optional Pirelli Trofeo RS tires, it will corner at 1.3 Gs.
The Supersports certainly looks the part as it descends into that most famous of Laguna Seca’s corners (which is being renamed the “Zanardi Corkscrew” next weekend). You don’t really notice the carbon-fiber roof that helps keep the center of gravity low, but you do see the aerodynamic appendages—a front splitter, winglets ahead and aft of the wheels, a rather large and curvaceous carbon-fiber spoiler at the rear together with a diffuser down below.
The bits are functional—Bentley told us it generates at least 661 lbs (300 kg) more downforce than the Continental GT Speed we reviewed last year and that the car’s aero balance has been tuned to shift rearward as speed rises (and downforce increases) from a 54:46 starting point.

From inside the cockpit, it feels the part, too. Despite the acres of carbon-fiber on the dash, the pair of sports seats are comfortable and offer plenty of electric adjustment, and they hold you in place even as you throw the car over a crest or down into the apex of the Corkscrew. Even taking some curb isn’t a problem. With a curb weight of “less than 4,407 lbs (1,999 kg),” the lightest Bentley in 85 years is still a pretty substantial thing, but it minded not being asked to ride over the red-and-white serrations, soaking up plenty of intrusion before it could reach the cabin.
Once the Trofeo RS tires are warm, there’s plenty of front grip, and as you apply power, the car’s electronic limited-slip differential helps tighten your line. The 4.1 degrees of rear steering also do their part to aid agility in the slower corners. And since the brakes are unchanged from the hybrid Continental GT, they’re more than up to the job of slowing down a car that weighs 1,100 lbs (500 kg) less.
The Supersports isn’t a difficult car to drive, and it’s easy enough to catch should it break loose—at least with the suite of traction and stability control systems still active. The two cars Bentley brought to Laguna Seca are the only two that have been built so far, and sullying either with a trip through the gravel or, worse yet, into a tire barrier, was definitely not on the agenda.

Shivraj reviews watershed scheme, calls for faster implementation to achieve drought-free India
New Delhi, Rural Development Minister Shivraj Singh Chouhan on Monday reviewed the progress of the watershed development component of the Pradhan Mantri Krishi Sinchayee Yojana and called on states to expedite projects and ensure measurable outcomes on the ground.
Chouhan said watershed development is an important tool in achieving the goal of a "drought-free India" for a developed India, according to a statement issued by the Rural Development Ministry.
"Watershed development is not merely a programme to create water structures; its real objective is to bring water to farms, increase land productivity and strengthen farmers' incomes and livelihoods," he said.
Under WDC-PMKSY 2.0, 1,220 projects covering 52.93 lakh hectares have so far been sanctioned at a total cost of ₹12,404 crore, including a central share of ₹8,134 crore. Of the central share, ₹6,955.75 crore, or 85 per cent, has been released, the ministry said.
Chouhan said the impact of watershed interventions was visible in increased cropping intensity, with nearly 1.40 lakh hectares of land that previously supported barely one crop now producing two crops and, in several places, three crops.
The expansion of horticulture, vegetable cultivation and high-value crops has also contributed to improved livelihoods, he said.
The programme has resulted in the construction and revival of 1.24 lakh water-harvesting structures, including check dams, nala bunds, percolation tanks, village and farm ponds, field bunding, trenches and reservoirs, according to the ministry.
These structures have helped conserve rainwater locally, recharge groundwater and improve water availability for agriculture, it said.
The interventions have provided protective irrigation to an additional 3.08 lakh hectares, helping farmers in rain-fed areas protect crops during periods of low rainfall or drought, the ministry said.
As many as 28.50 lakh farmers have benefited from the programme so far, while afforestation, horticulture and plantation activities have been undertaken across 1.45 lakh hectares. The programme has also generated 2.85 crore person-days of employment, it said.
Chouhan urged states and implementing agencies to adopt transparent, technology-enabled, performance-based and people-centric approaches and complete projects within the stipulated timelines.
He said watershed projects should not be assessed merely on the basis of expenditure, but on actual improvements in land development, water availability, irrigation, cropping intensity, land productivity and farmers' livelihoods.
Chouhan also said the government had sought to turn watershed development into a people's movement through the 'Watershed Yatra' and 'Watershed Mahotsav'.
He called for taking watershed development forward not merely as a scheme but as a national campaign for water and land security, agricultural security and rural prosperity.

A purported statement by Cockroach Janta Party (CJP) founder Abhijeet Dipke is circulating on social media. In the viral post, Dipke is quoted as saying, “We are demanding responsibility, not resignation from the chief minister (of Jharkhand), so that problems don’t arise regarding papers in the future.”
The apparent statement was shared by a verified Instagram handle named ‘indians’ on August 14. The post received has over 74,600 reactions till date. The page has around 9 million followers. (Archive)
The caption of the post reads:
“… Dipke said he does not want Soren to resign, but wants accountability to ensure such incidents do not happen again. His stand has sparked questions among citizens over why accountability is being sought instead of resignation in this case, while Dharmendra Pradhan faced demands to resign.”
After Union education minister Dharmendra Pradhan resigned following CJP’s Delhi protests, a similar protest erupted in Ranchi over alleged paper leaks and irregularities in Jharkhand’s government recruitment exams. Protesters, including students and activists, demanded chief minister Hemant Soren’s resignation.
It was against this backdrop that the quote attributed to CJP founder Abhijeet Dipke went viral. The viral posts reinforce the key BJP charge that CJP was comparatively restrained when allegations of exam irregularities emerged in Opposition-ruled states, particularly Jharkhand. BJP leaders have used this argument to accuse the group of selective outrage. In comments to the above Instagram post, many users replied saying Dipke’s stance showed his ‘hypocrisy’ or ‘double standard’.
The same quotation was also shared by Facebook pages named The Youth – India and Saale Dost Ko Thanks Bolta hai. The follower counts of the two pages are 141,000 and 4.9 million, respectively.
Fact Check
To find more on the purported statement by Dipke, we first went through his X timeline, since the CJP founder regularly posts about his media interactions and public statements on his X account. We could not find any post corroborating the viral claim.
We, however, found a post from August 2 where Dipke is speaking to the protesting students in Jharkhand on a video call. “The CJP stands with all the students in Jharkhand and support their demands,” he wrote. He makes the same point in the video as well.
Spoke to the students who are protesting in Jharkhand over irregularities in JPSC and JSSC recruitment exams.
The CJP stands with all the students in Jharkhand and support their demands. pic.twitter.com/lLSRhFVpv1
— Abhijeet Dipke (@abhijeet_dipke) August 2, 2026
Next, we performed a keyword search on Google, looking for news reports on the said statement. We used the keyword combination: “Abhijeet Dipke Jharkhand Hemant Soren resignation”.
We could not find a single report which mentioned that Dipke had said they were only seeking accountability and responsibility, and not the Jharkhand chief minister’s resignation. Instead, we found several reports on the CJP and its founder supporting the Jharkhand students’ stir. For instance, this report in The Hindu states that Abhijeet Dipke “was in touch with the protesters and supported their demands, and they will go to Ranchi to express solidarity.” Similar reports were carried by outlets like The Print and The Times of India.
None of the articles mentioned anything similar to what the purported quote claims.
We also found an ANI post containing Dipke’s detailed response to the Jharkhand situation. He says, “… We offer our full support. Our delegation has visited the area, and our people are distributing food there. We stand firmly with them and support all their demands… I, too, intend to go… Although, I am currently dealing with some health issues…”
#WATCH | Chhatrapati Sambhaji Nagar, Maharashtra | On students’ protest in Jharkhand, Cockroach Janta Party (CJP) Founder Abhijeet Dipke says, “We offer our full support. Our delegation has visited the area, and our people are distributing food there. We stand firmly with them… pic.twitter.com/R3XbAv5jaT
— ANI (@ANI) August 7, 2026
In another interview with PTI, Dipke said CJP would support demands for educational reforms, irrespective of which state was in question and which party was in power.
Alt News then reached out to Abhijeet Dipke and asked him whether he had made the statement shown in the viral posts. Dipke replied: “Never said this. These people (the social media pages) are running anything they want.”
To sum up, the viral post quoting Abhijeet Dipke as saying that they were seeking accountability but not Jharkhand CM Hemant Soren’s resignation is baseless. There is no credible evidence of the CJP founder having made such a statement. Dipke himself refuted the claim.

Greater awareness is needed to counter misinformation on social media and unproven products marketed for preventing or controlling myopia, experts said at a webinar organised by The Hindu on Sunday (August 30, 2026).
At the webinar titled ‘Excess Screentime: Is it Harming Children’s Eyes?’, Vasumathy Vedantham, ophthalmologist, vitreoretinal surgeon and paediatric retina specialist, Radhatri Nethralaya, and Vasudha Kemmanu, consultant paediatric ophthalmologist and public eye health specialist, Narayana Nethralaya, discussed the growing concern over myopia and refractive errors among children.
Dr. Vedantham highlighted the need for parents to be cautious about health information circulating on social media. She said misinformation and claims around various products and interventions for eye health were common online, and stressed that parents should rely on evidence-based medical advice rather than unverified products or remedies.
Dr. Kemmanu emphasised the importance of adequate time outdoors for children, noting that reduced outdoor exposure was a concern amid rising myopia. She said governments should introduce stronger public health measures to promote outdoor time among children and address the growing burden of myopia.
She said governments and schools needed to be part of efforts to create environments that support children’s eye health.
The experts also discussed the importance of regular eye screening, recognising early signs of vision problems and seeking timely evaluation, particularly when children develop difficulty seeing distant objects or show changes in their visual behaviour.
The session was moderated by Athira Elssa Johnson, Senior Reporter, The Hindu.

Japan Inc is betting big on India as China risks deepen
- Published
India's commerce minister Piyush Goyal led the country's largest-ever business delegation to Japan last week in a bid to expand trade and investment ties between the two countries. His visit came as Japan's deepening push into Asia's third largest economy has become increasingly more apparent.
If you visit a shopping mall or a high street in Mumbai, Delhi or Bengaluru, it's hard to miss the growing number of Japanese consumer brands that have set up shop across India.
Apparel giants Uniqlo and Muji and premium sneakers company Onitsuka Tiger have been around for a while, but are rapidly expanding.
Niche players are also here - Nitori, a Japanese furniture maker, entered the market recently, while convenience store chain Lawson, external is on its way, with a plan to reportedly open 10,000 stores by 2050 in India, starting with Mumbai.
It's not just retail. At a time when foreign lenders have been exiting their Indian bank portfolios, Japanese banks are aggressively bidding for Indian financial assets.
MUFG Bank - Japan's largest bank - closed a deal to buy 20% of Indian shadow lender Shriram Finance for $4.4bn last year in what was the biggest ever foreign investment in India's financial sector.
Last year also saw Sumitomo Mitsui Banking Corporation (SMBC) becoming the largest shareholder in India's Yes Bank with a 24.22% stake.
Japan Inc is now the largest contributor to India's booming ecosystem of global capability centres (GCCs) in the Asia Pacific.
More than 100 Japanese firms operate these GCCs in the country, according to a recent Deloitte report, external. GCCs are offshore innovation hubs of multinationals that perform business critical functions such as R&D, corporate strategy and artificial intelligence development among a plethora of other key jobs.
"Japanese companies are having to look to India for growth. With the local population declining for the past 16-17 years there isn't just a slowdown in domestic demand, but a permanent shrinking of the market," Vipul Nath Jindal, Founder of Next Bharat Ventures, an impact fund backed by Suzuki Motor Corporation, which recently announced a $200mn fund in India, told the BBC.
At the same time, Japan's traditional markets for expansion have become increasingly less attractive, he says.
"Investment into China has fallen sharply amid geopolitical tensions and changing economic dynamics, the US market is more challenging because of tariffs and domestic competition, and the market size of other Southeast Asian economies is limited."
Against this backdrop, India has become a natural target market for Japanese companies to drive long-term business growth.
Economic ties between the countries gathered pace at a government-to-government level when they signed an agreement to liberalise trade nearly a decade-and-a-half ago.
After Prime Minister Narendra Modi came to power in 2014, he elevated the relationship to a "special strategic and global partnership", setting a target of doubling the number of Japanese companies in India and launching marquee projects like India's first bullet train between Mumbai and Ahmedabad, built using Japanese Shinkansen technology.
But now, it is Japanese private firms that are driving business expansion in this latest investment up-cycle.
At a landmark summit in July held during Japanese Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi's first official visit to Delhi, Japanese companies announced $12.5bn in investments through some 120 agreements in sectors ranging from semiconductors to green energy. And Goyal has said , externalJapan could prematurely meet its target of investing 10 trillion yen in the country.
Beyond the large corporations, several Japanese small and medium-sized companies (SMEs) are also actively looking at tapping the Indian market, says Jindal.
Hamamatsu City - where companies like Suzuki, Honda and Yamaha were founded and which has one of the highest concentrations of manufacturing SMEs in Japan - recently set up the Hamamatsu India Committee to explore how the city's small companies could expand into India.
The rising interest in India has accompanied a fall in net Japanese investment in China which, as Toshiro Nishizaewa of the University of Tokyo wrote recently, external, is a reflection of "Japanese firms' autonomous market diversification strategies - a commercially driven reallocation of capital rather than a policymaker-led geopolitical shift from China to India".
But Japanese firms aren't abandoning China en masse. What they are doing is "reducing concentration risk after several years of supply chain disruptions and geopolitical tensions", Shruti Pandalai, India Chair at the Sydney-based Lowy Institute think tank, told the BBC.
India acts as a hedge against China-related risks, but there is also a growing overlap between Tokyo's economic security priorities and Delhi's manufacturing ambitions, which has strengthened the relationship despite significant political turnover in Tokyo, she says.
"With each successive government the targets have risen rather than fallen. That suggests the relationship has moved beyond leader-level diplomacy and become embedded in bureaucratic, corporate and strategic planning on both sides."
For Delhi, which is starved of foreign investment, the Japanese money comes at a crucial time.
India's burgeoning trade deficit with China has been a matter of grave concern and closer Japan-India cooperation could gradually reduce China's leverage in areas such as critical minerals and advanced manufacturing over the longer term, according to Pandalai.
But challenges to expanding the full scope of this relationship are many, say experts.
"Japan remains deeply integrated into Chinese manufacturing networks, while India's engagement is more uneven but still significant in key sectors," writes Pratnashree Basu from the Observer Research Foundation for the online portal Scroll, external.
"Economic interdependence, in this sense, constrains the scope for coordinated measures as these would impose significant commercial costs or provoke direct economic retaliation from China."
Also, India remains a tough country to do business.
Tax uncertainties, bureaucratic red tape, delays in land and environmental approvals are all long-documented challenges for foreign investors, including the Japanese.
An ex-Japanese minister recently publicly blamed the government in Delhi for delays in the bullet train project, saying India kept "pushing its own self interest" and "flipping on promises" - criticism which the Indian government immediately rebuffed, external.
Chinese state media, external was quick to pick up on the "rifts", using the incident as an example to highlight the gaps in India's ability to enforce contracts.
It underscores why, even as it seals a raft of big-ticket economic and defence agreements, Delhi will need to work doubly hard to ensure Japanese investment momentum isn't disrupted - especially given its growing struggle to attract sustained foreign capital from elsewhere.

Until recently, Natalie Harp was an omnipresent but low-profile aide to President Donald Trump: always there, but rarely part of the story herself. That changed abruptly earlier this month, when Sen. Jon Ossoff (D-GA), who is currently running for reelection, name-dropped her in a speech.
The presidential contender successfully trolling Trump’s White House
How Georgia Sen. Jon Ossoff became “the nation’s assignment editor.”
Trump “doesn’t want to do the job. He wants to build his ballroom and travel with Natalie on their apparently defenseless flying palace gifted by the Emir of Qatar,” Ossoff told supporters at a rally.
The line was a reference to reporting on Trump’s catering-cart maneuver as he was flying back from Turkey in July; Harp and other Trump aides joined the president on an alternate plane by way of a catering cart, while Secretary of State Marco Rubio was left behind on Air Force One.
The “Natalie” jab from Ossoff quickly took on a life of its own, spurred by a furious response from the Trump White House and right-wing media. Somewhat lost in the flurry of attention on Harp was Ossoff himself — but Greg Bluestein, chief political reporter for the Atlanta Journal-Constitution and co-host of the Politically Georgia podcast, told Today, Explained that the remark was “by design.”
Bluestein spoke with Today, Explained co-host Sean Rameswaram about Ossoff’s disciplined, savvy messaging strategy, his political rise, and why his rhetorical jabs at Trump are fueling speculation about an Ossoff 2028 presidential run.
Below is an excerpt of their conversation, edited for length and clarity. There’s much more in the full podcast, so listen to Today, Explained wherever you get podcasts, including Apple Podcasts, Pandora, and Spotify.
It’s time on this show, Greg, that we remind people who Jon Ossoff is. I’m told that is a job with which you can help.
I go way back with Sen. Ossoff. The first time I met him, or at least I talked to him, was way back in early 2017 where I got a call out of the blue from a name, a number I didn’t recognize, and the voice on the line said, “Hi, I’m Jon Ossoff and I’m running for US House, this special election.” And I said, “Well, welcome to the show. There’s about 17 other candidates already in the race.”
And he goes, “Well, I’ve got something they don’t. I have John Lewis’s endorsement, and I have about $250,000 in cash commitments.” So I was like, “Okay.”
It still was an uphill battle because we’re talking about a deep red Republican seat in the northern suburbs of Atlanta at a time when all those suburban seats were still Republican. So I said, “Okay, good luck, sir.”
But lo and behold, he became a national figure in that loss.
So you’ve been covering Sen. Ossoff just about as long as anybody. At any point over the course of that almost-decade, did you expect “Natalie” from him?
No. I mean, look, you expect him to be really, really careful and calculated about what he says. Even back then, he rarely uttered an imprecise statement. There have been times where folks have caught him off-message, but it’s been very, very rare even at the beginning of his political career, certainly now.
When he uttered the “Natalie” line that sparked a thousand thought pieces and national takes and all that, that was done by design.
Tell us a bit about his backstory for people who have forgotten who Jon Ossoff is.
When I first got that call in early 2017, I had no idea who he was. Little did I know he’d become a national figure that we’d be talking about in the context of a presidential campaign not even a decade later.
He’s a former documentarian, a former intern of the legendary Georgia Congressman John Lewis, whose parents, especially his mom, were involved in Democratic politics in Georgia, but definitely not household names — definitely not a known quantity when he called me all those years ago to say “I’m running.”
Ossoff came within a whisker of an outright win, which would’ve been a huge, monumental upset. But in the process, he showed that Democrats have a path with suburban voters that long voted Republican in the Trump era. He started with the sort of campaign slogan of “Make Trump Furious.”
He was leaning into the Democratic activism, but then within weeks shifted his message toward a more friendly, more mainstream argument about bringing jobs to the district, bringing more tech-savvy investment to the district.
When he announced for US Senate against David Perdue, very few people gave him a shot when he got in the race. But that race ended with this epic double-header runoff because Rev. Raphael Warnock was also in the race against [Sen.] Kelly Loeffler. Democrats hadn’t won in Georgia in decades. So it was an epic election and a real nail-biter to the end.
Ossoff becomes the first Jewish US senator in Georgia history, Warnock becomes the first Black US senator in Georgia history, and together they flip control of the Senate and allow Joe Biden to to actually implement some of his broad-ranging agenda those first two years that they were in office.
It makes a lot of noise when Ossoff helps flip the US Senate along with Warnock. And he’s making a lot of noise now with “Natalie.” But I can’t say that I feel like he’s made a lot of noise in the intervening six years. What’s he been like as a senator?
That’s by design. It’s only been really recently where he’s been very willing to go on the national cable shows, to talk to national reporters more, to do a lot of the things that you see other nationally prominent Democratic figures do much more regularly.
We both know there are folks in Washington who love going to the White House Correspondents’ Dinner and they love going to this or that luncheon or this or that dinner. Sen. Ossoff is much more likely to quietly go home and spend time with his two kids.
I’m not just saying that because that’s the senator I know. He is much more reserved and guarded about his private life and will bend over backwards to figure out ways to get back to Georgia — even when there are important votes, [he’ll] find ways after those votes to get back for events with his kids and that kind of thing.
It feels a little contrary to think about this guy who keeps a low profile, who wants to go back home to Georgia to be with his family, who doesn’t want the limelight, because as you’ve already mentioned, he isn’t just running for reelection in the Senate right now. Everyone seems to believe that he’s running for president.
I’m going to go out on a limb saying that I believe him when he said publicly — and privately too — to folks all over the spectrum, media folks and activists and supporters and you name it, that he is focused on this election and he’s not running for president.
If someone like Sen. Ossoff wins by a huge margin over Mike Collins in an important battleground state that is tilted both ways the last decade, the chatter will not stop. It’ll only get louder.
[He is] someone who is adept at making the arguments that so many core Democratic voters want to hear about President Trump, but at the same time can win over swing voters like he has in 2021. And he’s already seeming like he’s certainly making that outreach to them in 2026.
Do you think that if he does end up there, we’ll look back at Nataliegate as a big moment for him where it was just clear that this guy had the stuff? Or does this feel like, a week and a half out or whatever it is now, that it’s already fading into the background?
The biggest takeaway from that to me was how — and I think Jonathan Martin from Politico was the first to say it — Ossoff was essentially the nation’s assignment editor because it spurred countless stories for the next week and a half about who Natalie Harp is.
It was Ossoff who showed that he has this extraordinary staying power in the media. These rallies — he doesn’t hold them every day or every week. These are like once every month or so rallies.
The stagecraft is impressive. He’s got these multi-camera shots that are immediately farmed out to all these social media accounts who amplify them. It’s very, very impressive how he pulls this off. And they’ve become these sort of national spectacles that have inevitably given rise to more ruminations about whether he’ll run for president or not, but also of course boost his campaign itself.
That to me was one of the takeaways — that he has this impressive grip on not only what the media’s covering, but triggering them to cover even more of it.

The purported Trump post read as follows:
"The National September 11 Memorial and Museum commission decided I'm not allowed to speak at the remembrance. Imagine that? A native new Yorker. The greatest president in history. We're looking into shutting them down permanently, remove the memorial and building a statue of me as tall as the World Trade Center. Not to brag or anything, but I single handedly saved 500 thousand people in those burning buildings. I ran 110 floors at least 50 times within 30 minutes pulling people out of tight spaces. I almost died." DJT
According to a reverse image search of the supposed Trump post screenshot, users primarily shared the image on Facebook. It also appeared on the 9GAG meme website.
Snopes readers emailed us to investigate the alleged screenshot's legitimacy, asking, for example, "I believe the fact that he won't attend is true, but is this X post for real?"
To investigate the rumor, we first checked Trump's Truth Social page and found no such post. We then searched on DuckDuckGo, Google and Yahoo for reports about the supposed post possibly being shared then deleted. If Trump had falsely posted he saved 500,000 people and mentioned plans of building a massive statue after removing the memorial and museum, journalists with reputable news outlets, such as The Associated Press or The New York Times, would have widely reported on it, and our search inquiries would have uncovered such evidence. We found no such articles.
While some Facebook commenters questioned whether the post was real, many others recognized the image as fabricated humor, specifically calling it "satire."
In sum, the purported Trump Truth Social post screenshot's fake nature and extremely outlandish, false claims, suggested the image originated as satire. We will update this article if we locate the origin of the image.
Trump reportedly not going to NY ceremony
The story spread in the days before the 25th anniversary of the Sept. 11, 2001, terrorist attacks, which killed nearly 3,000 people. Ahead of that anniversary, Trump and the White House disputed a New York Times report alleging he decided against attending the New York remembrance because he couldn't speak at the event. The reporting cited three anonymous sources "with knowledge of the events." We did not locate evidence that might conclusively confirm or debunk that claim.
A spokesperson for the 9/11 Memorial & Museum previously told Snopes that the organization has historically "intentionally worked to keep the commemoration free of politics because remembering those we lost on 9/11 should never be a partisan issue," and that politicians are not to deliver remarks and must "remain in a designated area."
In an authentic post on Aug. 28, Trump posted (archived) an attack on Times journalist Maggie Haberman, one of several reporters who worked on the Times' story, calling her "Maggot Hagerman" and writing, "I would love not to speak, because I'm speaking all the time, and this is a day to remember the victims, and their beautiful family members."
Trump's post also said he plans to attend the remembrance at the Pentagon.
Via email, White House spokesperson Anna Kelly told Snopes of Trump's plans:
As a proud New Yorker, President Trump has spoken about his own experiences watching the horrific events of September 11, 2001. On the 25th anniversary of this tragic day, the President will remember those who were killed at the hands of evil terrorists, honor their loved ones, and pay tribute to the brave first responders who put their lives on the line to rescue their fellow Americans.
The White House also said Vice President JD Vance plans to travel to New York, as well as that all three 9/11 sites, including Shanksville, Pennsylvania, will be represented with administration officials in attendance.

Somali piracy surges as the impact of the US-Iran war ripples outwards
- Published
A surge in piracy near Somalia has increased threats to shipping already under pressure from maritime blockades and conflict due to the US war with Iran.
Two cargo vessels were seized in the Gulf of Aden within four days last week, rising to at least 13 the number of ships attacked since the start of the year and triggering unprecedented drone strikes against the pirates.
It is the biggest escalation in hijackings in more than a decade, renewing concern about security in this region vital to international trade.
"Piracy is always a crime of opportunity," says Omar Mahmood, a senior Somalia analyst for the International Crisis Group (ICG), "and right now the pirates see an opportunity."
That opportunity comes from the impact of the war on regional waterways further north.
Iran and the US continue to battle over control of the strategic Strait of Hormuz.
And Tehran's Houthi allies in Yemen have imposed a targeted blockade in the Bab al-Mandab Strait, which controls access to the Red Sea. This is focused on a dispute with Saudi Arabia but heightens insecurity for international shipping.
"I guess the pirates believe that with those two external events in Hormuz and Bab al-Mandab, they believe that the international forces will be dedicated to those crises instead of looking for pirates," says Vice-Admiral Ignacio Villanueva Serrano, operation commander for the European Union's naval force that protects shipping off Somalia's coast.
Among the latest vessels hijacked by the pirates was a Cameroon-flagged ship, the MV Lutuf, which was attacked off the coast of Somalia's semi-autonomous Puntland region on 17 August. A few days later pirates boarded an oil products tanker, the Eritrean-flagged MT Sibu 1, in waters near Yemen, on the other side of the Gulf.
The capture of the Lutuf has triggered unexpected consequences.
Thirteen men allegedly belonging to a network that supplies the pirates on the ship have been killed in two drone strikes since 18 August. No one has said they are behind the attacks, but local officials blamed them on Turkey, saying the vessel was carrying Turkish weapons.
The Lutuf is now among six vessels being held for demands of millions of dollars in ransom, four of which are anchored near the fishing town of Bander Beyla known as a hotbed for piracy, the BBC has learned.
That is nowhere near the peak levels of hijackings 15 years ago that cost the global economy billions of dollars. In 2011 Somali pirates carried out more than 200 attacks and held hundreds of crew members hostage.
A co-ordinated international naval response together with private security on commercial ships successfully drove down the scourge and contained a flare-up in 2023 and 2024.
But experts stress that while the pirate networks were suppressed, they remained intact, given the failure to address the poor economic and security conditions in Somalia that feed them.
Currently the resurgence is fuelled locally by anger over foreign trawlers which overfish in Somali waters, damaging the fishing industry that sustains communities in Puntland.
And there are more targets available now with a potentially bigger payload.
The regional maritime insecurity has driven some ships closer to the Somali coast as they divert south to avoid the conflict further north. Given the high price of oil, hijacking a tanker is more lucrative.
"You have that combined effect of less naval patrolling but more commercial shipping in these waters," according to the analyst Mahmood, "and that signals an opportunity.
"And once you've had a successful attack, I think that spurs other units to do copycat type incidents as well."
He and other researchers suspect there may be collaboration between the Somali pirates and Yemenis after several vessels were seized near Yemen's coast.
But Mahmood says these would more likely be criminal elements than Iran's Houthi allies, especially as one of the ships seized last week, the MT Sibu 1, allegedly belonged to an Iranian "shadow fleet" used to transport petroleum products trying to dodge US sanctions.
"I don't see something specifically Iran-directed," he says.
Turkey, however, reportedly has a stake in the latest hijackings.
Puntland security sources and a Somali government official have told the BBC that the Lutuf was carrying weapons bound for a Turkish military training facility in the Somali capital, Mogadishu. Ankara has an agreement with Somalia to strengthen its maritime security, as part of a wider defence and economic partnership.
The security sources say six international warships are now in the seas close to the Lutuf - two from Turkey and one each from Spain, Denmark, the US and India, something the BBC has not been able to independently verify.
"There is military equipment on the [hijacked] ship meant for Turkey's operations in Somalia," the Somali government official said, speaking on condition of anonymity, adding that the cargo included satellite equipment for a space station that Ankara is building north of the capital.
He alleged that Turkey had carried out the second drone strike that killed nine armed men on Sunday.
"The men who were killed were criminals and I don't have sympathy for them," he said, "but taking it to that level is escalating the situation even more."
Turkey's defence ministry has stated that its forces are providing "necessary support" to Somali authorities regarding the incident involving a hijacked vessel in Somali territorial waters, within the framework of their security agreement. But it stopped short of addressing the accusations that Turkey had carried out deadly drone strikes.
Publicly the government in Mogadishu has said only that it is aware of the operations against pirate groups and will take measures to address them.
Puntland authorities have been more outspoken.
Speaking to the BBC's Somali Service, Deputy Minister of Security Abdirahman Yusuf said his administration had evidence that Turkey was responsible for the attacks, citing information about Turkish activity around the vessel and along the Puntland coast.
The BBC has not independently verified his allegations.
The security ministry also issued a statement expressing opposition to "bombings by international warships targeting civilians" that "undermined co-operation… in combatting piracy", and demanded an immediate explanation for why they were carried out.
Puntland is wary of Turkey's close military relationship with the Somali government, and the incidents risk further complicating a long-standing political dispute between the semi-autonomous region and Mogadishu that hinders a co-ordinated effort to fight piracy, analysts say.
There is not yet a full-blown resurgence. But without an end to the US-Iran war, or increased international efforts at deterrence, Somali piracy stands to continue raising the threat level in a crucial maritime space that is already dangerously squeezed.

PM Modi called for dismantling the entire ecosystem that enables terrorism at SCO
NEW DELHI: Prime Minister Narendra Modi on Tuesday said there can be no “double standards” in the fight against terrorism and called for dismantling its entire ecosystem, including financing, recruitment, radicalisation and safe havens.Addressing the 26th Shanghai Cooperation Organisation (SCO) Summit in Bishkek, PM Modi described terrorism as a “grave challenge to all of humanity” and said the fight against it cannot be limited to a mindset of “action-reaction”.“We must dismantle the entire ecosystem of terrorism--its financing, recruitment, radicalization, and safe havens. We must speak in one voice that there can be no place for double standards on this serious issue,” he said.“Those countries that use terrorism as an instrument of their policy, and provide shelter and support to terrorists, must be sent a strong message that terrorism cannot be a ‘strategic asset’ for anyone,” the Prime Minister added.
He also outlined "Security, Connectivity and Opportunity" as the three pillars of India’s vision for the SCO, with peace and security forming the first pillar.“Our shared aspiration for a peaceful and secure Eurasia is also linked to peace and stability in Afghanistan,” he said, adding that India would continue its development and humanitarian assistance to the Afghan people.
On the West Asia crisis, Modi said conflicts in one region can have repercussions across the world, affecting “energy security, maritime trade, and supply chains of the entire world”.“The countries of the Global South have to bear the maximum brunt of this. Therefore, India's call has been that the solution to all tensions and wars is not possible on the battlefield, but only through Dialogue and Diplomacy,” he said.
The Prime Minister also flagged drug trafficking as a serious threat to the younger generation and regional security, calling for stronger cooperation through SCO mechanisms dealing with security threats, organised crime, information security and narcotics. “We must make them effective mediums for practical coordination and timely action,” PM Modi said.
He further stressed that SCO cooperation should translate into tangible benefits for people, with people-to-people ties placed at the centre of the grouping’s future agenda.“The true measure of our success should be how many new opportunities our efforts have created for young people, how many new markets have opened up for our entrepreneurs, how much our farmers have benefited from technology, and how much better the lives of our citizens have become,” he said.Kyrgyzstan President Sadyr Japarov is hosting the summit and serving as its chairman. PM Modi is attending alongside Chinese President Xi Jinping, Russian President Vladimir Putin, Pakistan Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif, Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian and other leaders of SCO member states.

A 24-year-old man allegedly stole a Cessna 172 aircraft in Hungary and flew it into a restricted airspace near the country’s only nuclear power plant before the plane crash-landed in a sunflower field. The man was intoxicated when the incident occurred. The aircraft was detected by military radar after entering the no-fly zone around the Paks nuclear power plant in southern Hungary, according to a social media post from the Hungarian Minister of Defense, Dr. Romulusz Ruszin-Szendi. Civilian aircraft are prohibited from operating within roughly two miles of the facility at altitudes below 20,000 feet. Hungary’s military immediately deployed two Gripen fighter jets after detecting the aircraft. The jets located the Cessna and remained nearby while emergency services were dispatched towards the area where it eventually came down. A few minutes later, the aircraft made an emergency landing in a sunflower field around four miles from the nuclear facility. The plane suffered extensive damage, but the pilot was able to escape without sustaining injuries. Police said the man sustained “slight injuries” during the landing. Following the crash, he reportedly made his way through the sunflower field and reached a nearby road, where he was found “in a confused state,” according to the police release. He was reportedly distressed and allegedly attempted to take control of the driver's car and flee in it. Officers intervened before he could drive away and arrested him. He was subsequently taken in for questioning. Initial tests suggested that he was intoxicated, while further examinations were being conducted to determine whether he had consumed any other drugs or substances. Investigators suspect that the man took the aircraft without permission from the nearby Kalocsa Airport. Authorities are looking into the circumstances surrounding the theft, including how he gained access to the aircraft and what prompted him to take it. Officials also plan to carry out inspections at other airports across Hungary as part of the investigation. The Paks nuclear power plant was unaffected by the incident.
