Soon after his appointment as the BJP’s national social media co-convenor, Arun Yadav made his X account private and then deleted more than 60,000 posts before making it public again. When the account was locked, it showed around 65,500 posts. By August 22, only 2,794 remained — a deletion exercise that wiped out virtually his entire publicly visible posting history.
At present, the oldest post that can be traced on Yadav’s timeline dates to August 19, 2026. All posts preceding it have been deleted. Many of those posts included abusive and racist remarks, attacks on women’s character, and content directly targeting Muslims in communally provocative terms.
On August 17, the Bharatiya Janata Party (BJP) announced a new social media cell where Deepak Mhaskey replaced Amit Malviya a the party’s IT cell chief. One of the newly inducted members of the social media cell was Yadav, who had previously been removed from his position as head of the Haryana BJP IT Cell.
When attention turned to Yadav’s old social media record following his new appointment, he locked his X account, @BeingArun28. Yadav has now made his account public again, but not before deleting the posts on a massive scale. The sequence of events indicates that making the account private might have given him the opportunity to remove his old controversial posts and wipe his social media record clean.
A review of Arun Yadav’s social media activity over the past several years reveals a clear pattern: abusive and racist remarks against opposition leaders, attacks on women’s character, and several explicit instances of directly targeting Muslim minorities and making communally provocative statements.
The Post that Led to his Ouster in 2022
Arun Yadav’s history of controversial remarks goes back several years. In 2017, he shared an image of the Kaaba in Mecca alongside a glass of whisky and wrote in an objectionable post that he could see “the Prophet in a peg of alcohol”. Questions continued to be raised over the remark for years. Finally, amid mounting pressure, Haryana BJP removed Arun Yadav from his post as state IT Cell chief on July 8, 2022.
The timing of the action taken against him was particularly significant. It came just a month after then BJP spokesperson Nupur Sharma’s derogatory remarks about prophet Muhammad of Islam had sparked a massive controversy in India and abroad. During a television debate, the BJP spokesperson had made offensive remarks about the prophet, triggering an international backlash.
Amid intense international pressure, the BJP had termed its spokesperson a “fringe element” and expelled her from the party. The following month, a screenshot of Arun Yadav’s old objectionable post went viral on social media. In this sensitive environment, Yadav’s removal was, in a sense, a tacit acknowledgement that his post had crossed a line the party was not prepared to publicly defend at the time.
The significant new responsibility handed to Arun Yadav within the party sends a serious political message: the conduct for which his own party had once sacked him has not stood in the way of his appointment to a higher position with greater responsibility.
“The Digging will Continue until God leaves India, Keep Digging”
In May 2022, Arun Yadav made another objectionable remark about Islam, writing: “The digging will continue until God leaves India, keep digging.”
The post was made at a time when the Gyanvapi Mosque dispute was before the Supreme Court. The Hindu side had claimed that a “Shivling” was present within the mosque complex. Given the sensitivity of the case, the Supreme Court transferred the suit filed by the Hindu side from the trial court to a more senior and experienced district judge.
In this tense legal and social environment, Yadav’s statement was not merely an inflammatory post or an insult directed at a particular religion. It also sought to frame the “digging” of sites containing mosques across the country as a coordinated campaign.
Attack on Rahul Gandhi
Political opponents have also been among Arun Yadav’s targets. In a post from January 2023, he shared a video of Congress leader Rahul Gandhi’s speech and used the phrase “the harvest of the brown aunty” for him.
The remark was not merely a deeply insulting personal attack but also reflected a clearly racist mindset. It was a direct reference to Rahul Gandhi’s mother, Sonia Gandhi, and her Italian origins. However, this is not an exception among BJP leaders. They have often been seen using such derogatory language targeting Sonia Gandhi’s foreign origins in the name of political opposition.
“…They Aren’t as Afraid Even when Their Wives Undergo Halala with other Men”
In a May 2022 post, Arun Yadav targeted Muslim women who were opposing surveys and excavations of mosques, making an obscene remark about them. Referring to the sensitive subject of “halala”, Yadav wrote: “As afraid as they are of the excavation of mosques, their wives aren’t even when they undergo halala with other men.”
In India, “halala” has long been the subject of an intense public debate. In Yadav’s post, the term was not merely used as part of a comment, but as a weapon to demean Muslim women.
More Islamophobia
In May 2022, Arun Yadav made another highly provocative post directly targeting Islam and the Muslim community. He wrote: “What kind of an ignorant community must those be whose Allah lives in temples stolen and looted from others?”
This was not simply a comment on the temple-mosque dispute. It was a direct attack on the Muslim community as a whole, using the dispute as a pretext. Yadav’s post was widely circulated.
“Who Got a Nine-month Recharge for Rs 500?”
One of the most shameful instances of Arun Yadav’s repeated targeting of Muslim women and making demeaning remarks about them emerged in May 2020. The case involved Jamia Millia Islamia student and activist Safoora Zargar.
Safoora was pregnant at the time and was imprisoned under the UAPA in connection with the 2020 Delhi riots case. While the detention of a pregnant woman was drawing criticism in India and abroad, Arun Yadav mocked Safoora’s pregnancy by comparing it to a mobile recharge plan.
Making a direct insinuation about her character, Yadav posted: “Who got a nine-month recharge for Rs 500?”
The matter did not end with the derogatory post. Yadav also actively endorsed other obscene and abusive comments posted under it. Arun Yadav was not the only BJP leader to make such remarks about Safoora’s pregnancy; several BJP leaders had also made demeaning comments about it.
The BJP’s IT Cell has long faced criticism over the spread of misinformation, targeting of minorities, promotion of regressive attitudes, circulation of controversial content and trolling. Its significance goes beyond the party’s own messaging: As one of the country’s most powerful political social media operations, it plays a significant role in shaping the information ecosystem — what millions of users see, discuss and believe online. Against that backdrop, Arun Yadav’s elevation is striking. A party that once disciplined him over communal posts has now entrusted him with a larger role in its national social media machinery. What was once grounds for his sacking has, years later, not come in the way of promotion.

Amstelveen has so far matched expectations: tidy and efficient, much like the Dutch hockey teams at this World Cup. Covering the Indian teams’ (mis)fortunes at the event meant setting up camp in this quaint Amsterdam suburb for the first 10 days, putting a visit to the other co-host, Wavre in Belgium, on hold.
Unlike the FIFA World Cup, where matches are spread across the host country, the hockey showpiece had games throughout the day at just two venues. At the Wagener Stadion, where India played all its group matches, the packed schedule left little scope to explore beyond the complex, home to Hoofdklasse club Amsterdam AH&BC.
Amsterdam AH&BC is the oldest hockey club in mainland Europe, with a history spanning 125 years. It has enjoyed so much success that its entire collection of honours can’t even fit in the clubhouse’s trophy case, with several having to wait their turn to make an appearance. One of the oldest trophies, jokingly referred to as the ‘goblet’ from the Harry Potter books, has won the lottery to make the cabinet this time around.
There is a popular saying in the Netherlands that there are more bicycles than people, and they are hard to miss. If you aren’t paying attention, you are arguably more at risk of getting hit by a biker than a car here. Cycling seems to be the preferred mode of commute for the locals, including England midfielder Thomas Sorsby, who moved to the city after recently signing for Amsterdam, which plays its home games at the Wagener.
Travelling supporters from India, England and Australia add colour to the setting, but Wales and Argentina fans, despite their small numbers, make a lot of noise. The home supporters at the Wagener aren’t like the ones you witness at a football game in the Netherlands on TV. There’s no rowdiness in the stands. Instead, there’s a real family atmosphere for every Netherlands game.
The home side’s matches have a real sombre setting, relying heavily on the PA system and goals from a Dutch hockey stick, which do come by the bucket-load There is an expectation for the Dutch to roll over opponents, particularly on the women’s side.
“We are at times too spoiled,” is how one local journalist put it.
Their women’s team, after all, is the undisputed queen of the sport. It even has its own song for the World Cup. The catchy number ‘Hockey Ladies’, created by the pop group Turfy Gang, is a massive hit with both the fans and the players. Some of the players took to the stage to dance to the song after their predictable clean sweep of the pool stage.
The only unpredictable element has been the weather. Playing host in the midst of the Dutch summer, it has been a cat-and-mouse game with the rain. Bright sunshine one minute can give way to a gentle drizzle or a downpour out of nowhere. I chose to leave my umbrella in the hotel room, opting for convenience and shedding the extra weight from my carry-on, which was already burdened with gadgets and a tripod. By day four, you know you can brave a passing shower. Disaster struck, however, on the second day of my arrival, in the form of my shoelaces, which seemed to take on a life of their own. Back home, I have to tie them back in place at least five or six times a day, which has become a reflex action by now. But, on tour, with my equipment in tow, it proved to be a recipe for disaster.
At first, it cost me a cracked phone screen and then, more importantly, a shattered mic connector — a key component for my interviews. A couple of alternative options didn’t pan out, and with no Swiggy Instamart to bail me out, a second phone in hand allowed me to carry on with the job.
With the Indian men’s side, there was some spikiness towards the travelling press pack from the outset. The general feeling is that criticism shouldn’t accompany victories, even if there is room for improvement. To be fair to them, having a microphone thrust in their faces to pick apart a chastening result minutes after the final hooter isn’t an ideal scenario.
Fortunately for them, Hockey India’s ingenious choice to change the jersey colour before the World Cup to a shade symbolic of the host country’s colours will allow them to slip away quietly without being troubled.
In the end, Amstelveen offered everything I could’ve ask for: hockey, rain, bicycles and, occasionally, a reminder that life on tour rarely goes exactly to plan.

The Bharatiya Janata Party (BJP) on August 17 announced a new national social media team, replacing Amit Malviya with Deepak Mhaskey as its IT cell in-charge. The party also named four new social media co-convenors — Priti Gandhi, Shivanand Dwivedi, Alok Bhatt and Arun Yadav.
Alt News had earlier reported that within minutes of BJP’s announcement, a search on X revealed that the accounts of the four social media co-convenors had either vanished or their posts had become inaccessible. However, screenshots and archived versions of their past tweets, often containing personal and contentious opinions, are available, raising concern over the sudden disappearance of their accounts. Yadav, for instance, deleted more than 60,000 posts before making her X handle accessible again. Mhaskey deleted at least 1,342.
Gandhi’s X account, which has over 500,000 followers, remains ‘protected’ or hidden from public view at the time of this article being published. A notice from the platform states “Only approved followers can see @MrsGandhi’s posts”.
An earlier screenshot of her profile captured by us shows her following 2,015 handles, which has now gone down to 1,875. In other words, she has recently unfollowed 140 X users.
Alt News spoke to Gandhi, and asked her why she had hidden her X posts, but she refused to comment. Her Facebook profile bio describes her as ‘IT & Social Media National In-charge for all 7 BJP Morchas’ and ‘Official Spokesperson, Maharashtra BJP’.
Recently, in November 2025, Gandhi courted controversy after targeting Indian cricketer Jemimah Rodrigues over her expression of faith during a post-match interview. After India’s semi-final victory against Australia, in which Rodrigues was named Player of the Match, she acknowledged her teammates’ support, said she had put her faith in God, and thanked Jesus in the post-match interview. Criticising this, Gandhi argued that while wearing the Indian jersey, Rodrigues represents Indians and “not her church”.
In her older tweets dating back to 2012-13, she expressed disdain for her surname, saying she would rather have ‘Modi’ or ‘Godse’ as a surname. She has repeatedly praised Nathuram Godse, the assassin of Mahatma Gandhi, in her tweets.
Declaring herself as a “huge fan and follower” of Godse, she has multiple tweets announcing that she “misses him” and that there is a need for “1000 more Godse’s” and that “India misses him.” Much of that record, however, is no longer readily accessible, but screenshots of her past tweets are shown below:
Long-time BJP Supporter
Her association with BJP, however, predates her formal organisational role. Gandhi has been a pro-BJP voice since around 2012. Initially, her X (then Twitter) handle was @pritirules. Aafter her anti-Congress posts were being shared by prominent BJP leaders, she changed her handle to @MrsGandhi. “I realised this name has a lot of potential, as there would be one Gandhi questioning the other. So I changed my handle,” she explained to the Telegraph.
In 2012, Modi started following Priti Gandhi on Twitter. According to her, she put forward her opinions aggressively — which caught Modi’s attention. Gandhi was even invited to Gandhinagar to meet Modi. “He [Modi] liked that I, as an independent person, defend him on social media”, Gandhi told The Telegraph.
In January 2014, Gandhi had falsely claimed that Julian Assange, the founder of WikiLeaks, had stated that “Modi is incorruptible”. Gandhi allegedly amplified a fake endorsement of Modi by Assange, featuring a poster of Assange alongside a quote that read, “America fears Modi because they know he is incorruptible.”
WikiLeaks responded:
#India: Here is the BJP’s Pritti Ghandi pushing fake #Assange endorsement of #Modi to 40k people https://t.co/kh8HsMlgqi
— WikiLeaks (@wikileaks) March 17, 2014
History Of Misinformation
Gandhi’s rise within the BJP’s digital ecosystem closely coincided with a long record of disseminating and amplifying misinformation. Alt News has fact-checked her claims repeatedly over the years.
For instance, in 2019, Gandhi circulated an edited video suggesting that Rahul Gandhi wanted to leave India and settle abroad. In 2020, Gandhi revived the ‘potato-gold’ remark, a claim that stemmed from a clipped video with distorted context, to mock Rahul Gandhi and mislead people.
In 2021, during the second wave of the COVID-19 pandemic, Gandhi also shared a misleading video purportedly showing an absence of crowds in Haridwar during the Kumbh Mela. The post appeared amid intense scrutiny of the religious gathering, where millions of pilgrims had assembled, and thousands of COVID-19 cases were subsequently reported among attendees and seers.
The video, however, did not depict the principal pilgrimage area around Har Ki Pauri. It was reportedly shot at Govind Ghat, several kilometres away, and at a time when the location did not see large crowds. The video was therefore misleadingly presented as evidence that Haridwar was not crowded during the Kumbh Mela.
During the 2021 West Bengal post-poll violence, Alt News had fact-checked a doctored video shared by Gandhi showing men wielding swords while dancing to the TMC election song, ‘Khela Hobe’.
In another instance, Gandhi shared a misleading video claiming that “Modi Modi” slogans were being raised inside Pakistan’s Parliament. Alt News found that the chants were actually “Voting Voting”.
More from the Archives: Propaganda & Disinformation
A recurring feature of Gandhi’s social media activity over the years has also been the amplification of communal or polarising misinformation.
In 2020, she shared an image of Priyanka Gandhi embracing the mother of the Hathras rape victim and described the woman as “fake Naxal-bhabi”. She falsely accused both Rahul and Priyanka Gandhi of consoling the “Naxal operative who had infiltrated the family’s home and was posing as the victim’s sister-in-law”.
The same year, she also circulated a clipped video of journalist Arfa Khanum Sherwani speaking about the Citizenship Amendment Act (CAA), using the edited clip to distort the context and present the speech in a communal light.
A Newslaundry article cites a 2021 Centre of the Study of Organised Hate (CSOH) paper, which identified Gandhi among BJP figures who amplified the ‘Love Jihad’ narrative in the aftermath of the killing of Nikita Tomar – a student who was shot outside her college in Ballabhgarh by a Muslim youth.
According to a 2020 report by Lokmat, Gandhi said in a tweet on October 27, 2020, “Those in denial of the existence of Love Jihad are only closing their eyes to reality, maybe even purposely. Unless we don’t accept the problem, finding a solution is impossible. Today it is Nikita, tomorrow it could be you!”
It is important to note that the chargesheet of the Nikita Tomar case had no sections of the IPC related to forced conversions and other associated crimes, as per a Times of India report.
In 2019, both Gandhi and Bengal BJP shared a clipped video to falsely claim a communal bias in a speech by then Bengal chief minister Mamata Banerjee. They shared a 12-second excerpt of her speech clipping out the part where Banerjee had recited Hindu scriptures. Alt News had fact-checked this.
In 2021, Gandhi shared a video of a man apparently blowing on food, suggesting that he was spitting on it, giving the footage an explicitly communal framing. In 2022, she claimed that participants at a Popular Front of India (PFI) protest in Pune had raised “Pakistan Zindabad” slogans. Fact-checkers found that the slogan was in actuality “Popular Front Zindabad”.
Again, in 2022, while sharing a photo of Rahul Gandhi with a girl, Gandhi falsely claimed that she was Amulya Leona, who raised ‘Pakistan Zindabad’ slogans during the anti-CAA protest in Bangalore in 2020. In reality, the girl with Rahul was Miva Jolly, an activist associated with the Kerala Students Union, the student wing of the Congress party.
During the 2024 farmers’ protest, Gandhi shared an image claiming a farmer was seen sitting on a Mercedes car worth Rs 3 crore, thereby portraying that the protesters were ‘rich’ and thus the movement was not legitimate. It was found in an investigation by Alt News that the car was actually an SUV Gurkha by Force Motors whicbh had been modified to look like a Mercedes vehicle. We spoke to the owner of the car as well.
In January 2022, Gandhi falsely claimed that Uttar Pradesh BJP MLA Vinay Shakya had been kidnapped after he had been pressured by Samajwadi Party to join them. Local police replied to her tweet clarifying that the abduction claim was entirely false. Gandhi, then, deleted her tweet.
Target of Misinformation Herself
Priti Gandhi herself became a target of misinformation when a viral thread in 2021 shared three genuine screenshots of her old posts alongside a fabricated tweet claiming that her husband had escaped the Capitol Hill riots. The thread, which gained over 10,000 likes and was amplified by several journalists and Congress members, falsely portrayed the manufactured tweet as part of a pattern in which Gandhi’s husband had narrowly escaped multiple major incidents. While three screenshots were genuine and referred to same incident (the 26/11 Mumbai attack), the Capitol Hill tweet was fake.

Trump’s fake AI video of Kharg Island ‘attack’ leaves US military scrambling to explain
President’s AI slop video forces Pentagon to step in with a denial
The Defense Department was forced on Monday to deny the U.S. had struck Iran’s main petroleum export facility after President Donald Trump posted a fake but very realistic AI-generated video showing a purported attack by American forces.
The video, posted to the president’s Truth Social account, appears to show oil storage tanks and refineries erupting in flames from the perspective of someone filming from inside a helicopter above the carnage, with an accompanying message describing the scene as “Kharg Island being blown to smithereens” and signed as “President DJT.”
But a U.S. official said no such attack had taken place, with Kharg Island not being among the locations targeted overnight in what has been the first exchange of fire between American and Iranian forces in weeks.
Additionally, the head of National Iranian Oil Co, Hamid Bovard, said on Monday that the president’s post was “laughable” and described conditions on Kharg Island as “calm and appropriate.”
Trump — whose White House has repeatedly stated that his Truth Social posts count as official statements from the commander in chief — also hit out at Iran again in a separate Truth Social post on Monday, writing that it was “officially a Failed Nation” and “DEAD.”
“They have no Navy, they have no Air Force, they have no currency, they are not paying their soldiers or police, Inflation is at 300%, and their leadership is in total disarray and incapable of properly representing the country. The only thing they have is FAKE NEWS from the USA, a willingness to kill their protesters (now over 100,000 people dead,” he said.
Iranian media outlets did report explosions near Larak Island in the Strait of Hormuz, where an American official said Tehran had been preparing to launch mine-laying rockets as part of the country’s bid to choke off the key waterway and hamstring the American economy in response to Trump’s war, which has now passed the half-year mark without end in sight.
In response, Iranian forces fired missiles at Jordan, but an American official told CNN those had been intercepted.
Speaking with Fox News on Sunday, President Trump defended the Iran campaign, arguing the U.S. was winning the war, even if a final, durable peace deal had not been inked.
“I don’t need a signature on a piece of paper,” Trump said.
He also argued that Democratic critics of the war were trying to sabotage the operation, invoking an argument used by Republican presidents defending unpopular wars from Richard Nixon in the Vietnam War era to George W. Bush after the invasion of Iraq.
“They want our country to lose the war with Iran, which isn’t going to happen because we are absolutely winning easily,” Trump added.
The strait, which carried about 20 percent of the world’s oil before the conflict, has remained a central obstacle. The U.S. insists it must remain open to unrestricted shipping, while Iran says it has the right to manage traffic through the waterway.
Recently, the Trump administration signaled a shift toward imposing economic measures against Iran. Last week, the Treasury Department unveiled a multi-pronged campaign to “sever the economic lifelines that sustain the Iranian regime.”
“If we need to use kinetic strikes, we’ll use them,” Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth said Monday. “But economic pressure hurts them the most right now.”

Senators are renewing calls for anti-vaccine Health Secretary Robert F. Kennedy to step down or be ousted—and at least one is calling for a criminal investigation—amid the release of documents they say prove Kennedy lied to them during his confirmation hearings last year.
“This is a pattern, not a slip,” Sen. Edward J. Markey (D-Mass.) said in a statement. “RFK Jr. has lied to the Senate, lied to the American people, and jeopardized the health of children to advance his anti-vaccine agenda.”
Sen. Ron Wyden (D-Ore.) said in a social media post Friday that the documents were “Proof we got RFK lying on the record during his confirmation hearing (a crime).” He called for the matter to be referred to the US Department of Justice for a criminal investigation. In a separate statement to The Guardian, Wyden added that “RFK’s platform is built on lies and grifts that leave a trail of dead children in their wake. There are consequences for lying to Congress.”
New documents
During Kennedy’s reality-bending confirmation hearings in January 2025, multiple senators raised concern about a trip Kennedy took to Samoa in 2019. At the time, Kennedy was a prominent anti-vaccine activist leading the rabidly anti-vaccine organization Children’s Health Defense (CHD). Just months after he visited the island nation, Samoa suffered a massive measles outbreak in which 83 people died, mostly children under the age of 5. The outbreak was largely fueled by a swell of vaccine hesitancy, drummed up by anti-vaccine activists. Vaccination rates had cratered to as low as 31 percent.

- A great way to record all your adventures: Insta360 X5 360 Camera for $465 ($85 off)
Can’t You Just Put Links to All Your Outdoor Guides Right Here?
Sure. Here you go:
Deals on Tents
The REI Half Dome 2 is the best budget two-person backpacking tent. I’ve toted it on many backpacking trips and found it plenty sturdy, quick to set up, and capable of fitting two people along with their gear. It even comes with a footprint (which I never bother with, but it's nice to have it if you have to deal with pointy rocks).
The Big Agnes Copper Spur series is our top pick among freestanding ultralight tents. This is the bike-packing model, which features shorter pole segments that are easier to haul on a bike, but I really prefer it for the more subdued colors. The Copper Spur is a high-quality, well-designed tent that's lightweight, easy to set up, and roomy enough to be livable in the backcountry. The “awning” design (with trekking poles or sticks) is a nice extra.
Nemo's Dragonfly tents are roomy for the weight. There's a generous amount of mesh at the top, which provides some nice ventilation on warm summer nights and is perfect for falling asleep under the stars when the weather permits. The Osmo fabric is a blend of nylon and polyester that absorbs less water than pure nylon rainflies.
MSR's Groundhog stakes aren't cheap, but they're the best tent upgrade you can make. They're superstrong—I've never had one bend or pull out on me—and considering their strength, they're pretty lightweight. I suggest carrying a mix of stakes when backpacking—some of these, some carbon fiber pegs, and some shepherd hooks. That way, no matter the terrain, you've got something that'll work.
Deals on Outdoor Clothing
Now is a great time to score some new base layers and mid layers ahead of the cooler months.
Smartwool's 100 percent merino base layer is my top pick for cooler weather in our guide to the Best Base Layers. Its loose fit allows it to work as a long-sleeve T-shirt in the shoulder seasons. That extra bit of roominess also makes it possible to use it as a second light layer over something thinner. Note that colors and sizes are limited on this deal.
This is an REI Outlet deal because it's been discontinued, which is a shame (hopefully that just means new colors are coming next year). REI's 100 percent merino base layers are some of the best values around, even at full price. On sale, they're a true steal. I like this half-zip for the extra ventilation the zipper provides, but if you prefer, the regular top (on sale for $30) is also on sale, as is the base layer bottom (on sale for $30).
Nothing says outdoors like a hatchet loop on your pants. Fjällräven Vidda Pro trousers give you that and great ventilation. The Vidda Pro uses Fjällräven's G-1000 fabric, a 65 percent recycled polyester and 35 percent cotton blend, with pockets everywhere and extras like ventilation zippers, reinforced knees (with openings for pads), and that sweet, sweet hatchet loop on the leg.
This deal is limited to one color, with sizes disappearing fast, but it's a pretty outstanding deal. The Ghost Whisperer Down Jacket is my top pick for a backpacking puffer jacket. The men's large I tested weighs just 7.3 ounces, packs down to a tiny little thing (stuffing into its own pocket), and the 800-fill-power goose down offers one of the best warmth-to-weight ratios on the market.
Camp Stove and Water Filter Deals
Nothing says camping like roasting marshmallows over open flames and burning beans on the camp stove. Check out our guides to the best backpacking stoves and best camping stoves for more picks.
MSR's PocketRocket Deluxe is our top pick for a backpacking stove. It wins the title thanks to its larger burner area, which allows the flame to spread out for faster boil times and better fuel efficiency, especially with larger pots. It also fared better in the wind than smaller burners. The genius of the deluxe model is the small curved lip around the burner, which helps keep wind from getting to the base of the flame. It's a small design element, and one that you certainly want. During long-term testing, I found it more effective at maintaining a simmer in the wind, should you want to do any actual cooking.
You can put together a lighter cooking setup, but Jetboil's Stash is the lightest all-in-one system out there, and it does boil water a bit faster than the rest. The heat diffuser design speeds up boil times (Jetboil claims 2.5 minutes, which I could only match indoors in still air), but the real appeal is how this kit packs down into itself and how simple it is to use.
Jetboil's larger all-in-one cooking system, the Flash, offers a larger capacity 1-liter pot that combines an integrated pot and burner into an easy-to-use system. I prefer the more compact Stash above, but if you're cooking for two and are all-in on dehydrated meals, this stove is popular for good reason.
While I prefer the larger burner head of the Deluxe model above, the MSR PocketRocket 2 is lighter at 2.6 ounces compared to the Deluxe's 2.9. It still has wide enough arms to support just about any one- or two-person pot. It's simple to use, even while wearing gloves, and it's efficient. At 947-foot elevation, it boiled 1 liter of water in 3 minutes, 47 seconds. You can even get it to simmer, though the flame radius is small, so fancier cooking isn't easy.
MSR's WhisperLite series is probably the most popular backpacking stove ever made. They last forever (mine is over 30 years old and still works great), and this model, the Universal, can use just about any fuel you can imagine—white gas, kerosene, unleaded gasoline, and isobutane-propane canisters, to be precise. The only downside is that it can be fiddly compared to stoves like the Jetboil. But if you're headed out on a long trip, buying fuel as you go, this is the most flexible option out there.
This is by far the most compact two-burner stove I've tested. It's my pick for any situation where space is at a premium—whether that's canoeing or just because you have a small car. The burners are large, and with some practice, I could get a light, simmer-friendly flame. My main gripe is the windscreen, which is not the best. The Basecamp version, with fitted pots, is also on sale for $300 ($100 off).
My favorite stove in Coleman's current lineup, the Coleman Cascade 3-in-1 features heavy-duty cast-iron grates and comes with a cast-iron griddle and grill. It'll comfortably fit a 12-inch pan and a 10-inch pan side by side, and it's significantly sturdier and more robust than other Coleman stoves, making it worth the extra money if you use it often. That said, the much cheaper stove below will get you by if you're only using it a few nights a year.
This stove is ubiquitous at campgrounds for a reason. It's well-built, sturdy on a table, and just works. It's not the most powerful stove, and it lacks frills like push-button ignition, but it's capable of holding a low flame, simmering soups, and cooking scrambled eggs without browning them. It's also incredibly durable.
The MSR Gravity Autoflow filter is a must-have for backpacking with a group. To use this filter, scoop up 10 liters of water in the dirty water bag, attach the hose, connect your water bottle, and sit back and relax. The filter is good enough to keep you safe from all the usual protozoa and bacteria, and the flow rate is a solid 1.5 liters per minute when the filter is clean.
The MSR Guardian is our pick for trips with sketchy water sources because it filters down to 0.02 microns, which will even remove viruses. It is heavy at 22 ounces and may be overkill for trips in the US, but it's a great option for overseas adventures. I really like that it's designed to be self-cleaning, which makes field maintenance incredibly easy, and that it screws right onto a Nalgene bottle. Also, because it's a pump filter, it's very fast. You can crank out a couple of liters in hardly any time at all. The gravity-fed version is also on sale at Backcountry for $232 ($78 off).
Camping Gear Deals
This camp chair is the coziest way to hang out around the fire. It is somewhat huge, heavy, and awkward to fold up and carry, but so long as you have room for it in your vehicle, there's no better way to relax under the stars with your loved ones.
The thing to keep in mind when you shop REI brand gear is the company's basic proposition: You get 90 percent of the designer item for 70 percent of the price. It's a strategy that works well and has produced some great, affordable gear. This chair is a good example: It's comfortable (it does wobble a little, side-to-side when you move, though) and less than half the price of competitors.
I've noticed that when people try to lighten their load with a smaller, lighter-weight backpack, they struggle to fit all their gear. The answer for sleeping bags and clothing is this compression stuff sack, which smashes anything soft down to about half the size of the same item in a regular stuff sack. This works well with sleeping bags and clothing, especially puffer jackets, but also fleece and merino wool.
Sleeping Bag Deals
Our favorite backpacking sleeping bag, the Bishop Pass 15 offers the best warmth-to-weight ratio while packing down small and staying affordable. I have slept in this bag for more than two weeks, with nighttime temps ranging from 28 to 65 degrees Fahrenheit, and, yes, it was too warm in the heat, but on those warmer nights, I unzipped it and used it as a blanket. It isn't perfect, but it's a versatile bag.
REI's Magma line of down gear is some of the best value around. The Magma 15 sleeping bag has long been an affordable option that's perfect for shoulder-season trips when the temperature potentially swings lower than you expect (the comfort rating is 21). There are three lengths and three widths, which makes it easy to find a perfect fit for your body, and the 850-fill-power goose down (Bluesign-approved) packs down nicely and small. If you don't need the shoulder-season coverage, the Magma 30 is also on sale for $262 ($87 off), and makes a great summer sleeping bag.
This down mummy bag has a spoon-shaped design for side sleepers and extra room in the elbows and knees so you can roll over onto your side without feeling like you're slipping into a straitjacket. It's built for temps down to 30 degrees Fahrenheit and has zippered gills you can open to avoid overheating when it's warmer.
The best budget ultralight quilt, the Magma Trail is a great value for the money. The lower price does mean that this one is a bit heavier (it uses 850-fill-power down), though at 24 ounces for the long, wide version I have, it’s competitive on the scale. The straps for attaching it to your sleep pad aren’t as nice as what you’ll get with something like the Enlightened Equipment's Revelation Quilt, but it’s just as warm and does a respectable job of keeping out drafts. There's even a zippered foot box with a drawstring for cooler nights.
Nemo's Pulse quilt uses RDS-certified, gold-infused 1,000-fill-power ExpeDRY down, which does a good job of shedding moisture from tent condensation and reportedly dries faster than standard down, though I've never figured out a good way to test this. The Karo Step baffle stitching keeps down well distributed, and at 12 ounces for the regular, this one is pretty dang lightweight.
This is our favorite sleeping bag for car camping. The REI Siesta is plenty warm and affordable. It's also not a mummy bag because you're not climbing Denali here. The rectangular cut makes for a much roomier, more comfortable sleeping experience. The 20-degree-Fahrenheit rating makes it warm enough for three seasons, and unlike most rectangular bags, the Siesta has a hood, which helps on those cold nights.
The Kindercamp makes a great car camping bag if you've got young children. Once your kids are about 4 feet tall, an adult sleeping bag works just fine. Prior to that, they'll benefit from a kids' sleeping bag like the Kindercamp, which is cut smaller so your little ones don't have to heat up a huge, adult-size sleeping bag to stay warm.
Deals on Action Cameras and Gadgets
If you snap a selfie in the woods and Instagram isn't around to see it, did it happen? You'll never have to answer that question if you've got one of our favorite action cameras or 360 cameras with you.
Insta360's X6 360 camera just launched—our review will be coming soon—but the X5 is still a great option, especially on sale. The twin 1/1.28-inch sensors capture 8K video, which means you can reframe your footage to fit rectangular video formats and still have nearly 4K clips sharp enough to mix with footage shot with your phone. The dynamic range is impressive, and the X5 also has great battery life.
If you're going to turn your action camera on yourself, consider the Ace Pro 2, our top pick for vlogging. It has a great lens and sensor co-engineered with Leica, is capable of recording 8K video at up to 30 frames per second (fps), and has some pretty darn nice color even in the default settings. My guess is that the Ace Pro 3 is coming pretty soon, but this is still a good deal.
Sure, phones have some of the features you'll get with a satellite messenger, but we still think you're better off with a dedicated device. Garmin's new inReach Mini 3 Plus now offers some of those phone features—like voice messaging—along with the emergency features and excellent service worldwide. It's also still tiny, well-built, and it has great battery life. A non-Plus model, which doesn't have a speaker and mic, is also on sale.

A jury on Monday (local time) found Duane “Keffe D” Davis guilty of killing rapper Tupac Shakur in Las Vegas in 1996, marking the first conviction in a case that has captivated hip-hop fans for decades. Davis, 63, was convicted on Monday on a charge of murder with a deadly weapon and is likely to be sentenced to life in prison. After a week-long trial in Las Vegas, the jury deliberated and reached its verdict in less than three hours, AP reported. The verdict came after a panel of 16 jurors, four of whom were alternates, heard testimony from at least 24 prosecution witnesses and three defense witnesses over nine days. After the verdict was announced in Shakur’s killing, his sister, Sekyiwa “Set” Shakur, cried and hugged the prosecutors, while the convict’s son covered his face with his hand. In closing arguments on Monday, Chief Deputy District Attorney Binu Palal told jurors that the accused acquired a gun and "went hunting" for Shakur and Death Row Records co-founder Marion “Suge” Knight after the two had beaten up Davis’ nephew earlier that night. Palal said, "He is responsible for the murder of Tupac Shakur," and added, "Tell him you hear him. Find him guilty.” Prosecutors noted that while Davis’ story has changed over the years, he has repeatedly placed himself inside a white Cadillac from which the shots were fired. They also maintained that, while he was not the shooter, the evidence indicated he had ordered the attack, using his influence as a senior gang member over the younger men in the car, including his nephew. Defense attorney Michael Sanft asked the jurors whether there was any evidence that Davis had ordered a shooting either before or after the attack. Citing logistical challenges involving witnesses, the prosecution said that it would seek to dismiss the gang enhancement charge. Davis’ trial reignited interest in a case that has fascinated hip-hop followers and true crime enthusiasts for decades. Shakur, widely regarded as one of the most influential rappers in music history, was in Las Vegas on 7 September 1996, when a white Cadillac stopped alongside his vehicle at a traffic signal, and gunfire erupted. Shakur succumbed to his injuries six days later. Knight was also injured in the attack but survived. For years, nobody was charged in Shakur’s killing until the accused started making public statements about his involvement and said that he was in the white Cadillac and gave the gun to others in the back seat, calling the rapper’s shooting retaliation for the beating of his nephew earlier that night. Davis was the only one alive among the four men who were in the Cadillac, according to prosecutors. According to reports, the case, which is roughly 30 years old, has affected the type of evidence presented in court. Prosecutors warned jurors that material collected in the 1990s is different from what law enforcement collects today, including hotel surveillance video from the night of the shooting. Phil Schiller reportedly steps down as Apple's App Store and product event chief
Schiller will remain an Apple Fellow and focus on "unspecified initiatives," according to Bloomberg.
As Tim Cook steps aside as Apple CEO and John Ternus takes over the top job, it seems there are other changes taking place at the company's executive level. Phil Schiller has reportedly stepped down from overseeing the App Store and product events. Schiller is said to be continuing at the company as an Apple Fellow and working on "unspecified initiatives." Apple hasn't publicly announced the transition, which was first reported by Bloomberg.
Schiller — who stepped down as senior vice president of marketing in 2020 — is one of the most publicly recognizable figures at Apple as he was a mainstay of its events for many years. Along with revealing new products and leading the creation of the App Store with Steve Jobs, Schiller helped shape devices like the iPhone and iPod.
As the head of the App Store, Schiller took charge of dealing with developers (including Epic Games amid the long-running legal battle between the two sides) and deciding whether to approve certain apps. He was also primarily responsible for policy updates and handling revenue share adjustments following court cases and new laws being enforced.
It appears Apple is taking this opportunity to restructure its teams. Bloomberg reports that the App Store will again fall under the remit of Eddy Cue, who is now in charge of the services division. Cue ran the App Store until Schiller took over in 2015.
Carson Oliver, one of Schiller's App Store deputies, will lead that team on a day-to-day basis, per the report. Schiller tasked Oliver with overseeing the App Store two years ago, with Ann Thai (who is now said to report to Oliver) then taking on responsibility for app distribution tools and third-party marketplaces. The head of Apple Arcade, Alex Rofman, is now reporting to Oliver too, according to Bloomberg.
Nola Weinstein, Schiller's deputy for product launches, will now reportedly lead Apple's events team. That group falls under the remit of Kristin Huguet Quayle, vice president of communications and public relations. The first event under Weinstein's leadership takes place on September 9, where we're expecting to see the iPhone 18 Pro models, new Apple Watch variants and the company's first foldable iPhone.

Following the attacks on the Cockroach Janta Party (CJP) workers in Rajasthan, several social media users claimed that CJP convenor Ashutosh Ranka was accompanied by a man who had earlier been found calling for demolishing the Parliament and provoking Nepal-like violence during the July 20 protest in Delhi.
As part of its ‘School Thik Karo’ initiative, a CJP team visited a government school operating from a buffalo shed at Rampura in Kanwarpura area of Jaipur district in Rajasthan when they were allegedly attacked. They reported being beaten with sticks and pelted with stones. CJP later accused the attackers of being affiliated with the BJP.
On August 21, X user Office of Vijay Patel (@VijayGajeraO) claimed that Ranka had arrived with “goons” who wanted to attack Parliament and trigger Nepal-style mass violence in India. The post featured a collage comparing a man accompanying Ranka with another man seen in a viral video from the CJP protest. The latter had allegedly said that Parliament would be attacked and a Nepal-like situation created if Dharmendra Pradhan did not resign. (Archive)
Ashutosh Ranka came with the goons who wanted to attack the parliament and wanted to cause Nepal-style mass violence in India. pic.twitter.com/yoKV2KnetZ

The handle is run by Right-wing influencer Vijay Patel who claims to be an investigative journalist. The post has garnered over 850,000 views.
Abhijit Iyer Mitra (@Iyervval), another Right-wing influencer, shared and amplified the claim. (Archive)
The most important part of this video isn’t what happened today. It’s the fact that this video captured a stated intent to commit violence on 20th July outside parliament. Also that far from being “outsiders”, the rioters were in fact core CJP members. https://t.co/r0VbwXGEfU

The post amassed over 150,000 views.
Another pro-BJP handle user, Raushan Sinha (@Mrsinha), also shared a similar comparison, claiming that the man who once threatened to turn India into a Nepal-like situation during the protest is now a CJP volunteer. His post read, “From threatening Parliament to becoming a ‘volunteer’ for CJP, quite a journey for the champions of democracy.”
The post gained around 100,000 views, and thereafter it was deleted.
This is not the first time that such comparisons have been made. Immediately after the July 20 protest, it was claimed that the man who called for Nepal-like violence had been seen sitting with Abhijeet Dipke, and was a CJP core member.
Fact Check
A closer examination of the two visuals — the Rajasthan video and the Jantar Mantar footage — reveals that the comparison is flawed, as they are two different people.
The man seen with Ashutosh Ranka and the CJP team is Vijay Sherawat, who hails from Jaipur, Rajasthan.
Alt News found a video that Sherawat had shared in response to the older claim, in which he defends himself against false accusations. He clarifies that he was not the same person who remarked that a Nepal-like situation would be created in India and the Parliament would be set afire if Pradhan did not resign.
In the video uploaded on July 31, Sherawat stated, “It is the IT cell people who are engaging in this low-level politics to defame the CJP team. To sum up, the individual who provoked violence and threatened to set the Parliament ablaze is not the same one as the one seen with Ashutosh Ranka during the CJP team’s visit to Rajasthan or with Abhijeet Dipke in an older video. Loud and clear calls. Great noise canceling. Very versatile uses. Surprisingly affordable.
TIRED
Bass-heavy without app-based tuning.
The Soundcore Liberty 5 Pro did something I wasn't expecting: It made me call my family more.
Here's my problem: I have aging parents who are losing their hearing, and I like to mumble. That's a bad combination for catching up over the phone during my New York City commute. I almost always have to talk loudly and repeat myself way more often than I would like. It makes the whole conversation feel unnatural, so much so that a little part of me dreads making that phone call.
I've tested over 50 pairs of wireless earbuds in my career as a headphones expert, and none of them have totally solved this problem. That is, until I started reviewing the Soundcore Liberty 5 Pro, with its Guinness World Records claim of “highest speech quality score.” And what sounded like pure marketing at first turned into something else—earbuds that are probably my new daily carry.
Put a Screen on It
Photograph: Harry Rabinowitz
The Soundcore Liberty 5 Pro has a new design from its predecessor. The buds have a larger, flat pill shape (similar to the second-gen Bose QuietComfort Ultra Earbuds) and are bigger and heavier than stem-shaped buds like Apple AirPods Pro 3. While they are a little big, they are very comfortable—I wore them for multiple hours without any irritation or fatigue. In the box, there are multiple alternative ear tips and wing-tip sizes to find your ideal fit.
The pill-shaped surface is touch-sensitive, so you'll be doing a lot of tapping, swiping, and holding to control things like media, volume, and noise-canceling modes.
The charging case has a touchscreen on the front that shows the buds' and case's battery levels, but if you swipe around, you can control settings for active noise cancellation (ANC), sound profiles, Dolby Audio, and more. The touchscreen is much larger and more useful than the display on the previous Liberty 4 Pro, but not as attention-grabbing as the giant screen that covers the entire case for the Soundcore Liberty 5 Pro Max. It's a nice addition, though I usually prefer to adjust settings using the on-ear controls or Soundcore app.
Inside the earbuds, there's an even bigger change that makes them stand out from Soundcore's previous headphones: the Anker Thus AI chip (Anker is Soundcore's parent company), which uses a combined CPU and memory design (compute-in-memory) for vastly increased efficiency. I'm not going to get too in the weeds, but this chip is a big investment from the brand compared to using an off-the-shelf option (like many of its rivals do). For the layman, the actual result is that these earbuds are excellent at processing your voice and outside noise. I expect to see it featured in many future Soundcore products.
King of Calls
Screenshot: Harry Rabinowitz
Video: Harry Rabinowitz
New York City is one of the best places to test noise-canceling and microphone quality in the real world. You have easy access to busy roads, bustling cafes, highway overpasses, and loud subway platforms, all within one commute.
In all of those environments, the Liberty 5 Pro sounded astonishingly good on a call. My voice was always loud and clear, and all background noise essentially vanished. Fire truck sirens, a busy highway overpass, a crowd of NYC commuters, a loud cafe—none of it came through in any of my calls or audio recordings using the Liberty 5 Pro. “You don't hear that truck?” was a common refrain during all my calls. Apple AirPods Pro 3, Bose QuietComfort Ultra Earbuds (2nd Gen), and Shokz OpenDots 2 sounded bad by comparison.
Noise canceling is also top-tier. The buds have the standard noise cancellation, transparency, adaptive, and off modes, and you can fine-tune ANC strength (from one to five) using the case or Soundcore app. The only earbuds that noticeably canceled more noise were the Bose QuietComfort Ultra Earbuds (2nd Gen) and Sony WF-1000XM6.
Video: Harry Rabinowitz
Video: Harry Rabinowitz
Out of the box, the sound profile (called Soundcore Signature) isn't an immediate slam dunk like call quality and ANC are. It's bass-heavy, so much so that I would bet even an untrained ear would notice the bass boost, especially compared to other earbuds from Apple or Bose. There are five preset sound profiles (I preferred Soundcore Balance), an eight-band custom equalizer to play with, and a personalized HearID mode, which tunes the profile to your preferences based on an audio quiz where you select which clip you prefer.
Using the Soundcore Balance or custom HearID profile, the Liberty 5 Pro sounds great. Again, it's not quite as detailed as AirPods Pro 3 or QuietComfort Ultra Earbuds, but it's close enough to be enjoyable for most people, especially given the significantly lower price.
Daily Versatility
Photograph: Harry Rabinowitz
It's not often that a new pair of earbuds becomes my go-to. The convenience of the Apple ecosystem usually means AirPods Pro 3 are, begrudgingly, my earbuds of choice. But I'm still using the Liberty 5 Pro; I'm using them as I write this review. The Liberty 5 Pro is comfortable, sounds good, has great ANC, works well on iPhone and Android devices, and fits securely, making it well suited for almost any task. An IP55 rating means the earbuds should hold their own against dust and light rain. Most importantly, it offers such dramatically better call quality that I enjoy phone calls more, even with my mumbling and NYC street noise.
Sure, sound clarity isn't perfect. Yes, the buds are a bit large. But when those are the only complaints I have about earbuds that cost nearly $100 less than most of my other top recommendations, that's a big deal. In 2026, the Liberty 5 Pro might be the best value earbuds you can get.
Harry Rabinowitz is a commerce editor at WIRED, where he covers headphones, earbuds, speakers, TVs, and fitness tech. Previously, he was the tech reporter at NBC Select, leading coverage and reviews of the same topics. Before that, he was a freelance writer for publications like Popular Science and Popular Mechanics. ... Read More

The Supreme Court on Tuesday quashed several first information reports (FIRs) registered by police in Delhi, Bihar, Maharashtra, West Bengal and Assam in connection with the recent agitation led by the Cockroach Janata Party (CJP) over academic issues, including alleged paper leaks, Bar and Bench reported. .
The Cockroach Janata Party, on Tuesday, 1 September, also informed the Supreme Court that it had called off its planned protest march on 5 September following developments regarding the closure of FIRs filed against students who participated in protests over the NEET paper leak.
According to a Bar and Bench report, a Supreme Court Bench comprising Chief Justice of India (CJI) Surya Kant and Justices Joymalya Bagchi and V Mohana invoked Article 142 of the Constitution to quash the criminal cases after the Central and respective State governments filed applications seeking their closure.
The report further stated that the Court directed that similar FIRs registered in other States and Union Territories, apart from Delhi, Bihar, Maharashtra, West Bengal and Assam, should neither be pursued nor investigated. Such cases would, therefore, be treated as closed for all intents and purposes.
The Court also directed that no fresh FIRs shall be registered with regard to the protests that took place between July 20 and 25.
CJP co-convenor Saurav Das appeared before a bench comprising Chief Justice Surya Kant and Justices Joymalya Bagchi and V Mohana to inform the court about the decision.
During the hearing, Solicitor General Tushar Mehta urged the top court to use its powers to close all FIRs against NEET protesters between July 20-July 25 across country.
Tushar Mehta told the Supreme Court bench that the Centre is committed to honour the assurance given to the CJP leaders and provide compensation to the families of students who ended their lives after the cancellation of the NEET exam.
Mehta told the apex court that it will pay compensation to families of the students who died and sought three months to work out the modalities, PTI reported.
The Abhijeet Dipke led-CJP had called for a protest march in Delhi on September 5, Teachers' Day. It had accused the Centre of failing to honour the promises made on July 25 to persuade the group to withdraw its 36-day agitation against irregularities in exams and the NEET paper leak.
According to the CJP, the march was to be led by families of students who committed suicide following the cancellation of the NEET exam and the subsequent re-test, as well as those who were allegedly subjected to police excesses during the July agitation.

A little over a month after the loss to Spain in the FIFA World Cup final, Argentine skipper Lionel Messi has retired from international football
“After this time that has passed since the final, after much thought, I want to announce to everyone that I am retiring from the National Team,” the 39-year-old said in a post on social media.
Looking back at Messi’s glorious career, one of the tournaments which stands out is Copa America.
From suffering multiple heartbreaks to eventually finishing on a high, Messi has experienced every possible emotion at the continental stage.
Messi, then only 20 years old, made his Copa America debut against USA in 2007 and provided an assist in La Albiceleste’s 4-1 win.
He scored a goal in both the quarterfinals and the semifinals. However, Argentina lost 0-3 to Brazil in the final.
Four years later, Argentina’s campaign ended in the quarterfinals after a 5-6 loss to Uruguay on penalties. Messi scored no goals in that edition.
In 2015, in his debut Copa America campaign as the Argentina captain, led his nation to the final. But the tournament ended in yet another heartbreak as the side lost 1-4 to Chile on penalties.
A year later, Argentina faced the same opponent in the summit clash of the centenary edition of the continental event but Messi’s team stumbled on the final hurdle once again. The team lost 2-4 on penalties with Messi failing to deliver from the spot.
A teary-eyed Messi announced his retirement from international football after the third Copa America final loss of his career.
A nationwide campaign convinced him to change his decision and return to the national side.
In 2019, under Messi’s leadership and the guidance of a new coach in Lionel Scaloni, Argentina reached the semifinals before losing 0-2 to arch-rival Brazil. The team beat Chile 2-1 to finish third.
After dealing with multiple setbacks, Messi finally had his moment in the 2021 edition as Argentina beat Brazil in Rio de Janeiro to become champion. Messi’s first Copa America title also ended a 28-year trophy drought for his nation.
Three years later, the then world champion Argentina successfully defended its Copa America crown by defeating Colombia 1-0 in the final.

Trump cuts to science advisory boards have long-lasting consequences, researchers say
Netia McCray recalls how excited she was to join the federal advisory committee on long COVID in 2025. She had been diagnosed in the early days of the pandemic — and symptoms such as fatigue, heart palpitations and shortness of breath had become a frustrating but inescapable part of life.
By joining this group of doctors, researchers and other experts advising on the disease, McCray, 36, had hoped to channel her years of experience as a long-COVID patient into "something that could benefit so many individuals like myself and my community," she says. The work, she felt, could make her part of the solution for a debilitating condition that impacts millions of Americans.
But McCray had only been on the committee for a few months when she received an email notice that the group was terminated, "effective immediately."
McCray's advisory group is one of more than 100 science-focused federal committees that have been terminated under the second Trump administration, according to a news analysis in the journal Nature. As of March of this year, more than a quarter of the country's healthcare-related committees have been shut down, according to the advocacy group Public Citizen.
As a result, McCray is one of hundreds of experts who are no longer meeting to work on some of the most intractable and urgent problems around health and science in the United States. The losses linked to the demise of these groups are difficult to quantify, but participants and advocates say the impacts will reverberate across federal agencies for years.
A rare team of cross-functional experts
McCray — who runs a nonprofit helping high school students access opportunities in STEM — was joined on the committee by pediatrician Dr. Alexandra Yonts, at Children's National Hospital in Washington, D.C. Yonts, one of the few experts in the country who specializes in long COVID in children, was also eager to contribute to the advisory group. Patients often travel long distances to be seen in her clinic. She has frustratingly few options.
" We need new therapeutics," says Yonts.
Twelve other experts from a cross section of relevant fields including public health, pulmonology, and critical care joined this group to think together about how to galvanize new solutions.
But the committee never had a single meeting.
A hallmark of American government
The U.S. has long relied on a system of gathering outside experts from a range of backgrounds in order to advise federal agencies on complex issues. It was formalized in 1972, when Congress passed the Federal Advisory Committee Act, or FACA. The committees are composed primarily of volunteers, and draw from across fields of relevant study and practice.
Today, the list of science-related issues that these committees are convened to explore is vast and ranges from astrophysics to public health to biomedical research — advising on questions such as when and which vaccines children should receive, how often people should be screened for cancer, or how best to prevent asteroids from hitting the Earth.
" The beauty of FACA is that it brings brilliant minds together for issues of the day, and allows them to openly adjudicate and to prioritize with limited resources how to get to next steps," says Michael Abrams, a health researcher at the group Public Citizen who published a report on these terminated committees and describes them as a kind of connective tissue that helps facilitate good government.
The Union of Concerned Scientists – an advocacy group for researchers and scientists – now counts 150 advisory committees at science agencies terminated in 2025 alone.
Officials from the White House did not respond to requests as to why specific committees were terminated, but said in a statement that the dissolved committees "were found to be redundant, unnecessary, or ineffective."
Yet outside science advocacy groups worry that without them, important issues of science and research will be neglected and siloed within federal agencies. " What advisory committees can do is give a diversity of viewpoints and an independence of viewpoints that no one organization will ever have," says Russ Paulsen, President and CEO of the the science advocacy group Research!America.
Terminated committees include those devoted to topics such as managing fisheries and sustaining U.S. seafood resources; planning future NASA space science and astrophysics missions; and reducing preventable infections in hospitals.
No substitute for real world perspective
People with real-world experience working in healthcare, says infectious disease researcher Hilary Babcock, offer invaluable perspective to officials at federal agencies like the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention — by helping them to put theory into practice. Babcock was on the Healthcare Infection Control Practices Advisory Committee, or HICPAC, before it was terminated.
"They don't need help necessarily knowing what the literature shows," says Babcock. "But what they don't do is work in hospitals and healthcare systems, so they don't necessarily understand intuitively what it means to try to operationalize findings from literature into guidance."
One example is the drug-resistant fungus Candida auris, one of many issues that Babcock and her colleagues were grappling with in their work on the committee.
Candida auris can live on surfaces in healthcare facilities and cause deadly infections in humans. Cases have risen sharply in recent years as clinicians have struggled to find interventions to treat it.
The fungus can spread between patients and resist some antifungal treatments. Babcock worries that the fungus is not getting the attention it deserves without the work of the committee. " There is some sort of interim guidance around Candida auris from the CDC, but we're not getting updated guidance," she says.
The fungus requires specific disinfectant practices in order to eradicate it..
Scott Roberts, an infectious disease doctor at Yale, has treated patients in the U.S. with Candida auris and worries that without a federal advisory committee to offer best practices on treating it, doctors like himself will be left with a patchwork of protocols, especially those at smaller or rural facilities. That patchwork, he says, could leave room for the fungus to spread.
"Losing a federal advisory committee on this is only going to make the problem worse," says Roberts.
Checks on authority
Other participants from advisory groups say these groups offer important checks on authority for officials inside the government.
"As a federal official, I found advisory committees to be really helpful to me in my thinking and policy development," says Carrie Wolinetz, who for years worked with advisory committees in her capacity as an official at the National Institutes of Health. Wolinetz now works outside government in healthcare policy and advocacy.
"They would bring up real-world issues that I — from within government — would not necessarily have thought of."
Juan Meza, a professor of applied mathematics at the University of California, Merced, has served on a number of advisory committees during his career. Meza recalls an occasion years ago when one committee he served on advised federal leadership at the Department of Energy against making an investment in supercomputers.
" The fact that we were supposed to be independent, I think gave us a certain amount of leeway to say, 'No. We've gotta go with what we think is right," says Meza. Reluctantly, he adds, leadership followed their advice.
Even when leadership does not take recommendations from committees, they create important transparency in government, says Kelly Holley-Bockelmann, a professor of astrophysics who until recently worked at Vanderbilt University. Holley-Bockelmann served on the Astrophysics Advisory Committee before it was terminated.
" There were a couple times where we offered expertise that was not listened to," says Holley-Bockelmann, "But nonetheless, we felt it was really important to get it down on record."
In a statement, NASA officials called the termination of the astrophysics committee a "restructuring," writing that they had merged several committees into one. The statement asserts that the agency "has remained committed to continuing to engage with the science community in a variety of ways."
But others who work in the NASA ecosystem say the previous structure of committees offered an important way to gather information from stakeholders at all levels.
The committees allowed the space agency's leaders to "hear almost directly from the community," says Amanda Hendrix, CEO of the Planetary Science Institute and a former member of another federal committee called the NASA Advisory Council.
That advisory group historically helped set the agenda for NASA priorities, she says, and pushed the agency to offer explanations as to why they made the investments they did for future years.
It's a rare tool of American government, says Hendrix, that provides this kind of accountability and window into decision making.
" I felt like the interactions with NASA folks at the different committee levels was very useful and important for the community," says Hendrix. "So it's really disappointing that that's all gone now."
